text_kjv: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah now pivots from exposing false fasting to defining true fasting—and the definition is startlingly concrete. This is not mystical or internal; it is about bread, shelter, clothing, and kinship. The rhetorical question structure ('Is it not...?') suggests these actions should be obvious to any who truly seek God's favor, yet the prophet's insistence implies they were being overlooked by a people who thought ritual compliance substituted for justice.

The four-fold action—feeding, housing, clothing, and not turning away—forms the skeleton of authentic covenant relationship. Notice the progression: food addresses immediate hunger; housing provides security; clothing restores dignity; and the final command ('hide not thyself from thine own flesh') reminds Israel that the poor are not strangers but members of the covenant family. The phrase 'your own flesh' (Hebrew: besarkha) carries the weight of kinship obligation rooted in creation itself—all humanity shares one physical substance.

word_study.meaning: To break or divide bread; to distribute or share. The root suggests breaking bread into pieces for distribution, emphasizing the act of division and sharing rather than mere giving.
word_study.significance: The verb choice is active and personal—not distant charity but intimate sharing of one's own sustenance. The Covenant Rendering's 'share your bread' captures this better than the KJV's 'deal thy bread.'

word_study.meaning: The afflicted or oppressed poor who are literally driven away or homeless. Mrudim (from the root meaning 'to drive or chase') suggests forcible displacement—people not merely poor but actively marginalized.
word_study.significance: Isaiah is not simply calling for charity toward the naturally destitute but demanding justice for those who have been systematically excluded or driven out, likely by the wealthy and powerful within Israel itself.

word_study.meaning: To turn away, conceal oneself, or ignore. The reflexive form suggests actively withdrawing or refusing to acknowledge.
word_study.significance: This is not merely a prohibition on denial but an active command to presence and accountability. You cannot simply ignore the poor; you must remain present and engaged with your own flesh.

word_study.meaning: Your own flesh; a blood relative or, in broader covenant terms, your own kinfolk. In Hebrew thought, sharing flesh implies shared substance and mutual obligation.
word_study.significance: This phrase universalizes the poor—they are not distant others but 'your own flesh.' In covenant theology, all Israel (indeed, all humanity) shares one flesh through creation. The translator notes from The Covenant Rendering emphasize this: 'the poor are not strangers but kin.'

cross_references.connection: Jesus directly echoes Isaiah 58:7 when defining judgment day righteousness: 'I was hungry...thirsty...a stranger...naked...sick...in prison.' The four concrete acts of Isaiah become the standard by which nations are judged.
The call to 'plead the cause of the poor and needy' reflects the same covenant obligation to advocate for the voiceless, echoing Isaiah's demand to 'bring the poor into your house.'
'Love thy neighbour as thyself' is the fundamental law underlying Isaiah's vision; true fasting is simply the enactment of this law through concrete mercy.

John echoes Isaiah's rebuke of those with material goods who withhold compassion: 'If anyone has material possessions...how can the love of God be in that person? Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions.'
King Benjamin teaches that all humanity are 'beggars' before God, establishing the leveling principle underlying Isaiah's ethic—the wealthy are not inherently superior to the poor.

commentary.historical_context: In eighth-century Judah, the gap between rich landowners and displaced agricultural workers was widening. The phrase 'poor that are cast out' likely refers to peasants who had lost ancestral land through debt slavery or royal expropriation—a systemic injustice. The Temple cult had become a refuge for the wealthy, who believed their elaborate sacrifices and fasts purified them regardless of their exploitation of the poor. Isaiah's radical claim is that such ritual is not merely ineffective but actually offensive to God when divorced from justice. The four acts he names—feeding, housing, clothing, and maintaining family bonds—were the basic obligations of kinship in Israelite society; his point is that these are not optional charity but core religious duty.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:28-29 presents a strikingly similar passage: 'And now, behold, I say unto you, then is the time to repent, for the time of the Lord cometh. But behold, do ye suppose that ye can lay aside your garments and suppose that ye are more righteous than others, and that God hath appointed you to be rulers over them? I say unto you, Nay.' This echoes Isaiah's unmasking of false piety. Additionally, Alma 1:26-30 describes how those who truly believe in Christ 'deal with the poor' and distribute their substance 'that every man might have according to that which he had need'—the practical outworking of Isaiah's vision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:30-39 articulates the law of consecration, wherein the Church is commanded to care for the poor and needy, directly implementing Isaiah's vision. Verse 30 states: 'And behold, thou wilt remember the poor, and consecrate of thy properties for their support' (see also D&C 104:15-16). The fast offering in the Latter-day Saint tradition traces its theological lineage to passages like Isaiah 58.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant emphasizes the washing of feet and the breaking of bread—two of the four acts Isaiah names. In the temple context, these rituals are not merely symbolic but prologue to covenant action in the world. The promise of eternal life in the temple is inseparable from the commitment to succor the weak (see Mosiah 18:8-10).

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah's four acts prefigure Christ's earthly ministry: He fed the hungry (John 6:5-13), provided shelter and restoration (Luke 9:58, yet offered eternal dwelling), clothed the naked in His own flesh taken from us (Hebrews 2:14), and never hid Himself from His own flesh—Israel—even unto the cross. More profoundly, Christ becomes the embodiment of this passage: the poor who are cast out become those who follow Him; the naked He covers is fallen humanity; the flesh He does not hide from is our flesh, assumed in the Incarnation.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse demands ruthless honesty: What does your fast actually support? Do you contribute to systemic displacement of the poor through indifference, complicity, or active participation in unjust economic structures? Isaiah names four concrete actions—feed, house, clothe, remain present—that remain non-negotiable for any who claim to fast before God. The final phrase, 'hide not thyself from thine own flesh,' may be the most searching: It is not enough to give anonymously or at a distance. The covenant requires you to know the faces of the poor, to acknowledge your shared humanity, and to remain accountable to their dignity. In a world of systems and abstractions, this is radically personal.

text_kjv: Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward.

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains the first 'then'—the conditional promise. Justice and mercy do not go unrewarded; they produce a cascade of blessings. But note: these blessings are not primarily personal comfort but the restoration of the community's wholeness and the presence of divine protection. The imagery is vivid and layered. Light 'breaks forth'—suggesting a sudden, even violent emergence from darkness, as dawn overcomes night. Health 'springs forth speedily'—using the same verb root as Isaiah 58:2 (growing, sprouting), emphasizing organic, life-giving restoration rather than external imposition.

The military metaphor in the final lines is crucial and often missed. 'Thy righteousness shall go before thee' positions justice like a vanguard leading into battle; 'the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward' stations divine presence as a rear guard protecting the flanks. The community practicing justice is not isolated or vulnerable but surrounded—led and protected—by righteousness and divine glory. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant in 'healing' (arukah, literally 'new flesh growing over a wound') emphasizes that this is not merely wellness but restoration—the healing of social wounds that oppression has created.

word_study.meaning: To break open, split, or burst forth. Often used for light breaking through darkness or water breaking through barriers.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not gentle dawning but forceful emergence—justice, when practiced, does not creep in but breaks through with power. The KJV captures this well.

word_study.meaning: Healing; literally, new flesh growing over a wound. The word evokes the biological reality of restoration after injury.
word_study.significance: The Dead Sea Scrolls variant uses a plene spelling here, emphasizing the word's full weight. This is not abstract wellness but the concrete healing of social wounds. As The Covenant Rendering translator notes point out, arukah 'literally means new flesh growing over a wound'—a vivid metaphor for social restoration through justice.

word_study.meaning: Justice, righteousness, or almsgiving. In Hebrew thought, tzedakah is not mere charity but the restoration of right relationship within the community. It carries covenantal force.
word_study.significance: This is not personal moral virtue but communal justice going before you as protection and vindication. In Jewish tradition, tzedakah became synonymous with charitable giving—a direct line from Isaiah's vision.

word_study.meaning: To gather, collect, or rear up; as a rearguard, to gather and protect those in the rear.
word_study.significance: The military metaphor positions God's glory as protective force. The KJV's 'rereward' captures the military sense better than more modern 'rear guard' translations might suggest—there is an active gathering and protective function.

cross_references.connection: A few chapters later, Isaiah again promises: 'Arise, shine; for thy light is come...for, behold, the darkness shall cover the earth...but the LORD shall arise upon thee.' The light breaking forth in 58:8 is part of Isaiah's larger vision of restoration for those who practice justice.

'For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.' The combination of light and divine protection echoes Isaiah's promise.
'But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.' The just have light that grows progressively brighter—aligned with Isaiah's promise.

The Lord's promise to accept Kirtland Temple worship: 'Your prayers have come up into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth, and are recorded in the book of the names of the sanctified.' True worship (linked to justice) is recorded and rewarded by God.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, the king was expected to embody justice and be protected by the gods as a result. Isaiah's radical claim here is that ordinary covenant people, practicing justice, inherit this royal privilege—they are surrounded by divine protection. The military imagery (vanguard and rearguard) would have been immediately recognizable to Judean audiences familiar with ancient military formations. The promise of healing and light breaking forth addresses the concrete suffering of the community: economic oppression had created actual poverty, sickness, and darkness (both literal and metaphorical). Isaiah promises that when justice is restored, so is health and illumination.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:41-43 presents a parallel promise: 'But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you...then, behold, will I grant unto you that your faith shall be increased' and later 'ye shall reap the rewards of your faith.' The conditional 'then' structure matches Isaiah's promise—righteous action produces blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:45 speaks of the Lord causing 'righteousness and truth to sweep the earth as with a flood, to gather out mine elect from the four corners of the earth.' The promise of righteousness going before and gathering God's people echoes Isaiah's military metaphor of vanguard and rearguard. Also, D&C 84:45-46 promises that 'the Spirit...shall be in your hearts; and my peace I give unto you' for those who keep covenants—paralleling Isaiah's promise of divine presence and healing.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple experience includes the promise that the faithful will be surrounded by divine light and protection. The progression through the endowment from darkness into light, and the wearing of temple garments as protective covering, embodies the promises made in this verse. Covenants made in the temple are precisely the kind of justice-bound commitments Isaiah calls for.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the vanguard and rearguard of those who follow Him. He leads the way through His own death and resurrection (light breaking forth) and gathers the rear through the Holy Ghost, ensuring no follower is left behind. The healing promised here—arukah, new flesh over a wound—is fulfilled in Christ's redemptive work, which literally heals the wound created by sin through His own flesh.
commentary.application: Modern readers often domesticate this verse into a promise of personal success—'if I'm generous, God will bless me with prosperity.' But Isaiah's actual promise is more profound and more challenging: When you practice justice, you become part of a community surrounded by God's protection and righteousness. The light is not yours alone; it is the community's. The healing is not personal wellness but social restoration. The question for today's member is this: Are you practicing the kind of justice that Isaiah describes in verse 7, and if so, do you trust that you are genuinely protected and led by God's righteousness, even when material circumstances suggest otherwise?

text_kjv: Then shalt thou call, and the LORD shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity;

commentary.narrative: The 'then' continues the conditional promise, but now shifts from external blessings (light, healing) to intimacy with God. The promise of immediate divine responsiveness—'thou shalt call, and the LORD shall answer'—echoes the covenant language of Abraham and Moses, who each responded to God with 'Here I am' (hineni). Isaiah's stunning reversal is that now God uses the same word in response to His people. This is not distant deity responding to formal petition; it is intimate presence. But the promise remains conditional. The next lines specify what must be removed: 'the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity.' These are not three separate things but three dimensions of one reality—the oppressive structures, the scornful mockery, and the false words that the wealthy direct toward the poor. The yoke is slavery and economic bondage; the pointing finger is contempt and dehumanization; speaking vanity (or wickedness—Hebrew: even) is the self-justifying lies the powerful tell themselves. Isaiah is saying: If you want God's presence, you cannot maintain oppressive structures while performing piety.

word_study.meaning: Here I am; present; ready to hear and respond. A profound utterance of availability and commitment.
word_study.significance: Abraham and Moses each used this word when God called them; it signified willingness to obey. The reversal here—God saying 'hineni' to His people—is theologically stunning. It means that when justice is practiced, God positions Himself as the eager responder to human need. The translator notes from The Covenant Rendering emphasize this: 'The reversal is stunning.'

word_study.meaning: A yoke; a symbol of servitude, bondage, or oppressive burden.
word_study.significance: The yoke recalls Egypt's slavery and Babylonian exile. Isaiah is demanding not just charity but the abolition of oppressive economic systems themselves. This is not merely individual kindness but structural justice.

word_study.meaning: To point; to stretch out one's finger in mockery, accusation, or contempt.
word_study.significance: This is the gesture of scorn—the wealthy mocking the poor, treating them as less than human. Isaiah names it as something that must be removed from 'your midst'—it is a communal practice, not merely individual vice.

word_study.meaning: To speak falsehood, wickedness, or iniquity; the lies and rationalizations used to justify injustice.
word_study.significance: This is not merely harsh speech but the false narratives the powerful construct to justify the suffering of the poor. In modern terms, it might be the 'blaming the victim' ideology that insists poverty is always deserved.

cross_references.connection: Abraham's 'Here I am' (hineni) in response to God's call establishes the covenantal language that Isaiah now inverts, with God saying 'hineni' to those who practice justice.
Moses' 'Here I am' (hineni) when called from the burning bush; Isaiah's vision is that the poor and marginalized will experience the same direct divine address that prophets received.

The prohibition against treating fellow Israelites as slaves, and the command to regard them as hired servants: 'thou shalt not rule over him with rigour; but shalt fear thy God.' This is precisely the removal of the yoke Isaiah demands.

The wicked 'winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers'—the pointing finger as a mark of the wicked. Isaiah's call to remove 'the putting forth of the finger' aligns with Wisdom's rejection of such mockery.

The promise that 'let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men' and 'thy dominion shall be an everlasting dominion' directly echoes Isaiah's promise that when contempt is removed and justice practiced, divine intimacy and power are restored.

commentary.historical_context: In Judean society of Isaiah's time, the wealthy elite maintained their power through both legal mechanisms (debt slavery, land confiscation) and cultural practices (contempt, dehumanization). The 'yoke' references not merely individual cruelty but codified systems of exploitation. The 'pointing finger' captures the social humiliation that accompanied economic bondage—the poor were not merely poor but scorned. Isaiah's demand to remove these practices addresses both the structural and the cultural dimensions of oppression. The theological innovation is to link these removals directly to covenant intimacy; you cannot maintain exploitation and expect divine presence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 5:2-8 presents a striking parallel where the people of King Benjamin, moved by his call to justice and covenant renewal, say 'Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us.' The intimacy promised by Isaiah—'the LORD shall answer'—is manifested in the Nephite community's direct access to God's Spirit through covenant renewal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 62:5 promises 'him that overcometh and keepeth my commandments until the end will I give all things.' But note the condition: keeping commandments, which in Isaiah's ethic means removing the yoke and pointing finger. Also, D&C 121:41-42 directly addresses this: 'No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned; By kindness, and pure knowledge.' This is the removal of the yoke and finger Isaiah demands.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant explicitly binds the member to use power and influence only in righteousness, never in oppression or contempt. The removal of 'the yoke' and 'the pointing finger' are preconditions for receiving the temple experience itself.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate 'Here I am' of God—the God who became fully present to humanity. He removed the yoke of sin through His Atonement and rejected the pointing finger of judgment from others, instead offering love. His resurrection 'breaks the yoke' of death itself.
commentary.application: For covenant members, this verse asks: What 'yokes' do I participate in or support? Are there systems of injustice—economic, social, racial—in which I am complicit? What 'pointing fingers' do I participate in—mockery, contempt, dehumanization of those different from me? And what 'vain speaking' do I engage in—rationalizations, blame-shifting, false narratives that justify inequality? Only when these are genuinely removed does God promise the kind of intimacy Isaiah names. This is not a promise that those who practice justice will be comfortable; it is a promise that they will not be abandoned. They will know God is present.

text_kjv: And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday:

commentary.narrative: This verse deepens and personalizes the call to justice introduced in verses 7-9. The phrase 'draw out thy soul to the hungry' is extraordinary—it is not merely giving bread but giving oneself. In Hebrew, 'soul' (nephesh) refers to the entire being, the vital center of personhood. To 'draw out' your soul is to expend your own life force, energy, and care. This is fasting redefined: Instead of denying yourself food, you are pouring out yourself for others. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant emphasizes this fuller sense of the word. The parallelism with 'satisfy the afflicted soul' (literally, 'the soul of the afflicted') creates a beautiful reciprocal image: You draw out your soul; you satisfy the soul of another. The promise that follows is climactic: 'thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday.' This is the inverse of normal experience. Normally, light fades in darkness, and darkness deepens at night. Isaiah promises that for those who pour out themselves for others, even in obscure places (where the work of justice is often hidden), light will emerge; even in darkness, noon-day clarity will shine. This suggests that the transformation is not external recognition but internal illumination and truthfulness.

word_study.meaning: To pour out, draw out, or expend one's soul (entire being) for the hungry. Tapeq suggests not static giving but active pouring, drawing from your own reserves.
word_study.significance: This is the heart of Isaiah's redefinition of fasting. The Covenant Rendering translator notes emphasize: 'not merely giving food but giving your very self. The fast becomes self-giving rather than self-denial.' It is a Christological image—to pour out oneself as Christ poured out His life.

word_study.meaning: To fill, satisfy, or satiate the soul of the afflicted; to address not merely physical hunger but the whole being's deprivation.
word_study.significance: The parallelism is crucial: Your soul poured out meets the soul of the afflicted and fills it. This is not transactional exchange but spiritual communion.

word_study.meaning: Your light shall dawn or shine forth even in darkness. Zarach (to shine, arise) is often used of the sun rising.
word_study.significance: The promise is not that darkness will be avoided but that light will emerge within it. This speaks to the inner illumination that comes from justice, even when external circumstances remain difficult.

word_study.term_english: thy darkness be as the noonday
word_study.meaning: And your obscurity or gloom shall be as the noonday; the deepest darkness will be illuminated as bright as midday.
word_study.significance: This is hyperbolic promise—even the worst obscurity is transformed to clarity. It suggests that the practice of justice brings not just spiritual but cognitive clarity; you see things as they truly are.

cross_references.connection: 'He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.' Isaiah's 'drawing out thy soul' prefigures Christ's teaching that self-loss leads to gain.
Paul speaks of being 'offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith,' of pouring out himself—echoing Isaiah's language and applying it to Christian witness.
'God loveth a cheerful giver'—and more deeply, giving emerges from love, not obligation. Isaiah's 'draw out thy soul' is this kind of joyful, self-giving generosity.

'I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.' Isaiah's promise that light rises even in obscurity for the just is ultimately fulfilled in Christ.

'Therefore, it must needs be that the righteous are called out from among all nations, and come unto Mount Zion, singing songs of everlasting joy.' The light and joy promised in Isaiah are the inheritance of the righteous.

commentary.historical_context: The social world of eighth-century Judah was deeply stratified. The wealthy elite could afford the temple sacrifices and fasts that gave them a sense of righteousness, while poor farmers and day-laborers had neither time nor resources for such practices. Isaiah's radical inversion is to declare that the true fast—the true religious act—is precisely what the poor must do (give what little they have) and what the wealthy were reluctant to do (give away their power and privilege). The promise of light in obscurity addresses a practical reality: Acts of justice toward the poor often went unrecognized and unrewarded by society. Isaiah promises that though society might not acknowledge such work, God sees it and transforms the practitioner from within.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin's address in Mosiah 2-4 emphasizes that all people are equal in God's sight and that the natural person becomes selfish and prone to oppression. The remedy is precisely Isaiah's redefinition: 'Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, through his atonement, may bring you into the presence of God' (Mosiah 5:15). The pouring out of oneself in service is the pathway to divine presence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 52:40 teaches that 'the poor shall rejoice' when the gospel is preached with power, implying that justice toward the poor is inseparable from divine blessing. More directly, D&C 42:30-31 commands that the Church care for the poor—implementing Isaiah's vision—and promises that this is remembered by God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The washing of feet in temple contexts symbolizes this pouring out of oneself in service. The principle of self-sacrifice, central to all temple covenants, is expressed through Isaiah's language: to give one's soul (entire being) in covenant with God and neighbor.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ literally 'drew out His soul' (poured out His life) for all humanity—He is the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's image. His light rises in the obscurity of the grave (Easter resurrection) and transforms all darkness to noonday clarity through the Atonement. To follow Christ is precisely to repeat this pattern: lose your life, find it transformed.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern members with a radical question: Am I merely performing religious duties (fasting, prayer, church attendance) while remaining self-protective and self-interested? Or am I actually 'drawing out my soul' for others—pouring out my energy, time, resources, and presence for those who are afflicted? The promise here is not safety or comfort but illumination: When you give yourself away in justice, you see reality clearly. You understand God's love. You know yourself. You are no longer divided between public piety and private selfishness. This is the light that 'rises in obscurity'—the internal clarity that comes from congruence between faith and action.

text_kjv: And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.

commentary.narrative: This verse promises a completely reversed condition. Where there was drought, there is now abundance; where there was depletion, there is now satisfaction; where there was withering, there is now flourishing. The progression through three promises—guidance, satisfaction, strengthening—moves from relational (God guides), to personal (soul is satisfied), to physical (bones are made fat, meaning strength and vitality return). The imagery then expands into one of the most beautiful similes in Isaiah: 'thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.' This echoes Genesis and the garden of Eden, suggesting that the practice of justice restores paradise. But crucially, this is not primarily about the individual being materially enriched (though satisfaction is promised). The person who pours out their soul for others becomes a source of life for others—they are a spring that never fails. They are not hoarding or becoming depleted but are themselves replenished by God so they can continue giving. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant uses a plene spelling for 'watered' (raveh), emphasizing the full hydration and life-giving quality. This is the ultimate promise: You will not run dry. You will not burn out from endless giving. God will sustain you.

word_study.meaning: The Lord will lead you, guide you, shepherd you continuously, always. Nachak suggests gentle leading like a shepherd, and tamid ('always') emphasizes the unbroken nature of this guidance.
word_study.significance: Unlike the contingent promises of verse 8-9, this is unbroken divine presence. The Lord does not guide only when you are performing the fast but 'continually'—always.

word_study.meaning: To fill, satisfy, satiate your soul even in scorched or arid places. Tzachtzachot (from a root meaning parched) conveys the extreme aridity of drought.
word_study.significance: This is an impossible promise in natural terms—to have your soul satisfied during drought. It suggests that inner spiritual satisfaction is independent of external scarcity. This anticipates the Beatitudes: 'Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled' (Matthew 5:6).

word_study.meaning: To cause your bones to flourish, be strengthened, or become vigorous. Yachalitz suggests straightening, strengthening, or making prosperous.
word_study.significance: Bones are the structural core of the body; making them 'fat' (full of marrow, vigorous) means restoring deep, fundamental strength. This is not superficial health but core resilience.

word_study.meaning: Like a garden that is irrigated, fully hydrated, flourishing. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant uses plene spelling for raveh, emphasizing the completeness of the watering.
word_study.significance: A watered garden in the Near East was a sign of abundance and blessing. Isaiah uses this to evoke Eden and the promise of restoration. The image suggests that the just person becomes a place where life flourishes.

word_study.term_english: spring of water, whose waters fail not
word_study.term_original: כְּמוֹצָא מַיִם אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יְכַזְּבוּ מֵימָיו (k'motza mayim asher lo yechazbu maimav)
word_study.transliteration: k'motza mayim asher lo yechazbu maimav
word_study.meaning: Like a spring or fountain of water whose waters do not deceive or fail. Yechazbu suggests failing, deceiving, or proving false.
word_study.significance: A spring that never fails in the Near East is an image of infinite blessing. Unlike cisterns that run dry, a true spring is fed by underground waters and never ceases. The just person becomes inexhaustible in their capacity to give.

cross_references.connection: 'He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul.' The guidance and restoration promised by Isaiah mirror the Psalmist's description of God's shepherd care.

'And a river went out of Eden to water the garden.' Isaiah's promise that the just person becomes 'like a watered garden' directly echoes the image of Eden watered by rivers—suggesting that justice restores paradise.

'Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is...he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river; and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought.' Nearly identical promises to Isaiah 58:11.

'Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools.' Those on pilgrimage to God's house transform even desolate places into sources of life—echoing Isaiah's image.

'Whoso receiveth my law and keepeth it, the same is my disciple; and him will I make free, that he may stand in the holy places; Therefore, prepare ye, prepare ye your houses for the coming of the Son of Man.' The promise of continual guidance in Isaiah is linked to D&C's promise of freedom and a prepared place.

commentary.historical_context: The drought referenced is both literal and metaphorical. Judah experienced actual periods of drought and water scarcity, especially during the eighth century BCE. But the drought is also spiritual and social—the exhaustion and depression that comes from living in injustice, from being exploited or witnessing exploitation. Isaiah's promise reverses both forms of drought. The image of the 'watered garden' would have been powerfully aspirational in a semi-arid land. Ancient irrigation techniques (dikes, channels, cisterns) allowed the wealthy to maintain gardens even during drought; Isaiah's promise is that through justice, this blessing becomes available to all, and more radically, to those who practice justice themselves.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:41-43 uses garden imagery strikingly similar to Isaiah: 'But behold, as ye have tried the experiment, and planted the seed, and it hath sprouted and begun to grow, thus I would ask, will not this strengthen your faith? Yea, it will strengthen your faith: for ye will say I know that this seed is good; for behold it sprouteth and beginneth to grow.' The just are like gardens that flourish through covenant practice. More directly, Alma 36:24-26 promises that those who repent and practice righteousness will be 'filled with joy' and their 'soul shall be satisfied'—the identical promise Isaiah gives.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:16-17 speaks of the New Jerusalem: 'And I will make it a land of peace and plenty, and the fulness of the earth shall be theirs.' The promise of a watered garden, of inexhaustible springs, is the promise of Zion itself. D&C 82:14 reinforces: 'For if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life, which is the greatest of all the gifts of God.' The continual guidance promised here is the gift of the Holy Ghost, which never ceases.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple garden imagery (flowers, trees, waters) in endowment and temple architecture symbolizes the watered garden Isaiah promises. Temples are built near water sources historically and symbolically; they represent the place where divine sustenance flows without ceasing. The person who keeps covenants (which includes the justice demanded in verse 7) is promised this same watering from heaven.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is both the watered garden and the spring of living water. John 4:13-14 records Christ's promise: 'Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.' Christ fulfills Isaiah's promise by becoming the source of inexhaustible life. To follow Christ is to become, through Him, like a spring that never fails.
commentary.application: This verse offers profound comfort to those engaged in justice work: You will not burn out. You will not become depleted. God will guide you (you don't need to figure this out alone). God will satisfy your deepest longings (not with material abundance necessarily, but with soul-deep fulfillment). You will be strengthened at the core (your bones will be fat with vigor). And crucially, as you give yourself away, you will become inexhaustible—like a spring that never fails, fed by sources beyond yourself. For modern members, this is an answer to the question every justice advocate asks: 'How do I do this work without burning out? How do I give without becoming empty?' Isaiah's answer: When your practice of justice is rooted in covenant, God becomes your source, and you flow without ceasing.

text_kjv: And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.

commentary.narrative: This is the culmination of Isaiah's vision of true fasting. The promises shift from personal blessing (light, healing, satisfaction) to communal vocation and identity. Those who practice justice become builders and restorers. The 'old waste places' are the broken communities, the systems of injustice that have devastated generations. The Hebrew word translated 'waste places' (charboth) carries the weight of ruin and desolation. To rebuild them is not merely material construction but the restoration of human dignity and community wholeness. The phrase 'raise up the foundations of many generations' is profound: The foundations are the deep structures—the laws, institutions, and relationships that hold a society together. Isaiah is calling for radical reconstruction at the foundational level, a work that spans generations. But then comes the vocational identity: 'thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.' These are not descriptive labels but covenantal names—the kind of names God bestows in Scripture (Abram becomes Abraham; Simon becomes Peter). To be called 'repairer of the breach' is to be given a divine vocation. The breach is both literal (the broken walls of a destroyed city) and metaphorical (the fracture between rich and poor, between justice and oppression). A repairer doesn't just patch superficially; they restore integrity. The phrase 'restorer of paths to dwell in' suggests not just opening roads but making habitation itself possible—transforming desolate places into homes. The Dead Sea Scrolls variant uses plene spelling for 'repairer' (goder), emphasizing the word's full theological weight.

word_study.term_original: וּבָנוּ מִמְּךָ חָרְבוֹת עוֹלָם (ubanu mimkha charboth olam)
word_study.meaning: And your people shall build from you the ancient ruins. Charboth (ruins, waste places) comes from a root meaning to be desolate. Olam means ancient or eternal—suggesting long-standing, structural desolation.
word_study.significance: The builders emerge from the people of justice. They are produced by the practice described in verses 7-11. This is not external reconstruction but organic rebuilding from within covenant community.

word_study.meaning: The foundations (mosdei) of generation after generation (dor-vador) shall you raise up or establish. This suggests work that spans centuries, laying structural foundations for future generations.
word_study.significance: Justice work is not a single act but multigenerational commitment. The foundations you raise support those who come after you. This is a calling, not a project.

word_study.meaning: The one who repairs or seals a breach/gap/break. Goder (from the root meaning to wall up or repair) and perets (a break, breach, or gap) together form an image of restoration.
word_study.significance: The Dead Sea Scrolls uses plene spelling here. The 'breach' is both the literal broken walls after siege or exile and the metaphorical fracture in society caused by injustice. The vocation of repairer is central to God's work itself—Christ repairs the breach between God and humanity.

word_study.term_english: The restorer of paths to dwell in
word_study.meaning: The one who returns or restores paths for dwelling; one who makes habitation possible. Netivot (paths) and shabat (to dwell, inhabit) together suggest restoring the possibility of home.
word_study.significance: A path is not merely a road but the way of life, the habitual practice. The restorer makes home and right dwelling possible. This is not charitable housing but the restoration of justice that allows human flourishing.

cross_references.connection: Nehemiah calls the people to 'build up the wall of Jerusalem' after exile—a literal fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that those who practice justice become rebuilders of ruined places.

'In the day that thy walls are to be built, in that day shall the decree be far removed.' Isaiah and Micah together prophesy that the restoration of justice brings the reconstruction of the community's protective structures.

'Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come...when her dust, and to favour the dust thereof.' The restoration of waste places is an act of divine favor toward Zion.

Alma teaches that the restoration of all things happens through Christ: 'Now, my son, all men that are in a lost and fallen state are in this same condition, and they are brought to view the resurrection of Christ, and his glory, and his righteousness...Therefore, the plan of restoration is requisite with the justice of God; for all things must be restored to their proper order.'

The promise of Zion in D&C speaks to the community's collective vocation: 'For the great Millennial work which I have covenanted with you...and my people whom I have chosen shall be my people, and I will be their God.' Those who practice Isaiah's justice become builders of Zion.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of eighth-century Judah (or possibly the exilic period, if later dating is correct), the 'old waste places' and 'ruins of many generations' likely refer to the destruction and exile that had devastated the land. Cities lay abandoned; social structures were fractured. The promise is that the people who practice justice will not merely survive return from exile but will become the active agents of communal reconstruction. This was not merely passive restoration but active rebuilding—both physical and social. The 'paths to dwell in' echoes the work of restoration described in Nehemiah and the post-exilic community's effort to rebuild society on foundations of justice and covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
Mosiah 29:40 describes the ideal Nephite society: 'And thus Mosiah had established a reign of peace in the land. And he also had established a law; and peace and good order had been established in the kingdom.' The Nephite society, when guided by the justice principles Isaiah describes, becomes a builder of stable, enduring communities. More directly, 4 Nephi 1:2-3 describes the post-Christ community as one where 'the Lord did pour out his Spirit on all the inhabitants of this land...and they were all converted unto the Lord, and none of them were fallen away...and they had all things common among them.'

The Latter-day Saint restoration itself is presented as a fulfillment of Isaiah's vision of restoration. D&C 35:24 speaks of 'the binding up of the law and sealing of the testimony' as part of the restoration work. The very language of 'restoration' in LDS theology—the Restoration of the Gospel—draws on Isaiah's prophetic vocabulary.
restoration_lens.dc_connections:
D&C 115:5-6 speaks of Jackson County, Missouri as 'the center place' where 'shall be the New Jerusalem...It shall be called the City of the New Jerusalem, a land of peace.' This is the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that those practicing justice shall raise up foundations for generations and restore paths to dwell in. More broadly, D&C 103:9-10 states: 'It is my will...to gather my people in time out of the nations, and to establish a holy city, unto me...that my people may be gathered in one in that day when I shall come down in my glory in the clouds of heaven to meet thee.'

Also, D&C 29:11 teaches of the final restoration: 'And in that generation shall the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled.' The work of restoration spans generations exactly as Isaiah promises.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the center of Zion. Those who make covenants in the temple—which include the commitment to justice expressed in Isaiah 58—are literally participating in the building of God's kingdom. The temple covenant obligates members to consecrate themselves and their resources to building Zion. The work of temple and the work of justice are inseparable. The 'waste places' are restored through covenant fidelity.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the supreme Repairer of the Breach and Restorer of Paths. The breach created by Adam's transgression and humanity's sin is repaired by Christ's Atonement. The paths that were lost through the Fall are restored through His Resurrection. Those who follow Christ and practice the justice He embodied become, in turn, repairers and restorers. They are called to continue His work of building the Kingdom of God.
commentary.application: This verse addresses the question: Does my practice of justice matter? Will it amount to anything? Isaiah's answer is yes—emphatically. But not necessarily in ways you control or see immediately. Your work of justice contributes to the building of foundations that will support many generations. You may be the first generation to practice the justice of verse 7, but you are laying foundations for your children and their children. This reframes the often-devastating feeling of activists and advocates that 'nothing changes.' Isaiah says: You are a repairer, a restorer. That is not merely what you do; it is who you are called to be. Your vocation is covenantal and eternal. For modern members, this means: The work of justice—whether it's advocating for the vulnerable, building sustainable communities, creating systems that protect the marginalized—is not tangential to the kingdom of God but central to it. You are being called, just as the ancient community was, to be 'repairers of the breach.' This is not political activism divorced from faith; it is the vocational identity given to those who practice true covenant.

text_kjv: If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 58:13 marks a decisive pivot in the chapter's argument about true fasting. The prophet has spent verses 3-12 exposing the gap between empty ritual and genuine devotion—a pattern that now extends to Sabbath observance. The conditional structure ('if you turn back your foot') signals that restoration of covenant relationship depends on a fundamental reorientation of how God's people treat His holy day. The Sabbath here is not presented as a restriction imposed from outside, but as a delight (oneg) to be discovered and claimed. This reframing is crucial: the Sabbath shifts from a day of prohibitions to a day of positive liberation from the tyranny of endless productivity and self-interest.

The verse operates on two levels simultaneously. Negatively, it demands the cessation of one's own pursuits, pleasures, and speech on the Sabbath—a comprehensive halt to the machinery of individual ambition. But this is not mere restriction; it is the condition for experiencing the Sabbath as it was intended: a day set apart for the presence and purposes of the Lord. The phrase 'turn away your foot' uses physical movement as a metaphor for moral reorientation. To turn your foot is to change direction, to stop going your own way and begin walking according to covenant rhythm. The 'holy day of the LORD' belongs to Him, not to us; our honor of it is simultaneously our honor of Him.

The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ) preserve this verse with a plene spelling of oneg ('delight'), emphasizing the fullness and richness of what the Sabbath offers. The theological stability of this verse across a millennium of textual transmission underscores how central this teaching about joyful Sabbath observance has been to Jewish covenant consciousness. Isaiah is not inventing a new doctrine but calling his people back to the original vision of Exodus 20:8-11, where the Sabbath is a sign of God's rest and blessing.

word_study.meaning: To turn back or return (shûb) one's foot (regel). Regel typically means 'foot' but can metaphorically represent one's course, path, or direction of travel. Shûb is one of the most theologically rich verbs in Hebrew, meaning to turn, return, or repent—implying a complete change of direction.
word_study.significance: The verb shûb carries the weight of teshuvah (repentance/return) in later Jewish theology. Isaiah uses it here not as condemnation but as invitation—calling the people to realign their movement and energy with covenant purposes. The foot as the instrument of travel becomes the image of moral reorientation.

word_study.meaning: Delight, pleasure, or luxurious enjoyment. Oneg is a positive noun denoting pleasure, joy, and satisfaction. It appears rarely in biblical Hebrew but carries connotations of richness and satisfaction. The root may connect to 'soft' or 'tender,' suggesting comfort and ease.
word_study.significance: This is the theological crux of Isaiah 58:13. The Sabbath is not to be experienced as a burden or restriction but as oneg—a true delight. This reframes the entire spiritual economy of Sabbath practice. Rather than emphasizing duty or obligation, Isaiah invites the people into joy. The Covenant Rendering's rendering preserves this richness: the Sabbath becomes something to be delighted in, not merely observed. For Latter-day Saints, this echoes D&C 59:13-14, where the Sabbath is explicitly framed as a day for the saints to rest from their labors and partake of spiritual nourishment.

word_study.meaning: Qadosh means 'set apart' or 'holy'—fundamentally, something separated from common use and consecrated to divine purposes. YHWH is the covenant name of God. Together, 'the holy day of the LORD' denotes a day consecrated and belonging exclusively to God's purposes.
word_study.significance: The Sabbath's holiness is not abstract or theoretical; it belongs to the LORD personally. To honor the Sabbath is to honor the God who owns and sanctifies it. This ownership language is critical—the day is not ours to use as we see fit, but the LORD's to shape our participation in His rest.

word_study.meaning: To honor, glorify, or make heavy/weighty. Kabad can mean to regard as significant, to treat with respect, or to ascribe weight and importance to someone. The root literally means 'heavy' or 'weighty,' suggesting that to honor something is to regard it as substantial and consequential.
word_study.significance: Honoring the Sabbath is honoring God. The verb kabad requires active recognition and respect. It is not passive or invisible but manifest in concrete choices: how we spend our time, energy, and attention. For Latter-day Saints, this echoes the principle of 'standing as witnesses of God' (Mosiah 18:9)—our Sabbath practice witnesses our regard for His holiness.

word_study.meaning: Pleasure, delight, desire, or will. Chephetz denotes what one finds pleasing or desirable—one's personal interests, ambitions, or preferences. It is morally neutral in itself but becomes problematic when pursued in violation of covenant obligations.
word_study.significance: The repetition of chephetz (vv. 13, twice) underscores the central tension: the Sabbath requires us to step back from the endless pursuit of our own desires. This is not because desire is inherently evil, but because on the Sabbath, the LORD's purposes and presence take precedence. The Covenant Rendering's phrase 'pursuing your own interests' captures this well—the Sabbath is a reprieve from the relentless machinery of self-directed ambition.

word_study.meaning: To speak or utter words (dabar as verb); a word or matter (dabar as noun). The phrase denotes speech, discourse, or the words one utters according to one's own will and purposes.
word_study.significance: Speech is included in the comprehensive Sabbath rest. Just as one ceases from work and the pursuit of personal business, so one ceases from idle, self-directed speech. This aligns with Talmudic interpretations that include certain categories of speech as violations of Sabbath sanctity. For modern readers, this suggests that even our conversational patterns reflect whether we are truly set apart for God's purposes or merely taking a surface break while our minds remain engaged in worldly preoccupations.

cross_references.connection: The foundational Sabbath commandment, establishing the day as a sign of God's covenant and rest. Isaiah 58:13 calls the people back to the original vision of the Sabbath as a day of blessing and restoration, not mere restriction.

The modern revelation on Sabbath observance, which frames the Sabbath as a day to 'rest from your labors' and 'pay thy devotions unto the Most High.' This aligns precisely with Isaiah's teaching that true Sabbath honor involves ceasing from one's own pursuits to focus on God's presence and purposes.

Nehemiah's enforcement of Sabbath rest against commercialism and labor, reflecting the same crisis Isaiah addresses—the tendency to treat the Sabbath as merely a break rather than a holy separation from self-directed activity.

Jesus' teaching on Sabbath observance in the New Testament, where He argues that Sabbath law serves human flourishing, not restriction. His mercy-centered reframing parallels Isaiah's emphasis on the Sabbath as delight rather than burden.

Earlier in Isaiah, the prophet promises blessing to those who 'keep the sabbath from polluting it' and 'hold fast' God's covenant. This passage reinforces the same message: Sabbath observance is central to covenant faithfulness and opens the door to God's blessing.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of post-exilic Judah (the likely setting of Isaiah 40-66), Sabbath observance had become a marker of Jewish identity and religious commitment during the long absence of the Temple's central sacrificial system. The Babylonian exile had stretched over decades, scattering the people and making pilgrim feasts and Temple sacrifice impossible. The Sabbath—a practice accessible anywhere and to anyone—became the primary expression of covenantal faithfulness. However, as commerce and survival pressures mounted in the post-exilic restoration, the tendency to use Sabbath as merely a respite while pursuing one's own concerns had grown. Archaeological evidence from Lachish and other post-exilic Judean sites suggests economic activity and trade continued even as religious reform efforts were underway. Isaiah addresses this gap between formal Sabbath observance and genuine heart-centered dedication to God's purposes. The prophet's emphasis on oneg ('delight') may also reflect how Sabbath was experienced in the post-exilic community—not as the joyful sanctuary it should be, but as an obligation resented or minimized.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes the spiritual economy of covenant observance throughout. Alma 37 teaches that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass'—a principle that applies to how we honor small things, like the Sabbath day. Helaman 12:1-2 describes how the people's hardness of heart led them to forget God's mercies, a pattern Isaiah addresses through Sabbath practice. The Sabbath becomes a 'small and simple thing' through which we remember and reaffirm our covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:13-14 is the capstone revelation on Sabbath observance: 'And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day.' The command to 'offer up thy sacraments' (the sacrament of bread and water) on the Sabbath ties Sabbath practice directly to sacramental covenant renewal. D&C 68:29 reinforces the teaching that the Sabbath is a day of worship and rest. These revelations show that in the Restoration, the principle Isaiah articulates—the Sabbath as a day set apart for God's purposes—remains central to LDS covenant life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Sabbath functions as a 'mini-temple' in covenant practice—a consecrated space and time set apart for God's presence. Just as the temple requires us to cease from worldly concerns and enter a sacred space, the Sabbath invites us to cease from our own pursuits and enter God's time. The injunctions against 'doing thy pleasure' on the Sabbath mirror temple covenants, which also require us to submit our will to God's purposes. President Russell M. Nelson has emphasized that Sabbath observance prepares us for temple worship and deepens our covenantal commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: The Sabbath itself is a type and shadow pointing to Christ and the rest He offers. Hebrews 4:1-10 explicitly teaches that the Sabbath rest foreshadows the eternal rest found in Christ—a rest from the works of the law and the burdensome striving of self-righteousness. Christ is the 'Lord of the Sabbath' (Matthew 12:8), who fulfills and perfects what the Sabbath signifies. His invitation in Matthew 11:28—'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest'—echoes Isaiah's framing of the Sabbath as oneg (delight). In Christ, the Sabbath becomes not a legal obligation but a joyful participation in His work and rest. Isaiah 58:13-14 can thus be read as a call to the deeper rest found in Christ, where we cease from our own works (Hebrews 4:10) and enter into His finished work of redemption.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Isaiah 58:13 invites a radical reconsideration of how we spend the Sabbath. The test is simple: Are we turning back our foot from pursuing our own interests, or are we finding ways to justify checking email, managing business, pursuing entertainment, and advancing personal agendas while calling it 'rest'? The verse challenges us to ask whether our Sabbath practice is genuine—a real turning away from self-directed pursuits—or merely surface-level compliance. The word oneg ('delight') is especially important: if the Sabbath feels like a burden, an inconvenient restriction on a busy week, we have missed the point. True Sabbath observance should feel like liberation, like stepping out of the relentless machinery of productivity and self-interest into a day where God's presence and purposes are primary. Practically, this might mean: genuinely resting (not disguising work as 'necessary'), speaking with greater intentionality (being present in conversation rather than distracted), worshiping wholeheartedly at sacrament meeting, serving in our callings, and allowing the Spirit to shape our experience rather than our personal agenda. The Sabbath becomes a weekly covenant renewal—a day when we demonstrate through our choices that we value God's purposes more than our own.

text_kjv: Then shalt thou delight thyself in the LORD; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 58:14 is the promise that completes the conditional structure begun in verse 13. The 'then' (Hebrew 'az) marks the hinge point—if you turn back from your own pursuits and honor the Sabbath with genuine delight, then the LORD promises something far greater: you shall delight yourself in the LORD. This is the inversion at the heart of Isaiah's teaching: true Sabbath rest does not deprive us of delight; it transforms the source of our delight. We trade the thin, empty satisfaction of pursuing our own interests for the fullness of joy found in God's presence and purposes. The language of 'riding upon the high places of the earth' invokes themes of dominion, elevation, and divine empowerment. In the Ancient Near Eastern context, high places were seats of power and visibility; to be raised to the high places is to be exalted and honored. The 'heritage of Jacob' recalls the covenant promises given to the patriarch—the land, descendants, and blessing that form the foundation of Israel's identity. This is no small promise. The verse ends with the solemn formula 'for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it'—a seal of divine certainty and irrevocability.

What is remarkable about verse 14 is its parallel structure with verse 13. Verse 13 commands: 'call the Sabbath a delight' and 'honor it.' Verse 14 responds: 'delight yourself in the LORD.' The same Hebrew word for 'delight' (oneg in v. 13, ta'ang in v. 14—both carrying the sense of pleasure and satisfaction) appears in both verses. The Covenant Rendering makes this connection clear: the delight of the Sabbath observance leads to delight in the LORD Himself. This is the progression of covenant experience—outward obedience opens the door to inward joy. The promise is not merely spiritual or emotional; it includes material blessing ('feed thee with the heritage of Jacob'). This reflects the full covenantal vision: faithful Sabbath observance reconnects us to the entire sweep of God's promises, restoring us to the full inheritance meant for God's covenant people.

The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ) preserve verse 14 without significant variant, reinforcing that this promise of elevation and abundant feeding has been stable in Jewish tradition for over two thousand years. The closing words 'for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken' explicitly ground the promise in divine speech—the same word that called creation into being, the same word that established covenant with Abraham. This is not contingent blessing dependent on human effort; it is the sure word of God's sovereign mouth. Isaiah began chapter 58 with the LORD's mouth speaking rebuke (58:1); he closes with the LORD's mouth speaking promise (58:14). The pivot from rebuke to promise marks the entire arc of true repentance and covenant renewal.

word_study.meaning: Then, at that time, or in that case. Az is a temporal adverb marking a sequence or consequence—indicating what follows from a prior condition.
word_study.significance: The word az signals the causal relationship between verse 13 (the condition) and verse 14 (the promise). It is not 'if and possibly then,' but 'if, then certainly'—affirming God's reliable covenant structure. This linguistic marker reinforces that the promise is not speculative but certain, contingent only on the condition being fulfilled.

word_study.meaning: To delight in, to enjoy, or to take pleasure in. Related to the noun oneg (delight/pleasure) from verse 13, the verb anag carries the sense of luxurious enjoyment, comfort, and satisfaction. The root conveys softness, ease, and the absence of struggle.
word_study.significance: The use of the same root (oneg/anag) in verses 13 and 14 creates a powerful wordplay: 'call the Sabbath a delight [oneg]' leads to 'delight yourself [anag] in the LORD.' True obedience opens the way to authentic joy. This is not legalistic drudgery rewarded with distant blessing, but the experience of finding genuine satisfaction in covenant relationship with God. The Covenant Rendering preserves this: 'you shall delight yourself in the LORD,' emphasizing that God Himself becomes the source of joy and satisfaction.

word_study.meaning: Rakab means to ride, mount, or be carried; bamot refers to high places, elevations, or ridges. Together, 'to ride upon the high places' evokes images of elevation, dominion, and empowerment. The high places in Ancient Near Eastern cosmology were seats of divine presence and power.
word_study.significance: The image of 'riding' suggests not just elevation but movement, journey, and agency. This is not passivity but dynamic participation in God's purposes. In Isaiah, riding often accompanies themes of vindication and restoration (cf. Isaiah 40:31, 'they shall mount up with wings as eagles'). The promise connects external vindication (elevation, honor) with internal transformation (delight in the LORD). For Latter-day Saints, this resonates with the language of being 'exalted' or 'raised up' in covenant relationship—not through pride but through alignment with God's will.

word_study.meaning: Nachalah means inheritance, portion, or allotted land—something passed down from ancestors and belonging by right to descendants. Jacob (Israel) is the patriarch through whom the covenant promises were transmitted. The 'heritage of Jacob' refers to the full scope of covenant blessings: the promised land, descendants, and divine relationship.
word_study.significance: The word nachalah emphasizes that what God promises is not something earned through works but inherited through covenant lineage. To feed the people 'with the heritage of Jacob' means to restore them to the full blessing package of Abrahamic covenant. This addresses a deep yearning in post-exilic Judah: after exile and dispersion, did they still possess their covenant inheritance? Isaiah's answer is yes—true Sabbath observance reconnects them to the full scope of what God promised to their fathers. This is crucial for understanding Latter-day Saint concepts of restoration: we inherit promises given to the fathers (D&C 86:8-11), and covenantal faithfulness (including Sabbath keeping) connects us to that inheritance.

word_study.term_english: the mouth of the LORD hath spoken
word_study.meaning: Pi (mouth), YHWH (the covenant name of God), diber (spoke, said). The phrase emphasizes divine speech as the source and guarantee of the promise. In Hebrew theology, God's mouth is the instrument through which creation comes into being (Genesis 1) and through which covenant is established.
word_study.significance: This closing formula is not mere rhetoric; it is a covenant seal. To say 'the mouth of the LORD has spoken' is to invoke the absolute reliability of divine speech. This language echoes throughout Isaiah and appears in contexts of the most solemn promises (e.g., Isaiah 1:20, 40:5). For the post-exilic community hearing these words, it was a reassurance that despite their present circumstances, God's word remained active and would accomplish what He purposed. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this phrase without variant, showing its centrality and stability in the tradition.

cross_references.connection: The blessing section of the covenant, which promises that if Israel obeys God's commandments, they will be exalted 'above all nations' and possess abundant blessing. Isaiah 58:14 echoes this covenant structure: obedience (Sabbath keeping) leads to elevation and blessing.

The promise that 'they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles.' Isaiah 58:14's image of riding upon high places parallels this theme of supernatural elevation through trust and covenant faithfulness.

The New Testament's teaching that 'there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God' for those who enter His works. Isaiah 58:14's promise of delight and satisfaction in the LORD foreshadows the rest available through Christ.

The modern revelation affirming the covenant pattern: 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' Isaiah 58:13-14 exemplifies this reciprocal covenant structure: faithful Sabbath observance obligates God to fulfill His promise of blessing.

Alma teaches that 'all things denote there is a God' and that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass.' The Sabbath, a small and simple practice, becomes the vehicle through which the great promise of the heritage of Jacob is accessed.

commentary.historical_context: In the post-exilic context, the promise of riding 'upon the high places of the earth' and inheriting 'the heritage of Jacob' would have carried profound weight for a community that had recently returned from exile or was still experiencing the limitations of Persian imperial rule. The Judeans of this period were not truly independent; they were a small province within the Persian Empire, with no king of their own (since Zedekiah's deposition in 586 BCE). Isaiah's promise of elevation and dominion would have sounded almost absurd from a geopolitical standpoint. Yet it was a promise grounded in covenant theology, not in current circumstances. The 'heritage of Jacob' referenced not merely material possession of land but the entire covenantal identity and blessing-structure that defined the people. By connecting Sabbath faithfulness to this heritage, Isaiah affirmed that even in imperial subordination and geographical limitation, the people retained their covenant status and could access God's promised blessing through faithful practice. The emphasis on the 'mouth of the LORD' speaking this promise was a reassurance that divine speech, not human circumstance, was the ultimate determinant of reality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms the pattern of Sabbath observance leading to covenant blessing. Nephi's exhortation in 2 Nephi 31:19-20 teaches that endurance in covenant obedience leads to the receipt of the Holy Ghost and eternal life. The concept of 'riding upon the high places' finds parallel in 1 Nephi 13:37, where Nephi is shown that 'the Lamb of God' will be 'lifted up upon the cross' yet ultimately exalted. The connection is that covenantal faithfulness, including the regular practice of Sabbath observance, connects us to God's promises of exaltation and inheritance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:15-16 continues the revelation on Sabbath observance: 'And inasmuch as ye do these things with thanksgiving, with cheerful hearts and countenances, not with much laughter, for this is sin, but with a glad heart and a cheerful countenance—Verily I say, that inasmuch as ye do this, the fulness of the earth is yours.' This directly parallels Isaiah 58:14's promise that faithful Sabbath observance leads to abundance and blessing. The promise of the 'heritage' finds its Restoration parallel in D&C 88:15-16, where the Lord teaches that all things are 'spiritual' and belong to His covenant people. D&C 84:37-40 teaches that the sacrament (taken on the Sabbath) is 'that you may more fully keep yourselves unspotted from the world,' connecting Sabbath practice to the path of exaltation and ultimate inheritance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The 'heritage of Jacob' in verse 14 carries deep temple significance. In Latter-day Saint theology, the temple is the place where we receive our inheritance—where we learn of the ordinances and covenants that connect us to all the blessings promised to the fathers. The Sabbath, as a weekly covenant renewal experience, prepares us for and points us toward the fuller covenantal experience of the temple. President Brigham Young taught that the Sabbath is a day when we should 'lay aside the cares and concerns of the world' and devote ourselves to God, much as we do in the temple. The promise of 'riding upon the high places' can be understood as the exaltation promised through temple ordinances and covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 58:14 points to Christ in several ways. First, the promise of 'delight yourself in the LORD' finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who is the embodiment of God's presence and purpose. In John 1:14, we are told 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us'—God's ultimate self-revelation and the source of our greatest delight. Second, the image of being 'lifted up' or 'riding upon the high places' prefigures Christ's exaltation. In John 12:32, Jesus says, 'And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me'—His exaltation becomes the means of our elevation and salvation. Third, Christ is himself the 'heritage of Jacob'—the fulfillment of all the covenant promises given to the patriarchs. In Luke 1:54-55, Mary's Magnificat celebrates that God 'hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy; as he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever.' The ultimate heritage promised to Jacob finds its completeness in Christ, who is 'the seed of Abraham' (Galatians 3:29) and the source of all blessing. The Sabbath observance commanded in verse 13, leading to the promise in verse 14, thus becomes a type of the rest we find in Christ—the cessation from our own works that allows us to enter into His.
commentary.application: Isaiah 58:14 invites us to test the promise through covenant practice. The verse assumes that when we genuinely turn back from pursuing our own interests on the Sabbath and honor God's day, we will experience the fulfillment of God's word. The application is not merely about accumulating good works or checking off spiritual practices, but about entering into the lived experience of covenant blessing. Ask yourself: Do I delight in the LORD? Or am I still chasing delight from other sources—productivity, entertainment, comfort, status? The verse suggests that true joy, true elevation, true satisfaction comes from covenant alignment, not from worldly pursuits. Practically, this means: (1) Protect the Sabbath from the relentless incursion of worldly concerns. (2) Use Sabbath time to reconnect with what matters most—God's presence, family relationships, spiritual nourishment. (3) Trust that God's promise is reliable ('the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it'), even when external circumstances seem to contradict it. (4) Understand the Sabbath not as a restriction but as a pathway to the inheritance of all God's blessings. The 'high places' are not distant or inaccessible; they are found in the weekly rhythm of covenant faithfulness.

text_kjv: Behold, the LORD's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear:

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah opens this stark indictment of Judah with a crucial reversal: the problem is not divine inability or indifference. The prophet addresses a fundamental misdiagnosis he hears in the community — people attributing their exile and suffering to God's weakness or deafness. This verse operates as a diagnostic correction. The phrase 'hand is not shortened' draws on ancient Near Eastern language of divine power and capacity; a shortened hand implies impotence, just as a heavy ear implies failure to hear. The Covenant Rendering captures the meaning sharply: 'the hand of the LORD is not too short to save.' This is not mere comfort; it is an accusation. If God's power and attentiveness are intact, then the rupture of relationship must stem from elsewhere — a truth the next verses will expose relentlessly.

The rhetorical force here is devastating because it denies Israel the consolation of blaming God's limitations. Ancient Near Eastern parallels show that when nations experienced divine silence, they sometimes attributed it to the deity being overwhelmed by other demands or weakened by rival powers. Isaiah categorically denies this. The opening 'Behold' (hinneh) functions as an urgent summons to pay attention, as if the prophet is demanding that listeners stop and reconsider their entire theological framework. God's hand remains extended, His ear remains attentive. The separation between God and His people is not due to divine withdrawal but to human sin — a far more uncomfortable diagnosis that demands personal repentance rather than mere waiting for divine intervention.

word_study.meaning: to be short, to cut short, to diminish. In the context of the 'hand' (yad), it suggests a shortened reach or limited capacity for action. The root conveys both physical and metaphorical shortening — a hand that cannot extend far enough to save.
word_study.significance: This language of divine capacity is crucial in Isaiah's theology of redemption. To say God's hand is 'not shortened' is to affirm His unlimited power and reach. The Covenant Rendering's 'not too short' captures the sense that this is about adequacy and sufficiency for the task at hand — salvation.

word_study.meaning: to be heavy, to be weighed down, to be dull. When applied to the ear (ozen), it means the ear has become insensitive or unresponsive — not that God cannot hear, but that He has become disinterested in listening.
word_study.significance: The ear metaphor is deeply relational in Hebrew thought. A 'heavy ear' suggests God has turned away in judgment, not that He has lost auditory capacity. This word choice emphasizes that any divine silence stems from relational rupture, not mechanical failure.

cross_references.connection: Moses uses similar language about God's hand and power, emphasizing that God's actions are never constrained by inability but only by His sovereign will and covenant purposes.

The psalmist asks why God 'hidest thou thy face' in times of trouble — the very question Isaiah addresses by clarifying that divine hiddenness is not about divine capacity but about sin creating separation.

The Book of Mormon uses remarkably similar language to affirm that 'the arm of the Lord is lengthened out all the day long,' establishing that divine power and willingness to save are never the limiting factor.
Paul echoes Isaiah's logic when addressing Israel's apparent rejection, arguing that God has not cast off His people — the fault lies in human unfaithfulness, not divine withdrawal.

commentary.historical_context: In the context of exilic Judah (or the post-exilic period, depending on Isaiah's dating), the community had experienced what appeared to be divine abandonment. The destruction of Jerusalem, the temple's devastation, and the deportations created a theological crisis: Had God been overcome by the gods of Babylon? Had He grown weary of His covenant people? Ancient Near Eastern literature shows this was a common response to catastrophe. Isaiah's opening refutation — 'the hand of the LORD is not shortened' — directly counters this despair. The prophet insists that God's covenant power remains fully operative. This would have been a shocking and even offensive claim to ears accustomed to viewing exile as evidence of divine failure or weakness.
