The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'I will not keep silent,' underscoring divine speech as the vehicle of change.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, right conduct, moral vindication. Often paired with salvation as the two great acts by which God restores His covenant people. Can mean both the state of being right and the act of making things right.
word_study.significance: In Isaiah's eschatology, tzedâqâh is not merely personal moral virtue but the corporate reality of a people restored to covenant relationship with God. It 'goes forth' (יָצָא, yâtzâ)—actively emanating from Zion—suggesting that righteousness will be Zion's characteristic, visible to all nations. This is the renewal of the covenant community, not just individual piety.

word_study.meaning: Brightness, radiance, light. Often used to describe the glory of God's presence or the illumination of divine truth. A concrete, visible phenomenon.
word_study.significance: The choice of nôgah rather than a vaguer term emphasizes visibility and recognition. Zion's righteousness will not be hidden or theoretical but luminous, undeniable. This echoes Isaiah 60:1-3, where Zion's light rises and the nations come to her brightness.

word_study.meaning: A lamp, torch, or burning flame. Emphasizes sustained, active illumination rather than passive reflection of light.
word_study.significance: Salvation is not just a state but an active, ongoing reality—a flame that continues to burn. The image of the torch reinforces that Zion's deliverance will be conspicuous and perpetual, drawing the world's attention.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 60 announces 'Arise, shine; for thy light is come,' the same eschatological brightness motif. Isaiah 62:1 fulfills this vision as the prophet renews the commitment that Zion's light will shine until nations are drawn to it.

The psalm proclaims 'He that keepeth thee will not slumber,' reflecting the theme of God's unwearied watch over Zion. Isaiah 62:1 mirrors this divine wakefulness—'I will not rest' until Zion is restored.
The Lord declares His covenant people shall 'flourish and abound in the land,' echoing the restoration language of Isaiah 62. The connection between divine promise and vindication unites both texts.

Nephi quotes Isaiah's prophecies of Jerusalem's restoration, explicitly connecting Zion's future glory to the Lamb of God. The Book of Mormon contextualizes Isaiah 62 within Christ-centered eschatology.

John's vision of the New Jerusalem echoes Isaiah's language: the city has no need of the sun, for God's glory illuminates it, and the nations walk in its light—the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah 62:1's promise of Zion as a burning lamp.

commentary.historical_context: Isaiah 62 was composed during or after the Babylonian exile (after 539 BCE), when Jerusalem lay in ruins. The historical context of the audience was devastation: the temple destroyed, the walls broken, the population decimated or deported. To these people, the promise of restoration was not abstract theology but desperate hope. The language of 'not holding peace' would have resonated powerfully with those who felt abandoned by God. The speaker's refusal to be silent echoed the cries of the remnant themselves, suggesting that God's silence was about to end and His voice would restore what was lost. The imagery of brightness and burning lamp was drawn from ancient Near Eastern royal iconography: a city's glory was its light, visible from afar, drawing merchants and allies. For a ruined Jerusalem, the promise that it would shine again as a beacon was a promise of restored significance in the international order.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 10:8-10 quotes this section of Isaiah and places it squarely within the messianic framework: Nephi explicitly states that the 'Lamb of God' will be the agent of restoration, suggesting that the 'I' who will not hold his peace in Isaiah 62:1 may be the Savior Himself, interceding for Zion. The Book of Mormon interprets Isaiah's eschatological vision through the lens of Christ's central role in redemptive history.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:62-92 discusses the restoration of all things and God's work to sanctify and prepare His people. Isaiah 62:1's refusal to rest echoes the urgency and totality of the Restoration—God will not rest until all is fulfilled. The parallelism between divine persistence and the work of the Restoration runs throughout Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The brightness and light emanating from Zion (Isaiah 62:1) connects to the temple as the source of God's presence and truth in the latter days. The temple Mount is the literal and spiritual center from which God's light radiates to the nations (D&C 110:1-8). Isaiah's vision of Zion as a burning lamp finds its counterpart in the temple as the house of light and holiness.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'I' who will not hold his peace until Zion is vindicated can be read as the Messiah, the eternal Intercessor. Christ's role as advocate for His people finds expression in this relentless commitment to Zion's restoration. The refusal to rest parallels Christ's intercession at the right hand of God (Hebrews 7:25). Moreover, the visibility of righteousness and salvation 'as brightness and a lamp' points to Christ as 'the light of the world' (John 8:12), whose sacrifice and resurrection are the source of Zion's ultimate vindication. The eschatological fulfillment of Zion's restoration depends on and flows from Christ's atonement.
commentary.application: For modern members of the Church, Isaiah 62:1 invites reflection on personal and communal advocacy. Just as the speaker refuses silence and rest until Zion is restored, members are called to speak and work for the advancement of God's kingdom without ceasing. The verse challenges spiritual passivity. Zion in the latter-day context is not only Jerusalem but the Church itself—God's covenant community. The promise that righteousness and salvation will 'go forth as brightness' speaks to the visible, undeniable witness of a Christlike people. The invitation is to align oneself with God's purposes for the latter-day restoration, recognizing that His work cannot be hurried or hindered, but neither can it be silent. Members can embody the watchmen's role (referenced in verse 6) by speaking without ceasing about the restoration of all things in Christ.

text_kjv: And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness, and all kings thy glory: and thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the LORD shall name.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 expands the vision of verse 1 with a concrete result: the nations will witness Zion's vindication. The movement from internal reality (righteousness and salvation in Zion) to external recognition (the Gentiles and all kings seeing it) defines the eschatological reversal. Zion, long despised and dismissed by the nations, will become so visibly righteous and glorious that even the kings of the earth—symbols of worldly power—cannot ignore it. This is a radical inversion of exile experience, when Jerusalem was looked upon with contempt by foreign powers. The promise reaches beyond political vindication to spiritual and moral transformation: the nations will see not merely that Jerusalem is restored but that it embodies righteousness and glory.

The climactic element is the new name. In ancient Near Eastern thought, a name was not a mere label but an identity. To be given a new name by God was to have one's essential nature transformed and God's ownership declared. The insistence that this name comes from 'the mouth of the LORD'—not chosen by committee or merely adopted through cultural change—emphasizes God's direct agency. The name speaks what God sees: Zion is no longer the city of exile but the city of divine delight and restoration. This theme will be fully developed in verse 4, where the specific new names are revealed: 'Hephzibah' (My Delight Is in Her) and 'Beulah' (Married).

word_study.meaning: Nations, peoples, typically non-Israelite peoples or the international community at large. The term carries no inherent negative connotation but marks otherness from Israel.
word_study.significance: The gôyim seeing Zion's righteousness signals the internationalization of Israel's restoration. This is not private vindication but public, universal recognition. The Gentiles' witness becomes part of Zion's vindication—their testimony that God's people have been transformed.

word_study.meaning: Glory, honor, weight, substance. Often denotes God's manifest presence and splendor. Can refer to wealth, reputation, or the visible evidence of divine favor.
word_study.significance: Kâvôd is the substance of presence, not mere appearance. All kings seeing Zion's glory means they perceive the weight of God's favor resting upon it. This is not superficial reputation but the visible evidence of divine endorsement.

word_study.meaning: A new or fresh name. The adjective châdâsh emphasizes newness and freshness, suggesting something unprecedented, not merely a restoration of an old name.
word_study.significance: The 'newness' of the name indicates that Zion's restored identity is not simply a return to a former state but a transformation into something unprecedented. This aligns with Isaiah's broader theme of God making 'new things' (Isaiah 43:19). The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on this name coming from God's mouth underscores divine authorship of identity.

word_study.meaning: The mouth of the LORD—a personified image emphasizing God's direct speech and decree. God's word spoken from His mouth is the instrument of creation and restoration (as in Genesis 1).
word_study.significance: God's mouth is the locus of creative power. Just as God spoke creation into existence ('Let there be...'), He speaks Zion's new name into existence. This is not a bureaucratic renaming but a creative act of divine speech. Names given by God's mouth carry ontological weight—they declare not merely what is desired but what shall be.

cross_references.connection: God declares to Israel, 'I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.' Isaiah 62:2 extends this promise: the new name itself becomes a public declaration of ownership and restoration.

The eunuch and the foreigner are promised a name within God's house that is 'better than of sons and of daughters.' Isaiah 62:2 shows that Zion itself receives a new name from God's mouth—the ultimate bestowal of identity and belonging.

The overcomers are promised 'a new name written in a stone, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.' The theme of God bestowing new names as marks of restoration and redemption continues in Revelation's eschatology.

The Lord states that all things that pertain to God have a celestial name. The promise that Zion receives a name from God's mouth aligns with Doctrine and Covenants teaching on the cosmic significance of divine naming.

Jacob teaches that the wise and great shall become as nothing, and the wicked shall perish while Zion is established. Isaiah 62:2's vision of all kings seeing Zion's glory is the culmination of this spiritual reversal Jacob announces.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic and post-exilic period, Jerusalem and Judah bore the names of their shame: 'Forsaken' (Azuvah, which appears in verse 4) and 'Desolate' (Shemamah). These were not merely descriptive but were internalized identities. The exile itself was understood in terms of name: Israel was called by the name of its enemy, Babylon. To be given a new name by God was to reclaim identity and agency. In the ancient Near East, when a conqueror took a city, renaming it was a standard act of annexation. Isaiah 62:2 reverses this: God, not a foreign enemy, claims the right to rename Zion, and the renaming signifies restoration, not subjugation. The promise that 'all kings' shall see Zion's glory would have been extraordinarily bold to an audience living in the ruins of Jerusalem, with the city's former kings dead or exiled. This is eschatological language: the promise belongs to a future when the balance of world power is fundamentally reordered.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 13:37 speaks of the restored gospel going forth 'unto the ends of the earth' and the nations seeing the light of Israel. Isaiah 62:2's theme of the nations seeing Zion's righteousness and glory parallels the Book of Mormon's vision of the Restoration reaching all peoples.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 65:2-6 describes how the kingdom of God shall fill the whole earth and all nations shall see the glory of the Lord. The Restoration explicitly fulfills Isaiah 62:2's promise that the nations and kings shall witness Zion's vindication. Joseph Smith's call as prophet in D&C 21:4 includes the promise that his 'word shall be my word'—direct divine speech—echoing the Isaian principle that God's mouth authorizes all declarations about His people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the mechanism by which the nations come to see Zion's glory. D&C 110:7-10 describes the Lord's appearance in the Kirtland Temple and His acceptance of the building, with the promise that His glory shall be upon the house. The visible light and presence associated with the temple fulfill Isaiah's vision of nations seeing Zion's glory.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the one whose name is above every name (Philippians 2:9-10), given by the mouth of God. Isaiah 62:2's promise that Zion receives a new name from God's mouth prefigures the transformation wrought by Christ. The 'new name' motif applies both to Zion corporately and to individual members of the body of Christ (Revelation 2:17, 3:12). Christ's name, spoken by God, is the power by which all things are renamed and restored. In Isaiah's Christology, the Servant who speaks on behalf of God (Isaiah 42:5, 51:16) is the one through whom God's mouth accomplishes restoration.
commentary.application: For members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the promise that the nations will see Zion's righteousness and glory is a call to live as representatives of that glory. The covenant community is known by its fruits (Matthew 7:16-20). When non-members observe the ethical conduct, generosity, and devotion of Latter-day Saints, they witness 'Zion's righteousness' in action. The new name promised in this verse can be understood personally as well: each individual in covenant with God receives a new name through the sealing ordinances of the temple, signifying transformation and belonging to God's household. The verse invites reflection on whether one's personal conduct, and the Church's corporate witness, reflects the righteousness and glory that would draw the world to recognize God's hand in Zion.

text_kjv: Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 presents one of scripture's most profound reversals of status. Zion is not crowned; Zion is the crown. The city is not adorned by a crown but is itself the object of ultimate value and honor, held in God's hand. This is a complete inversion of the exile experience, when Jerusalem was trampled and its treasures looted by Babylonian conquerors. Now, instead of being stripped of crowns and jewels, Zion becomes the crown that God wears. The image contains a stunning intimacy: the crown is not merely possessed by God but held in His hand—close, precious, constantly attended to.

The parallelism reinforces the exclusivity of Zion's honor: 'crown' and 'royal diadem' are near-synonyms, both symbols of supreme authority and beauty. The repetition of 'in the hand of' (בְּיַד) emphasizes personal possession and care. God does not merely acknowledge Zion as restored; He holds it, treasures it, displays it. The corporate meaning is clear: the covenant community has been elevated from the lowest humiliation to the highest honor in God's estimation. Nothing in the international order—no kingdom's military might or wealth—compares to the value God places upon His restored people.

word_study.meaning: A crown, wreath, or circlet. Denotes royal authority and beauty. Often used metaphorically for honor and dignity.
word_study.significance: Atéret emphasizes the circular, encompassing nature of honor—it goes all around, complete and total. Zion is not partially honored but fully crowned in divine estimation. The term connects Zion's restoration to its role as the seat of God's kingdom on earth.

word_study.meaning: Glory, beauty, splendor, adornment. Often denotes aesthetic and spiritual radiance. In Kabbalah, Tiferet represents the central sphere, the heart of creation.
word_study.significance: Tiferet adds a dimension beyond kingship: not merely political authority but beauty and radiance. Zion's crown is not only a sign of power but of comeliness. The restoration is aesthetic as well as moral.

word_study.meaning: A turban, headdress, or diadem worn by kings and priests. Denotes both royal and priestly dignity. Associated with the high priest's mitre in the Temple service.
word_study.significance: Tzníf connects Zion's restoration to both kingly and priestly functions. Zion is not only a political entity but a spiritual center, a place where God's people exercise priestly authority before the nations. The dual crown-and-diadem imagery indicates both temporal and spiritual sovereignty.

word_study.meaning: Hand, arm, or power. Metaphorically, signifies agency, possession, protection, and authority. 'In the hand of' typically indicates possession, control, or intimate care.
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'in the hand of the LORD' and 'in the hand of thy God' (twice in one verse) emphasizes personal, protective possession. God does not set Zion on a distant throne but holds it close, in His hand, suggesting both power and tenderness. The hand that creates and sustains also holds and treasures.

cross_references.connection: The nations shall bring Israel's sons and daughters: 'Thus saith the LORD God, Behold, I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles...and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles.' Isaiah 62:3 completes this vision—Zion is lifted up as a crown in God's hand.

The psalm laments that God has 'cast off the crown of thy servant' and brought him low. Isaiah 62:3 is the answer to this lament: God restores and lifts up the crown of His people, holding it in His hand.

Zechariah prophesies that the LORD will save His people on that day 'as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land.' The same imagery of God's people as precious stones in God's hand appears here.

The Lord promises that the light of those who have forsaken all shall shine 'as the sun' and their 'dominion shall be an everlasting dominion.' Isaiah 62:3's promise of Zion as a crown in God's hand is the fulfillment of this covenant promise to the faithful.

Peter calls the Church 'a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people' chosen to show forth God's praises. Isaiah 62:3's image of Zion as a crown and diadem in God's hand describes the exact status Peter announces for the body of Christ.

commentary.historical_context: In the historical context of post-exilic Judah, the promise that Zion is a crown in God's hand would have been received as restorative medicine for a deeply wounded people. Archaeological and textual evidence shows that Jerusalem in the early post-exilic period was a modest settlement—the walls broken, the temple rebuilding incomplete for decades, the population still reduced. To such a community, the assertion that they were God's crown would have functioned as a proclamation of invisible worth beneath visible weakness. The image also invoked royal ideology: in ancient Near Eastern thought, a king's crown was his most precious possession, the symbol of his authority and legitimacy. For God to claim Zion as His crown was to assert that Zion held the same centrality in God's kingdom as a crown held in an earthly king's estimation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 10:8-9 states that the Lamanites shall 'become a righteous people...and there shall be no more wars and contentions among you; and the Lord shall dwell in the midst of you, and ye shall be called the children of the Lord.' The covenantal elevation promised here mirrors Isaiah 62:3's vision of Zion exalted as God's crown.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 105:12 declares that the Church shall be established and shall be reckoned as God's kingdom. D&C 86:1-2 calls the Church 'the church and kingdom of God' and connects it explicitly to the covenant with Abraham. Isaiah 62:3 describes the Church's status in God's hand—precious, held, honored.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple crown—the mitre worn by the high priest in ancient worship—is connected to this verse. In latter-day temple worship, members are promised blessings and crowns of glory. Isaiah 62:3 suggests that the covenant community itself functions as the crown of God's restoration, and the temple is the place where this relationship is sealed and sanctified.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is described in Hebrews 1:3 as 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.' Zion, as God's crown, points to Christ as the jewel of creation, the one held in God's hand. Furthermore, Christ is crowned with many crowns (Revelation 19:12), and those who overcome are promised crowns (2 Timothy 4:8). Isaiah 62:3 suggests that Zion's exaltation is inseparable from and dependent upon Christ's centrality to God's plan. The crown rests in God's hand because Christ, through His atoning sacrifice, made possible the restoration of God's covenant people.
commentary.application: For modern Church members, Isaiah 62:3 is a profound statement about personal and communal worth. Each individual who enters into covenant with God is part of Zion, God's crown. This is not earned through worldly achievement but is a gift of God's grace—a status that is 'in the hand of the LORD,' secure and precious. The verse invites a recalibration of values: in a world that judges worth by wealth, status, or power, Isaiah's vision declares that the covenant community's worth is determined solely by God's own estimation. They are His crown. Practically, this should inform how members view themselves and the Church. When facing trials or living in a world that dismisses or mocks the Church, members can hold fast to this truth: in God's hand, the Church is His crown, His most precious possession. The challenge is to live in a manner worthy of that crown—to reflect the beauty and righteousness befitting God's crown held in His hand.

text_kjv: Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 moves from metaphor to direct declaration: Zion's names are changed. The old names—'Forsaken' (Azuvah, עֲזוּבָה) and 'Desolate' (Shemamah, שְׁמָמָה)—are erased and replaced with new names that express God's relationship to Zion. This is not merely symbolic renaming but a reversal of identity and destiny. During the exile and its aftermath, Jerusalem and Judah were known by the names of their shame. These names were internalized by the people themselves—they believed themselves forsaken and desolate. The promise here is that these internalized identities will be obliterated by new names spoken by God Himself.

The new names carry extraordinary significance. 'Hephzibah' (חֶפְצִי־בָהּ) literally means 'My Delight Is in Her'—a radical reversal of the exile theology that God had abandoned His people. God now explicitly declares that He delights in Zion, that she is the object of His joy. Historically, Hephzibah was the name of Hezekiah's wife (2 Kings 21:1), creating a link to Judah's royal past and suggesting restoration of not just political but dynastic continuity. 'Beulah' (בְּעוּלָה) means 'Married' and evokes the marital covenant imagery that will dominate verse 5. The land, widowed by exile, is now claimed and possessed by God as a husband claims a bride. These names are not ornaments but declarations of restored covenant relationship. The reasoning is explicit: 'for the LORD delighteth in thee'—God's delight is the source of restoration.

word_study.meaning: Forsaken, abandoned, desolate. The Hebrew root עזב (â-zav) means to abandon, to leave behind. Azuvah is the feminine form, indicating a forsaken woman or place.
word_study.significance: The old name embedded in Zion's identity the theology of abandonment. To cease being called Azuvah is to claim that God's abandonment during exile was not permanent and does not define her ultimate identity. The name change is existential restoration. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the dramatic erasure of this name from Zion's identity.

word_study.meaning: Desolate, waste, destruction. The Hebrew root שמם (shâ-mam) means to be stunned, astonished, desolate. Shemamah describes physical ruin and the emotional state of devastation.
word_study.significance: Shemamah was the experiential reality of post-exilic Jerusalem. The promise that this name will no longer apply indicates not just physical reconstruction but the end of spiritual devastation. The land will be healed not merely materially but in its essential nature.

word_study.meaning: My Delight Is in Her. Literally: חֶפְצִי (my delight, my pleasure) + בָהּ (in her). Expresses God's emotional and volitional joy in Zion.
word_study.significance: This name inverts the exile experience entirely. Instead of 'Forsaken,' Zion is now 'My Delight.' God's pleasure, not His judgment, characterizes His relationship to Zion. The name makes divine emotion—specifically, God's delight—the foundation of Zion's identity. The historical bearer of this name (Hezekiah's wife) anchors the promise in royal history. The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'My Delight Is in Her,' preserving the intimate, personal declaration.

word_study.meaning: Married. The Hebrew root בעל (ba'al) means both to marry/possess sexually and to be lord/master. Be'ulah indicates a land that is claimed, possessed, and loved by a husband.
word_study.significance: Beulah signals the end of widowhood—the state of a land abandoned and ownerless (implied in Shemamah). The covenant relationship is expressed through marital imagery: Zion is no longer a widow but a married woman, claimed and cherished. The Covenant Rendering notes that ba'al implies both marriage and lordship, suggesting that God's claim on the land is intimate and complete. Verse 5 will extend this imagery.

word_study.meaning: To delight in, to take pleasure in, to have favor toward. Indicates not mere obligation but emotional affection and active goodwill.
word_study.significance: The verb châ-fetz moves beyond judgment or duty to affection. God's relationship to Zion is characterized not by distant sovereignty but by delight. This word becomes the basis for the new name Hephzibah and grounds the entire promise in divine emotion, not just divine decree. The presence of this verb 'for the LORD delighteth in thee' provides the reason for the renaming—God's pleasure in Zion is not contingent on her performance but is the source of her restoration.

word_study.meaning: To marry, to take a wife, to possess. In some contexts, to be lord over. The verb expresses both conjugal and proprietary relationship.
word_study.significance: The verb bâ-'al as applied to the land indicates that Zion will be possessed and cherished as a bride is possessed by a bridegroom. The covenant relationship is marital: intimate, exclusive, and permanent. The promise 'thy land shall be married' (passive voice in KJV) indicates that God is the active agent—He will marry the land, claiming it as His own.

cross_references.connection: Earlier in Isaiah, the prophet promises that shame and reproach will be forgotten and the woman (Zion) will remember no more the reproach of widowhood. Isaiah 62:4 fulfills this promise: the old names of shame (Forsaken, Desolate) are erased.

Hosea describes God betrothing Israel to Himself 'in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.' The marital covenant imagery in Isaiah 62:4 parallels Hosea's vision of divine marriage to the people.

Hephzibah was historically the name of Hezekiah's wife. Isaiah 62:4's use of this name creates a deliberate link between eschatological restoration and royal history, suggesting that Zion's future includes the restoration of Davidic kingship.

The kingdom of God shall triumph, and 'all nations shall see the glory of the Lord.' Isaiah 62:4's promise that Zion will no longer be called Forsaken but Hephzibah describes the kingdom that D&C 65 promises will fill the earth.

Those who overcome are promised that 'I will write upon him the name of my God...and I will write upon him my new name.' Isaiah 62:4 prefigures this promise of divine renaming as the mark of ultimate restoration.

commentary.historical_context: The historical situation was acute. After the Babylonian exile (587-539 BCE), Jerusalem remained in ruins for decades. The temple rebuilding (begun c. 520 BCE) proceeded slowly and incompletely. The population remained drastically reduced—many who were exiled never returned. The psychological and spiritual weight of this situation cannot be overstated: the people themselves had internalized names of shame. The book of Lamentations, composed in the same period, expresses the anguish of Zion's abandonment in raw terms. To such a people, Isaiah 62:4 offered not just political hope but existential restoration. The specific use of 'Hephzibah'—a royal woman's name—would have invoked memories of Hezekiah's era, a time of relative stability and prosperity before the final catastrophe. The promise was that such restoration would return. The marital imagery ('Beulah,' 'married') was drawn from ancient Near Eastern concepts of land ownership and covenant: a land without a lord was considered desolate and vulnerable; when claimed by a powerful and loving husband-figure, it was restored and protected.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 3 Nephi 20:32-35 quotes Isaiah 54:1-2 and applies it to the restored covenant people. The theme of erasing shame and restoring identity through God's covenant is central to Book of Mormon theology. Isaiah 62:4's renaming fits this pattern: the restored people's old names of shame are replaced by new names of covenant belonging.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 103:19-20 describes the New Jerusalem that will be built: 'Blessed are you for receiving mine everlasting covenant, even the fulness of my gospel.' The renaming of Zion in Isaiah 62:4 parallels the establishment of the New Jerusalem in latter-day revelation. The names Hephzibah and Beulah express God's covenant relationship to His restored people in the Latter-day Saint context.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where Zion's restoration is sealed and sanctified. In temple worship, covenants are renewed and identities are transformed through covenant making. The renaming in Isaiah 62:4 is reflected in the promises given to endowed members that they will receive 'a new name' in the temple—a name known only to God and the holder, signifying transformation and covenant belonging. The temple makes literal and personal what Isaiah speaks of corporately.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's renaming in Isaiah's prophecies is significant: He is called 'Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace' (Isaiah 9:6). The principle that God renames His covenant people as an act of restoration and redemption centers on Christ. He is the one through whom all identity is renewed in the Restoration. The Apostle Paul speaks of being 'in Christ' as receiving a new identity (2 Corinthians 5:17: 'old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new'). Isaiah 62:4's promise of new names for Zion is inseparable from Christ's role as the agent of that transformation.
commentary.application: For Church members, Isaiah 62:4 speaks to the transformative power of covenant. Each individual who enters into covenant with God in the temple receives a new name and a new identity: no longer defined by the world's judgments (Forsaken, Desolate, limited, unworthy), but claimed by God as His own (Hephzibah, Beulah—Delight, Married to the Divine). The verse challenges members to release the old names the world has given them—whether of shame, failure, or limitation—and accept the names God speaks: worthy, beloved, claimed. Corporately, the verse invites members to understand the Church's mission as the restoration of Zion's true identity in the world. The Church is not 'forsaken' by history or irrelevant to the modern world; rather, it is the object of God's delight and the bride of Christ. Living this identity means reflecting in conduct and testimony the reality that the Lord delights in His people and His Church, and that membership is a marital covenant—intimate, binding, and transformative.

text_kjv: For as a young man marrieth a virgin, so shall thy sons marry thee: and as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 extends the marital covenant imagery of verse 4 and adds an extraordinary element: divine emotion. The verse contains two parallel comparisons, both drawn from the joy of a wedding. The first—'As a young man marrieth a virgin, so shall thy sons marry thee'—has generated interpretive discussion. The KJV reading 'thy sons marry thee' suggests that Zion's own children will rebuild and repossess the land, extending the marital imagery to familial restoration. An alternative reading (reflected in some scholars' analysis of the Hebrew) might have 'builders' (bonayikh) instead of 'sons' (banaikh)—a single letter difference—making the sense 'as a young man marries a virgin, so shall thy builders rebuild you.' Either way, the point is clear: restoration comes through committed, joyful engagement (the joy of new marriage) on the part of those who belong to Zion.

The second comparison climaxes the verse and arguably the entire passage: 'As the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee.' Here is the apex of Isaiah's vision: God's emotion toward Zion is not merely protective or providential but joyful, exuberant, celebratory. God rejoices over Zion as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride—with delight, wonder, and love. This is not the God of judgment alone but of covenant intimacy. The Covenant Rendering brings out the tenderness: the affection is mutual and reciprocal. God does not merely restore Zion from above; He delights in her, and His delight is the ground of her restoration. For an audience that had experienced exile as divine abandonment and punishment, this promise—that God would rejoice over them—was radical grace.

word_study.meaning: To marry, to take as wife, to possess with conjugal and proprietary right. The verb encompasses both the emotional bond of marriage and the legal claim.
word_study.significance: The verb bâ-'al emphasizes that marriage is both intimate bonding and public, covenant commitment. When Zion's sons marry her (or builders rebuild her), they engage in an act of possession and protection that echoes God's marriage to the land in verse 4.

word_study.meaning: A virgin woman, a young woman of marriageable age. Signifies both youth and purity, often evoking a woman's complete availability for a new covenant bond.
word_study.significance: The comparison of Zion to a virgin suggests that despite the devastation of exile, Zion retains the potential for new, unblemished relationship. The virgin state implies hope and renewal, not corruption or permanent defilement.

word_study.meaning: A bridegroom, a newly married man. In biblical thought, the bridegroom represents the height of human joy and celebration.
word_study.significance: The use of châ-tan elevates the comparison: God is not merely a husband but a bridegroom—one in the first flush of marital joy. This suggests that God's rejoicing is not a settled, distant approval but an active, present, joyful state. The imagery draws on the wedding imagery of the Psalms (Psalm 45) and Song of Solomon.

word_study.meaning: To rejoice, to be glad, to take joy in. A strong verb indicating exuberant, active delight.
word_study.significance: The verb sus is not quiet contentment but active, expressed rejoicing. When God rejoices over Zion as a bridegroom over his bride, He is not merely satisfied but delighted, exultant. This verb appears in contexts of celebration and triumph (Psalm 68:3: 'the righteous be glad; let them rejoice before God: yea, let them exceedingly rejoice'). For Isaiah's audience, the assertion that God would actively, exultantly rejoice over them was almost incomprehensible grace—the inverse of exile.

word_study.meaning: A bride, a newly married woman. The feminine counterpart to bridegroom, emphasizing youth, beauty, and the beginning of a covenant bond.
word_study.significance: The pairing of bridegroom and bride in Isaiah 62:5 evokes the mutual joy of new marriage. When God rejoices over Zion 'as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride,' the comparison suggests a relationship of mutual beauty and delight, not merely one-way command or dominance.

cross_references.connection: This royal wedding psalm describes a king rejoicing over his bride, declaring 'Hearken, O daughter...forget also thine own people.' Isaiah 62:5's image of the bridegroom rejoicing echoes this psalm's vision of conjugal joy as the model for covenantal relationship.

Solomon's bride is celebrated: 'Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals.' Isaiah 62:5 applies bridal imagery to Zion corporately, making the entire city the object of divine joy.

Jeremiah prophesies restoration: 'I will cause the captivity of Judah and the captivity of Israel to return...and I will cleanse them from all their iniquity...and it shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and an honor before all the nations.' Isaiah 62:5's promise of God's rejoicing parallels Jeremiah's vision of restoration as God's joy.

The prophet declares that the Lord 'will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.' This passage explicitly expresses God's rejoicing over His people, mirroring Isaiah 62:5's climactic vision.

The Lord describes His work as preparing the earth and His people for glory: 'I am the Lord your God, even the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.' The covenant joy promised in Isaiah 62:5 is the basis of the Restoration's central promise: that God takes pleasure in His faithful people.

commentary.historical_context: In the post-exilic period, wedding celebrations in the ancient Near East were occasions of communal joy lasting several days. The choice of wedding imagery to describe Zion's restoration would have resonated with a culture that understood marriage as the apex of human joy and commitment. The dead who returned from exile or their descendants faced the daunting task of rebuilding Jerusalem—politically, spiritually, and psychologically. To be told that their work of rebuilding was not a grim duty but an act of joyful participation in God's work (like a young man marrying a virgin, taking possession with joy) was transformative. Moreover, the assurance that God Himself rejoiced over the restored Zion inverted the theology of exile, where God's silence and apparent absence had seemed to indicate abandonment or wrath. Isaiah's promise reconnected the people to the covenant theology of their ancestors, in which God's delight in His people was the foundation of all blessing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 8:1-2 cites and applies Isaiah 54:1-2 to the covenant people in the Latter-day context, promising that 'the barren shall have many more children than she which hath an husband.' The imagery of Zion as a joyfully restored woman, blessed with increase, parallels Isaiah 62:5's vision of covenant joy and fruitfulness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:72-74 (Kirtland Temple dedication prayer) expresses the covenant relationship between God and His people in terms of mutual delight and belonging. The concept of God rejoicing over His covenant people, central to Isaiah 62:5, is echoed in Joseph Smith's theology of eternal covenant relationship. D&C 131-132 on celestial marriage extends this imagery: marriage is the highest covenant, reflecting the relationship between God and His people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sealing ordinance of marriage in the temple is the personal, familial counterpart to Isaiah 62:5's vision of Zion as God's bride. When a couple is sealed in the temple, they enter into a covenant that reflects the bridegroom-bride relationship Isaiah describes. The joy of sealing is understood as a foretaste of the joy with which God receives His covenant people. Temple marriages, in Latter-day Saint theology, are an enactment of the cosmic marriage between God and His restored people.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the Bridegroom, and the Church is His Bride (Ephesians 5:25-32; 2 Corinthians 11:2; Revelation 19:7-9). Isaiah 62:5's image of the bridegroom rejoicing over the bride is ultimately fulfilled in Christ's relationship to His Church. The rejoicing of God over Zion is expressed through Christ, who 'loved the church, and gave himself for it' (Ephesians 5:25). The marital covenant imagery, stretched through Isaiah's entire restoration prophecy, culminates in Christ as the Bridegroom who lays down His life for His bride and will rejoice over her eternally.
commentary.application: For Church members, Isaiah 62:5 communicates a radical truth about the covenant relationship: God is not distant or grudging in His relationship to His people, but actively, joyfully delighted in them. This should transform how members understand prayer, service, and the spiritual life. Just as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so God rejoices over those who enter into covenant with Him. This joy is not earned through perfect performance but is the foundation of the covenantal relationship itself. Practically, this verse invites members to experience covenant not as burden but as joy—the joy of belonging to God and of participating in His work of restoration. For those who are married, the verse invites them to see their marriage as a reflection of God's covenant joy, a sanctuary in which divine delight is experienced in human form. For the Church corporately, the verse affirms that the work of restoration—rebuilding Zion, making disciples of all nations—is not grim obligation but participation in God's joy. This reframes service and mission: members are not laborers toiling at a thankless task but partners in God's exultant restoration of all things.

text_kjv: I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,
text_kjv_continued: and give him no rest, till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 shifts from promise to calling. God has already set watchmen on Jerusalem's walls—but these are not military sentinels. They are intercessors, prophetic voices whose entire function is intercession. The phrase 'make mention of the LORD' (hamazkirim et YHWH) literally means 'those who remind the LORD,' suggesting a stunning theology: these watchmen have a vocation that includes reminding God of His promises. This is not a picture of humans manipulating a forgetful God but of authorized intercessors engaging in covenant advocacy. Their refusal to be silent 'day nor night' indicates the totality of their commitment—not occasional prayers but constant, unceasing intercession.

The command structure is remarkable: 'keep not silence, and give him no rest, till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.' Here is an instruction to God Himself (or more accurately, in Jewish prayer tradition, an instruction to human intercessors to press their petition before God) to not rest until Jerusalem is established as a praise throughout the earth. This is not disrespectful presumption but covenant partnership. The intercessors are not imposing their will on God but persistently holding Him to His own promises. They are standing in the gap, as Moses stood in Exodus 32:11-13, pleading for God's people and reminding Him of His covenants. For a people who believed they had been forsaken and were powerless to change their circumstances, the gift of this intercessory vocation was empowering: they could not rebuild Jerusalem by military might or political maneuvering, but they could cry out in prayer, and in doing so, they became God's agents of restoration through persistent intercession.

word_study.meaning: Watchmen, guards, keepers. Those who keep watch, maintain vigilance, guard and protect. In prophetic literature, often metaphorically referring to prophets or intercessors who maintain spiritual vigilance.
word_study.significance: The shomerim in verse 6 are not military sentries but spiritual watchmen. Their 'watching' is prayerful intercession. The term connects to God as Israel's 'keeper' or 'watchman' in Psalm 121:4 ('He that keepeth thee will not slumber'). Human watchmen mirror God's own vigil over His people. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'watchmen' as those posted on the walls to maintain the city's spiritual vigilance.

word_study.meaning: Walls, ramparts, defenses. Literally, the physical walls surrounding a city. Metaphorically, the spiritual protection and sanctity of the covenant community.
word_study.significance: The watchmen are positioned on the walls—the boundary between Zion and the outside world. Their intercession is a spiritual wall, a protective prayer covering over the city. In Isaiah's eschatology, Zion is defended not by military strength but by prayer and righteousness. The walls are spiritual before they are physical.

word_study.meaning: To be silent, to keep quiet, to refrain from speech. Here used negatively: they shall NOT hold their peace.
word_study.significance: This echo of verse 1 ('I will not hold my peace') ties the human intercessors to the divine speaker. Just as God refuses silence for Zion's sake, the watchmen refuse silence. They are aligned with and participating in God's own refusal to abandon Zion. The repetition of this term connects divine and human advocacy.

word_study.meaning: Those who remind, those who cause to remember. Literally, 'those who remind the LORD.' A unique phrase in Scripture emphasizing the function of intercessors as those who hold God to His covenant promises.
word_study.significance: This phrase is extraordinarily important. It suggests that intercessors have the authorized role of reminding God of His own covenants and promises. This is not human manipulation but covenant partnership. The intercessor stands before God and says, in effect, 'You have promised to restore Zion; I remind you of Your promise and press You to fulfill it.' The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'You who remind the LORD.' This vocation is empowering—it means that prayer is not passive petition but active, authorized partnership in God's work.

word_study.meaning: Give no rest, do not allow silence. The phrase carries the sense of pressing one's petition relentlessly, not allowing the matter to be dropped or forgotten.
word_study.significance: The instruction 'give him no rest' is extraordinary: human intercessors are commanded to persist in prayer until God acts. This is the language of Jacob wrestling with the angel (Genesis 32:26: 'I will not let thee go, except thou bless me'). Prayer is portrayed not as submissive acceptance but as urgent, persistent advocacy. The watchmen are given license to press their petition before God with unrelenting intensity.

word_study.meaning: Praise, glory, renown, acclaim. Can mean both the praise offered to God and the renown or reputation of a person or place. Often connected to public recognition and witness.
word_study.significance: Tehillah moves the vision beyond political restoration to public recognition and acclaim. Jerusalem will be 'a praise in the earth'—known throughout the world not for its military might but for its righteousness and God's favor upon it. The watchmen's intercession aims at this: that Jerusalem will become so blessed and righteous that it will be a subject of praise among all nations.

cross_references.connection: Moses stands in the gap, interceding for Israel and 'reminding' God of His covenant with Abraham: 'Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, thy servants, to whom thou swarest by thine own self.' Isaiah's watchmen mirror Moses' intercessory role, authorized to petition God persistently.

The psalm declares, 'He that keepeth thee will not slumber: behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.' Isaiah's watchmen participate in God's sleepless watchfulness over Zion, maintaining the vigil on earth that mirrors God's vigil in heaven.

Jesus teaches the parable of the persistent widow who continues asking the unjust judge until he grants her petition. He concludes: 'Shall not God avenge his own elect which cry day and night unto him?' Isaiah 62:6's watchmen who refuse silence day and night exemplify this authorized persistence in prayer.

The Lord declares, 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me.' Isaiah's watchmen who persistently remind God of His promises embody this principle of authorized, urgent intercession that invites God's engagement.

The saints in John's vision 'serve him day and night in his temple.' The watchmen of Isaiah 62:6 who refuse silence day and night are precursors to this vision of eternal, unceasing intercession before God's presence.

commentary.historical_context: In the post-exilic period, Jerusalem's actual walls were broken and undefended. The returnees from exile were a remnant, politically insignificant in the Persian empire. To promise that watchmen would be set on the walls who would 'never hold their peace' was to invert the reality of military powerlessness with spiritual power. The image draws on ancient Near Eastern watchtowers and city defenses, but spiritualizes them: Zion's defense is prayer, not weaponry. This was revolutionary theology for a small, weak community that could not defend itself by force. It affirmed that their primary power lay in covenant relationship with God, accessed through intercession. The phrase 'those who remind the LORD' also reflects ancient Near Eastern covenant language: in Hittite suzerainty treaties, the vassal was bound to 'remember' or 'invoke' the suzerain's name and covenant. Isaiah inverts this: Israel reminds God of His obligations to His people as vassal reminds suzerain of the treaty terms. This reflects post-exilic Judaism's development of intercession and prayer as central to covenant relationship, especially in contexts of political powerlessness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:17-18 describes how Alma cried 'nothing can save me except it be the condition of repentance; see, I am bound by the chains of my sin.' Isaiah 62:6's watchmen who intercede for Jerusalem prefigure the Book of Mormon's theology of persistent prayer and covenant renewal as the power that transforms communities and individuals.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109 (the Kirtland Temple dedication prayer) exemplifies intercessory prayer at length, with Joseph Smith leading the covenant community in reminding God of His promises and petitioning Him to establish Zion. The entire prayer embodies the intercessory role Isaiah describes for the watchmen—holding God (in covenant terms) to His promise to establish His kingdom. D&C 42:45-51 discusses the role of prayer and testimony in advancing the Lord's work, echoing the vocation of the watchmen.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where intercessory prayer is most fully realized. In temple worship and prayer, members stand in the literal and symbolic presence of God, interceding for their own salvation and the salvation of all people. Isaiah 62:6's watchmen who refuse silence and call upon God to remember His promises find their fullest expression in temple intercession. The temple endowment and sealing ordinances are understood in Latter-day Saint theology as authorized intercession, whereby those who enter the temple participate in God's work of salvation for all humanity.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate Intercessor, the one who 'ever liveth to make intercession for us' (Hebrews 7:25). Isaiah 62:6's watchmen who refuse silence and persistently remind God of His promises mirror Christ's eternal intercession. Christ stands before the Father and 'reminds' Him—in covenant terms—of His work for the salvation of humanity. Moreover, Christ as the High Priest enters once into the holy place, bearing the prayers of all God's people (Hebrews 9:24-26). The watchmen on Jerusalem's walls participate in this intercessory office. The ultimate fulfillment of verse 6 is that Christ's intercession is so powerful and persistent that all things are brought into submission to God's sovereign purposes, making Jerusalem—and by extension, all of Zion—'a praise in the earth.'
commentary.application: For Church members, Isaiah 62:6 contains a revolutionary calling: the vocation of intercessor is not reserved for prophets or priests but is available to all members who enter into covenant. Each member can be a watchman on Zion's walls, refusing to hold peace, persistently reminding God (in prayer) of His promises to establish His kingdom. The verse invites members to understand prayer not as a private, passive activity but as active, authorized participation in God's work. The specific phrase 'give him no rest' liberates members from the notion that persistent prayer is somehow presumptuous or bothersome to God. Rather, God invites and empowers His people to press their petitions before Him, to remind Him of His covenants, and to hold Him (in covenant terms) to His word. Practically, this means that when a member feels burdened for a family member's salvation, for the advancement of the Church, or for the establishment of Zion in the world, that burden is not a distraction but a call to intercessory vigilance. The watchmen's vocation—to speak and pray without ceasing—is open to all who covenant to stand on Zion's walls and refuse to let God rest until His promises are fulfilled. This transforms prayer from supplication to authorized advocacy, from hoping God will act to claiming in covenant language that He will.

text_kjv: And give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.

commentary.narrative: This verse presents one of scripture's boldest theological statements: the people of God are authorized—even commanded—to give the Lord no rest until His promises are fulfilled. This is not disrespectful presumption but covenant boldness rooted in God's own character and commitment. The prophet addresses those who serve as watchmen on Jerusalem's walls (verse 6), calling them to relentless intercession. The doubling of the condition—'till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth'—links two aspects of restoration: the internal establishment of the city and its external vindication before all nations. This reflects the pattern seen throughout Isaiah: Zion's restoration is not merely local but cosmic in significance, affecting how all peoples regard God's work.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew phrase translated 'give him no rest' (al-titnu domi lo) carries extraordinary weight. As the TCR notes, 'The boldness is breathtaking.' In ancient Near Eastern thought, the gods could be wearied or swayed by persistent petition, but the biblical God—who neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4)—is here portrayed as deliberately making Himself available to His people's prayers. This is not manipulation but covenant reciprocity: God has bound Himself to respond to the prayers of His people. The watchmen are told that their vigilance in prayer mirrors God's vigilance over the city. They are not praying against God's will but aligning themselves with His determined purpose. The restoration of Jerusalem as a 'praise in the earth' means that her redemption will become a testimony to all peoples of God's power and faithfulness.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The temporal markers—'till he establish' (ad yekhonen) and 'till he make' (ad yasim)—indicate that this prayer is not timeless but directed toward a specific eschatological moment. The watchmen are called to pray toward the future fulfillment that God has already decreed. This transforms prayer from passive waiting into active participation in God's redemptive timeline. The 'praise' (tehillah) that Jerusalem becomes is not mere human applause but recognition of divine majesty. Just as the heavens declare God's glory (Psalm 19:1), Jerusalem's restoration will declare His justice and mercy to the nations.

word_study.meaning: do not give silence/rest to Him; from dumi (silence, rest) and natan (give). The phrase expresses persistent, unrelenting prayer that refuses to accept delay or silence.
word_study.significance: This is covenant language asserting the people's right to hold God to His promises through prayer. The use of negative imperative ('do not give rest') rather than positive petition ('grant us') creates a tone of authorized boldness. In Abraham's intercession for Sodom (Genesis 18:27-33) and Jacob's wrestling with the angel (Genesis 32:26), we see similar patterns of God's people refusing to release Him until the covenant is honored.

word_study.meaning: to establish, make firm, set in place; from kun. Often used of God establishing His kingdom, covenant, or people in a place of security and permanence.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in the Hiphil stem, emphasizing God's active establishment. It carries both literal meaning (settling Jerusalem, rebuilding walls) and covenantal meaning (establishing the city as capital of God's kingdom). The same root appears in Psalm 89:37 regarding the establishment of David's throne.

word_study.meaning: praise, song of praise, glory, renown; that which is praised or admired. Often refers to praise offered to God, but here refers to something that elicits praise—Jerusalem becoming the object of universal admiration.
word_study.significance: The same word appears in the title 'Psalms' (Sefer Tehillim). Jerusalem is not merely restored but becomes a witness—a 'praise in the earth'—that testifies to all nations of God's faithfulness. This echoes the vision of Isaiah 2:2-3, where all nations stream to Zion because they recognize God's authority there.

cross_references.connection: God neither slumbers nor sleeps, yet the watchmen are called to keep vigilant prayer. This paradox—divine wakefulness combined with human intercession—shows that prayer participates in God's own watchfulness over His people.

Jacob refuses to let the angel go without a blessing, saying 'I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.' This is the same covenant boldness shown by the watchmen in Isaiah 62:7—authorized persistence in intercession.

The theme of God's reward coming with Him ('his reward is with him') is first introduced in 40:10. Isaiah 62:11 echoes this language, establishing continuity between the Servant's coming and the city's vindication.

Nephi sees that Zion 'shall be established in the last days' and all nations shall desire to know her. The Book of Mormon affirms that Jerusalem's restoration is central to the Lord's latter-day work.

commentary.historical_context: In the exilic and post-exilic period, Jerusalem's walls lay in rubble, and the city's status among nations was negligible. Foreign powers had stripped the temple and dispersed the people. When Isaiah speaks of making Jerusalem 'a praise in the earth,' he addresses a community whose very identity as a people is threatened. The watchmen on the walls (both literal guards and spiritual intercessors) represent a community clinging to God's promises when circumstances offer no visible confirmation. The practice of persistent prayer for national restoration reflects the ancient Jewish practice of corporate intercession during national crisis. In Nehemiah's time, the literal rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (which begins in 445 BCE) becomes the historical outworking of this spiritual reality: prayer and faithful action together accomplish restoration.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's vision in 1 Nephi 13:36-37 parallels this passage, showing that Zion will be established in the last days and will become a source of light and knowledge to all nations. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that Jerusalem's restoration is inseparable from the Restoration of the gospel itself. The watchmen motif also appears in Helaman 13-14, where prophets serve as watchmen warning the people to repent.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 113:7-10 directly quotes and interprets Isaiah 62:11, identifying the one who comes with His reward as the Savior and connecting it to latter-day redemption. This makes clear that the eschatological fulfillment Isaiah envisions is tied to Christ's second coming and the final gathering of Israel. The emphasis on persistent prayer and covenant boldness reflects D&C 46:7, where the Lord promises that all who ask in faith shall receive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The watchmen on Jerusalem's walls echo the role of temple workers and ordinance workers who serve in sacred space. Just as the watchmen maintain vigilant prayer for the city's restoration, those who participate in temple work maintain covenant connection between heaven and earth. The restoration of Jerusalem and the building of the temple are inseparably linked in Jewish restoration theology.

commentary.christological_typology: The persistent intercession commanded here points to Christ's own intercessory work at the right hand of the Father (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). Jesus, as the ultimate High Priest, makes perpetual intercession for the saints. Additionally, verse 7 anticipates the Savior's coming 'to establish and to make Jerusalem a praise'—His work of redemption transforms the city and all Zion into a testimony of divine justice and mercy. The 'watchmen' who refuse to give God rest anticipate the Latter-day Saint practice of covenant keeping and faithful intercession that hastens the Lord's work.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern members to understand prayer not as passive petition but as active covenant participation. The 'watchmen' are not waiting idly for God to act; they are engaged in vigilant, persistent intercession. For contemporary Latter-day Saints, this means refusing to accept spiritual complacency or to give 'rest' to our own prayers for family reconciliation, missionary work, temple completion, or the gathering of Israel. It authorizes boldness in prayer—not disrespectful presumption, but covenant-based confidence that God has bound Himself to respond. The verse also invites us to pray for Zion's vindication in the latter days, knowing that Jerusalem's restoration is integral to the Lord's redemptive plan. Our prayers for the success of the gospel, for temples to be built and dedicated, and for the promised return of dispersed Israel are not presumptuous but authorized by this very covenant language.

text_kjv: The LORD hath sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength, Surely I will no more give thy corn to be meat for thine enemies; and the sons of the stranger shall not drink thy wine, for the which thou hast laboured:

commentary.narrative: Having authorized His people to hold Him to His promises through prayer (verse 7), God now responds with an oath—the strongest possible assurance. The covenant formula 'The LORD hath sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength' invokes the most solemn self-binding language available to Him. As Hebrews 6:13 notes, 'for when God made promise to Abraham...by himself he sware.' Because there is none greater than God to swear by, He swears by His own person—His right hand (symbol of power and agency) and His mighty arm (symbol of redemptive strength). This oath is not a distant theological statement but directly addresses the people's historic trauma: foreign powers have systematically confiscated their harvests, consumed their grain, and drunk their wine.
commentary.narrative_continued: The specificity of the promise matters profoundly. God does not merely promise abstract blessing but addresses concrete, material injustice. For centuries, the people have labored in fields only to watch enemies take the harvest. This is not merely economic exploitation; it is a violation of covenant dignity. When a people cannot keep the fruit of their labor, they are reduced to servitude. The oath declares an end to this condition: 'I will no more give thy corn to be meat for thine enemies.' The repetition—no more, no more (the parallel clause about wine drives the point home)—creates an emphatic negation of the exile condition. This follows the theological pattern throughout Second Isaiah: restoration is not merely spiritual uplift but material, embodied dignity restored to God's people.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The phrase 'for the which thou hast laboured' shifts the focus from the enemy's consumption to the people's labor and legitimate claim to its fruits. This echoes Deuteronomy's covenant blessing: if you obey, you will eat what you sow (Deuteronomy 28:33 warns that foreigners shall eat what you labor for). The promise here reverses the curse: the people's labor will no longer be stolen. God's oath thus restores not just property but the right relationship between labor and its reward—fundamental to human dignity. The foreigners (sons of the stranger, benei nekar) represent not merely foreign nations but all forces of domination and injustice. When God swears this oath, He positions Himself against all systems that exploit the vulnerable and confiscate the laborer's due.

word_study.meaning: to swear an oath, take an oath, bind oneself by oath; from shebua (oath). The Niphal form indicates God placing Himself under oath obligation.
word_study.significance: This is the language of covenant binding. Unlike ordinary promises, an oath cannot be broken without God violating His own nature. The TCR translator notes that God 'swears an oath—the strongest possible assurance.' This appears in Hebrews 6:13-18, where the author explains that because God could swear by no one greater, He swore by Himself to confirm the promise to Abraham. Isaiah 62:8 is God's equivalent oath to the post-exilic community.

word_study.meaning: right hand; the hand of power, authority, and redemptive action. In covenant language, God's right hand is the instrument of salvation and judgment.
word_study.significance: Throughout Isaiah and the Psalms, God's right hand is the hand that saves (Isaiah 41:10), that leads (Psalm 23:6), and that executes justice. When God swears by His right hand, He places His redemptive power itself as surety for the oath. This echoes Exodus 15:12, where God's right hand 'becomes glorious in power' in delivering Israel from Egypt.

word_study.meaning: arm of His might/strength; uzza means strength, might, power. The arm represents capability; the strength emphasizes divine might that cannot be overcome.
word_study.significance: God's arm is the instrument by which He redeems His people (Isaiah 51:9, 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD'). When God swears by His arm of strength, He guarantees that His power stands behind the promise. No force of resistance can prevent the fulfillment.

word_study.meaning: grain, cereal crops, particularly wheat and barley; the staff of life in agrarian societies. Dagan was also the name of a Canaanite agricultural deity.
word_study.significance: The use of 'corn' (grain) rather than abstract blessing grounds the promise in the material necessities of survival. God cares about His people's ability to eat, to sustain life, to prosper in their fields. This is not spirituality divorced from material reality but integrated covenant care.

word_study.meaning: food, that which is eaten; from achal (to eat). In this context, it means the enemies will consume the grain—it will become their food.
word_study.significance: The simple word carries the weight of deprivation for the people and spoliation by enemies. God promises to end this reversal where the laborer loses his sustenance to the plunderer.

word_study.meaning: new wine, fresh wine, juice of the grape; specifically the produce of the vineyard before fermentation. Tirosh is often paralleled with 'corn' as the products of the Promised Land's agricultural blessing.
word_study.significance: Wine appears throughout Scripture as symbol of abundance, covenant blessing, and celebration. That the foreigners will not drink Jerusalem's wine means they will not share in her joy or partake of her covenant blessings. The promise restores the community's exclusive right to their own joy.

word_study.meaning: to labor, toil, weary oneself; implies strenuous work toward a specific end.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that the people's suffering was not passive but active—they worked, they labored, they exerted themselves. God acknowledges their effort and commits that it will not be in vain. This reflects the principle in Deuteronomy 28:33 and 2 Corinthians 10:10 that the laborer deserves his wages.

cross_references.connection: The Hebrews passage explains that God swore an oath to Abraham because He could swear by no one greater, and uses this principle to assure believers that God's oath is unchangeable. Isaiah 62:8 is God making the same kind of binding oath to restore His people.

The curse pronounced for covenant unfaithfulness includes that 'a nation which thou knowest not shall eat up the fruit of thy land.' Isaiah 62:8 reverses this curse: foreigners will no longer consume what Israel has labored for.
The earlier passage celebrates God's arm awakening to redeem His people 'as in the days of old.' Isaiah 62:8 invokes that same redemptive arm as surety for the oath of restoration.
God's right hand becomes glorious in power at the Red Sea, drowning the enemy. The right hand that rescued Israel from Egypt is the same hand by which God swears in Isaiah 62:8.

The Lord promises that 'he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad.' Isaiah 62:8 establishes that those who would scatter Israel—take her harvests, confiscate her labor—place themselves against God's sworn purpose.

commentary.historical_context: In the post-exilic period, the Judean community lived under Persian suzerainty and later under Hellenistic and Roman rule. While the people had returned from exile, their economic and political sovereignty remained severely limited. Local populations and foreign overlords could exact taxes and tributes that left the Jewish farmers with minimal return on their labor. The promise of verse 8 must have resonated powerfully with a community that experienced ongoing economic exploitation. The specific mention of grain and wine—the two primary products of Judean agriculture—indicates knowledge of the actual economic conditions of the post-exilic period. Archaeological evidence from the Persian period shows relatively modest material culture in Judea, suggesting that the community's labor was indeed taxed heavily by imperial authorities. God's oath addresses this historical reality: the future restoration will include economic freedom and the dignity of keeping one's own labor.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar language of God's covenant protection for His gathered people. In 3 Nephi 22 (Nephi's quotation of Isaiah 54), the theme of protection and vindication appears, with the people being assured that no weapon formed against them will prosper. The principle that God's people will enjoy the fruits of their labor without foreign exploitation is central to the Book of Mormon's vision of Zion.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:43-62 promises that 'the Lord shall have power over his enemies' and that Zion shall be established without foreign domination. The principle of verse 8—that God's people will enjoy peace and the fruits of their labor—is central to the latter-day restoration of Zion. D&C 42:30-39 establishes the law of consecration, which ensures that no person's labor is exploited and all are provided for according to need.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of grain and wine connects to the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, where bread (grain) and wine become symbols of covenant participation. God's oath to protect the people's harvest and wine production is ultimately about protecting their capacity to offer a broken heart and contrite spirit—the deepest fruits of labor—to Him.

commentary.christological_typology: The oath sworn by God's right hand and mighty arm ultimately points to Christ's redemptive work. Jesus 'sat down on the right hand of the throne of God' (Hebrews 10:12) and continues to intercede with His Father. The 'arm of strength' recalls Isaiah 52-53's description of the Servant, through whose stripes we are healed and by whose obedience many are made righteous. God's oath to protect His people's labor and dignity is fulfilled through Christ's redemption, which secures for believers the fruit of eternal life.
commentary.application: This verse teaches modern believers that God cares about material justice, not merely spiritual salvation. When members labor faithfully—in callings, in family work, in the building up of God's kingdom—they can trust that their labor is not in vain. The principle of the oath reassures us that God stands behind His commitment to His people: those who give their strength to the work of the gospel will not lose their reward. Furthermore, this verse invites us to examine our economic lives through a covenant lens. Are we, as individuals and as a Church, honoring people's labor and ensuring that those who work receive fair compensation? The verse also calls us to trust in God's protection of the Church and members: no force, no persecution, no economic hardship can ultimately rob us of the promised blessings of covenant faithfulness. Finally, it invites personal prayer for the literal restoration of Jerusalem, which remains central to the Lord's latter-day work.

text_kjv: But they that have gathered it shall eat it, and praise the LORD; and they that have brought it together shall drink it in the courts of my holiness.

commentary.narrative: Verse 8 established God's oath that enemies will no longer consume Israel's harvest; verse 9 now describes the positive reality: the people themselves will eat what they gather and drink what they produce, praising God in the process. This is not merely a return to normal economic life but a transformation of the relationship between labor, sustenance, and worship. The TCR translator notes the profound simplicity: 'you will eat what you grow. After centuries of foreign powers confiscating harvests, this is restoration of the most basic dignity.' The doubling of phrases—'they that have gathered' parallel with 'they that have brought it together'—emphasizes thoroughness: all who labor will participate in the joy of the harvest, not merely the wealthy or privileged.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'in the courts of my holiness' transforms the scene from ordinary agricultural consumption to sacred covenant celebration. This is not secular eating and drinking but worship. The people will eat and drink 'in the courts of my holiness'—the temple precincts. This echoes Deuteronomy's vision of covenant meals (Deuteronomy 12:7-12), where families brought their tithe and shared a meal before the Lord, 'eating there before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice in all that you put your hand unto, you and your households, wherein the LORD your God hath blessed you.' The restoration Isaiah envisions is not merely economic but sacramental: the people's labor is sanctified through being offered up and consumed in the presence of God. The praise of the Lord becomes as essential as the consumption itself.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The return from exile is often portrayed in purely political or spiritual terms, but verse 9 emphasizes the material and embodied dimensions of restoration. God cares that His people eat, drink, and find joy. This is not a spiritualization away from physical reality but an affirmation that the body, sustenance, and celebration are all part of covenant relationship. The phrase 'praise the LORD' appears at the moment of consumption, suggesting that gratitude and recognition of God's provision are inseparable from the act of eating. Modern readers may miss the scandal of this: in the ancient world, for a conquered people to gather and eat their own harvest while offering praise in their own temple would be revolutionary. It represents full restoration of national, economic, and religious autonomy.

word_study.meaning: those who gather, those who gather in; the participle form of asaf (to gather, collect, harvest). Refers to the laborers and harvesters.
word_study.significance: The participle emphasizes the ones who perform the action of gathering—the actual laborers. This is significant because it asserts that the workers themselves (not absentee landlords or foreign overlords) will benefit from their own harvest.

word_study.meaning: shall eat, will consume; from achal (to eat). The future tense emphasizes the certainty of the promise.
word_study.significance: The simple verb carries weight: to eat is to survive, to thrive, to live. After exile's deprivation, the right to eat one's own harvest is restoration of the right to live.

word_study.meaning: and they shall praise God; from halal (to praise, celebrate, make famous). The verb in the Piel stem intensifies the meaning to 'praise greatly.'
word_study.significance: Praise becomes the natural response to the restoration of basic dignity. The same verb appears throughout the Psalms. Here it connects material blessing to doxological response: proper eating leads to proper worship.

word_study.meaning: those who gather together, those who collect; from qabatz (to gather, assemble). Often used of gathering people as well as produce.
word_study.significance: This verb emphasizes community gathering. Not only will individuals eat what they grow, but the community will gather together to share. This connects to the communal meal imagery.

word_study.meaning: shall drink, will drink; from shata (to drink). The future tense parallels 'eat,' suggesting equal certainty.
word_study.significance: Wine, in Israelite culture, represents blessing, celebration, and covenant joy. That the people will drink 'their own' wine is restoration of not merely sustenance but joy.

word_study.meaning: in the courts of My sanctuary; hatzera (court, courtyard); qodash (holy, sanctified). The temple courtyard where covenant meals were consumed.
