word_study.significance: The phrase roots the celebration in sacred space. The temple courts were where God's people gathered to offer sacrifice and share covenant meals. This is not secular eating but sacramental consumption in God's presence. The adjective 'my holiness' (qodshi) is possessive: these are God's courts, God's sacred space, and the people will eat there as God's covenant community.

cross_references.connection: Moses instructs that families should eat their tithes and sacrificial meals 'before the LORD your God' and 'rejoice in all that you put your hand unto.' Isaiah 62:9 echoes this vision of covenant meals in God's presence.
The Psalmist calls God's servants to praise Him. The structure of verse 9—eating followed by praise—follows this same pattern of material blessing prompting doxological response.
Samuel explains the practice of blessing before eating at a covenant meal. Isaiah 62:9 assumes this sacramental understanding where food consumed in sacred space becomes an act of worship.

Christ institutes the sacrament at the temple in the Americas, commanding His people to 'do this in remembrance of me.' Isaiah 62:9's vision of eating in the courts of holiness while praising God prefigures this sacramental pattern in the Restoration.

commentary.historical_context: In Second Temple Judaism, the practice of offering portions of the harvest to God and consuming tithe portions in the temple precincts was a central aspect of religious life (see Leviticus 23, Deuteronomy 12-14, Numbers 18). The post-exilic community would have been familiar with these practices, though the actual conditions of Persian-period Judea limited the scale of such celebrations. Jerusalem in this period was a modest hill town, not a major city, so the vision of abundant gatherings in the temple courts would have seemed aspirational. The verse envisions a future restoration where the community has both the agricultural surplus and the political freedom to celebrate together in the temple. This contrasts with the actual experience of many returned exiles, who struggled with debt, poor harvests, and heavy taxation (see Nehemiah 5:1-13). The prophet thus offers hope grounded in concrete promises: the future community will not merely survive but will celebrate together.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon, particularly in Helaman 6:10-11, describes the righteous people enjoying abundance and the fruits of their labor. The principle that covenant-keeping leads to material blessing and that such blessing should be shared in community and celebrated in sacred space is consistent throughout Book of Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The law of consecration in Doctrine and Covenants 42 and 78 establishes that the Lord's people should have all things in common and that the fruits of labor should be distributed according to need. Isaiah 62:9 anticipates this principle: a community where all eat the fruit of their labor, where celebration is shared, and where worship is central. D&C 88:119 promises that the Lord's people will gather at Adam-ondi-Ahman, suggesting that the eschatological vision includes community gathering and celebration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the setting for the eating and drinking described in verse 9. In latter-day context, this connects to the sacrament (the eating and drinking of bread and wine in the temple context) and to temple feasts and celebrations. The principle is that eating and drinking in sacred space, offered to the Lord, transform ordinary sustenance into covenant participation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus frequently taught through meals and eating: the feeding of the five thousand, the marriage feast at Cana, and most significantly, the Last Supper. In Matthew 26:29, Jesus promises that He will 'drink of the fruit of the vine' anew in His Father's kingdom, suggesting that eating and drinking with God is the ultimate covenant blessing. Isaiah 62:9's vision of the people eating and drinking together in the courts of God's holiness points toward the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), where the redeemed celebrate with their Redeemer.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern members to cultivate gratitude for the fruits of their labor and to understand that eating, drinking, and celebration are not separate from worship but central to covenant life. The principle extends beyond material food: whatever we labor for—spiritual growth, family relationships, service—should be received as God's blessing and offered back to Him in thanksgiving. The verse also affirms that joy and celebration are not indulgences but essential to the covenant community. The Latter-day Saint practice of family home evening, ward socials, and temple celebrations echoes Isaiah's vision that believers gather together to enjoy God's blessings while maintaining sacred focus. Furthermore, the verse calls us to examine whether we are allowing all people—not just the privileged—to participate in and benefit from shared blessings. The principle that 'they that have gathered it shall eat it' invites us to work toward economic justice where laborers receive the fruit of their work.

text_kjv: Go through, go through the gates; prepare ye the way of the people; cast up, cast up the highway; gather out the stones; lift up a standard for the people.

commentary.narrative: Verse 10 shifts from promise and oath to immediate action. The doubled imperatives—'Go through, go through!' and 'cast up, cast up!'—create a sense of urgent momentum. This is not a distant future hope but a present call to prepare. The verse echoes Isaiah 40:3 ('Prepare ye the way of the LORD') but applies it to the people's return and restoration. Rather than preparing a way for God (40:3), the people now prepare a way for themselves—for the gathering of the dispersed community returning to Zion. The TCR translator notes: 'The doubled imperatives create urgency: go through, go through! Build up, build up! This echoes the highway language of 40:3 and 57:14.' The progression from promise (verses 7-9) to imperative (verse 10) mirrors the covenant pattern: God swears, then calls His people to respond through action.
commentary.narrative_continued: The specific commands break down into four parallel actions: (1) 'Go through, go through the gates'—exit from exile's confinement; (2) 'prepare ye the way of the people'—clear obstacles; (3) 'cast up, cast up the highway'—build up the road itself; (4) 'gather out the stones'—remove impediments to travel; (5) 'lift up a standard for the people'—raise a signal/banner to gather the dispersed. Each command addresses a different aspect of restoration. The gates likely refer to Jerusalem's gates, which lay in ruins during the exile period (Nehemiah spent years rebuilding them). The imagery of 'going through' suggests both literal passage from exile to homeland and spiritual passage from separation to restoration. The 'way of the people' is the path along which the dispersed community will return.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The 'highway' (mesillah) is a technical term in Isaiah for the great processional road that will be established for God's people (40:3; 57:14). Building the highway is not merely practical engineering but spiritual preparation—clearing away what obstructs the journey home. The 'standard' (nes) is a rallying point, an ensign that gathers the scattered. This echoes Isaiah 11:12, where a standard is raised to gather 'the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.' The verse thus encompasses the literal physical work of road-building and the spiritual work of gathering scattered Israel. It calls for agency and effort: the community itself, not merely God, must participate in the restoration. The exiles cannot simply wait for deliverance; they must rise up and prepare the way.

word_study.meaning: Go through, pass through, cross over; from abar (to pass, cross, transit). The doubled infinitive absolute creates emphasis and urgency.
word_study.significance: This verb echoes the great crossings in Israel's history: crossing the Red Sea, crossing the Jordan. To 'go through' means to transit from exile to homeland, from separation to restoration. The doubling indicates that no hesitation or delay is acceptable.

word_study.meaning: gates; from shaar (to open, to serve as an entrance). City gates were the controlled entry/exit points and served as centers of community life and judgment.
word_study.significance: In Nehemiah's account, rebuilding Jerusalem's gates was central to restoring the city's integrity. 'Going through the gates' means exiting exile's boundaries and entering the restored city. This is both literal (passing through Jerusalem's gates upon return) and symbolic (entering a new era).

word_study.meaning: prepare, make ready, clear; from panah (to turn, to clear). Often used of clearing obstacles.
word_study.significance: This verb encompasses both literal clearing (removing stones, leveling obstacles) and metaphorical clearing (removing impediments to the journey home). It suggests active work, not passive waiting.

word_study.meaning: way/path of the people; derekh (way, path, journey); am (people, nation). The 'way' is the route of return and the condition of restored relationship.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes that the restoration is not for individuals but for the people collectively. The way belongs to 'the people'—the covenant community as a whole.

word_study.term_english: cast up, cast up the highway
word_study.meaning: Build up, build up the highway/raised road; from salal (to pile up, raise, build up). Mesillah is a raised, constructed road—not a natural path but a engineered thoroughfare.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests intentional construction and elevation. A raised road was a Roman-era engineering achievement, suggesting that Isaiah envisions restoration involving sophisticated infrastructure. This is not merely clearing a natural path but building a constructed way.

word_study.meaning: gather/remove stones; from sakal (to stone, to remove by stoning). The phrase means to clear stones from the path.
word_study.significance: This is the practical, unglamorous work necessary for travel. Stones represent obstacles—literal barriers to the journey. Removing them requires effort. The verse thus acknowledges that restoration requires unglamorous labor: road-building, stone-clearing, practical work alongside grand spiritual vision.

word_study.meaning: Raise a banner/signal; nes (standard, banner, signal fire). From rum (to lift, raise, exalt).
word_study.significance: The nes (standard) appears in Isaiah 11:12 in the context of gathering the dispersed. Here it serves as a rallying point for the scattered people. This is the spiritual work: providing a sign around which the exiled community can gather and organize their return.

word_study.meaning: over the peoples/nations; amim (peoples, nations). The standard is lifted 'over' the peoples, suggesting visibility to all nations.
word_study.significance: The restoration of Israel is not a hidden event but a visible sign to all nations. The standard raised over Israel becomes a witness to the world of God's faithfulness and power.

cross_references.connection: That verse commands 'Prepare ye the way of the LORD' for His coming. Isaiah 62:10 applies the same language to preparing the way for the people's return, showing that restoration of Israel is an act of God as significant as His appearing.

A previous passage states 'Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people.' This is nearly identical language, reinforcing the urgency of clearing the way.
Isaiah promises that 'He shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel.' The standard raised in 62:10 is this same ensign for gathering dispersed Israel.
The historical account of rebuilding Jerusalem's gates and walls illustrates the literal fulfillment of 62:10's command to go through gates and clear the way.

The Lord commands the Church to prepare for the gathering of Israel, stating 'Behold, I say unto you, the redemption of Zion must needs come by power.' Isaiah 62:10 establishes that the gathering requires active human participation in preparation.

commentary.historical_context: The literal gates Isaiah references lay in ruin. The Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem (586 BCE) left the city's fortifications devastated. When the first exiles returned under Cyrus (539 BCE) and subsequently under Zerubbabel, the immediate tasks were clearing the site, rebuilding the temple, and eventually (decades later, under Nehemiah in 445 BCE) reconstructing the walls and gates. The verse thus speaks to the concrete, unglamorous work required for restoration. The image of building highways echoes later Hellenistic road-building projects, suggesting that Isaiah's vision encompasses the ongoing process of reconstruction across centuries. The 'stones' to be cleared are not metaphorical but literal ruins of destroyed structures. The 'standard' or banner would have been a familiar sight in the ancient Near East as armies and populations used them to organize and rally followers. The verse thus grounds the eschatological hope in concrete, achievable tasks that the community could undertake.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently uses the language of 'preparing the way' in connection with the Restoration (1 Nephi 10:7-10). Nephi sees that the Restoration will prepare the way for the Lord's second coming, echoing Isaiah's call to prepare the way. The metaphor of building highways and removing obstacles appears in Nephi's vision and in Alma's missionary labors.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 65 calls the Church to 'let the solemnities of eternity rest upon your minds' and to work toward building Zion. Isaiah 62:10's call to active preparation resonates with D&C 136:31, where the Lord instructs: 'Organize yourselves...prepare every needful thing.' The Restoration teaches that gathering Israel requires human labor aligned with divine purpose.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gates and courts of the temple are spaces through which the faithful pass. Building and maintaining temples and the paths to them is a modern application of preparing the way. The spiritual work of temple building corresponds to Isaiah's literal call to build highways and clear gates.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the Way (John 14:6), and the preparation of the way is ultimately about preparing the way for His coming. Matthew 21:4-5 applies Isaiah 40:3 to John the Baptist's preparation of the way for Jesus' ministry. Isaiah 62:10's call to prepare the way for the gathering of Israel ultimately points to Christ as the center of that gathering—He is both the way and the destination toward which Israel returns.
commentary.application: This verse transforms restoration from something we passively await into something we actively participate in creating. Modern members are called to 'go through the gates' by taking concrete steps toward missionary work, temple building, and family gathering. 'Preparing the way' means removing obstacles to the gospel—doubt, complacency, fear—from our own lives and from others'. The command to 'gather out the stones' invites us to identify what impedes progress (in the Church, in our families, in our communities) and systematically remove these obstacles. 'Lifting up a standard' for our families means maintaining clear, visible commitments to covenant values that can rally family members around shared purpose. The doubled imperatives ('Go through, go through!' 'Cast up, cast up!') convey that procrastination has no place; the work is urgent and must begin now. For those involved in temple construction, missionary work, educational institutions, or Church service, this verse affirms that their often-unglamorous labors—building, organizing, clearing away obstacles—are sacred work that literally fulfills Isaiah's prophecy.

text_kjv: Behold, the LORD hath proclaimed unto the end of the world, Say ye to the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy salvation cometh; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.

commentary.narrative: After the call to action in verse 10, verse 11 announces the purpose toward which all preparation points: the coming of salvation. The 'proclamation to the end of the world' emphasizes that this is not a private or local event but a proclamation with cosmic significance. The phrase 'daughter of Zion' personifies Jerusalem/the covenant community as a woman awaiting her redeemer. The announcement 'thy salvation cometh' is not conditional but assured. The phrase 'his reward is with him, and his work before him' echoes Isaiah 40:10, establishing continuity between the promise of salvation announced in the book's middle section and its fulfillment in these final chapters. The TCR translator notes: 'The salvation that comes is not an abstraction but a person arriving.' This personification is crucial: salvation is not merely a condition or state but a Being—the Savior Himself.
commentary.narrative_continued: The structure of verse 11 moves from proclamation (God announces to all peoples) to address (Say to the daughter of Zion) to substance (thy salvation comes). This three-fold movement shows that the announcement is not merely about external reality but about addressing the people specifically with news directed to them. The 'daughter of Zion' motif appears frequently in Isaiah (40:9, 49:18, 52:1-2; see also Zechariah 9:9-10). She is the awaiting bride, the nation personified as female, vulnerable and awaiting redemption. The coming salvation is thus not merely political restoration but personal rescue—the return of a beloved. The phrase 'his reward is with him, and his work before him' indicates that the Savior comes with full vindication: the reward He carries is for His people, and His work—His completed redemptive task—accomplishes their restoration.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: This verse connects to the New Testament application in profound ways. The TCR translator notes that 'Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 echo this verse when Jesus enters Jerusalem.' Both Gospel accounts quote a modified form of this verse when Jesus enters the city as the Messiah. The 'salvation that comes' is ultimately identified with the person of Christ. Isaiah's proclamation in 62:11, announcing salvation to the daughter of Zion, is fulfilled when Jesus Himself enters Jerusalem as the promised King. Yet the ultimate fulfillment awaits His second coming, when the proclamation to the end of the world will finally be realized in full. Thus, verse 11 contains both a Christological reference (Jesus' first coming as the promised salvation) and an eschatological reference (Jesus' return to complete the restoration of Zion).

word_study.meaning: has proclaimed, made heard, announced; from shamea (to hear, listen). The Hiphil stem indicates active proclamation to be heard.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that this is an announcement meant to be heard, broadcast, made known. It is not a quiet promise but a proclamation of sufficient importance to reach 'the end of the world.'

word_study.meaning: end of the earth, far places, extremities of the inhabited world; qetzeh (end, extremity); aretz (earth, land).
word_study.significance: This phrase indicates that the proclamation is universal in scope. It reaches not just to Jerusalem or Judea but to all peoples everywhere. This universality suggests that Israel's salvation has significance for all nations.

word_study.meaning: daughter of Zion, personification of Jerusalem/the covenant community as a woman; bat (daughter); tziyon (Zion, Jerusalem).
word_study.significance: This motif appears throughout Isaiah (40:9, 49:18, 52:1-2, etc.). It personalizes the city/nation as a woman who has suffered exile and awaits vindication. The term carries emotional and intimate associations: she is vulnerable, awaiting rescue, deserving of honor and protection.

word_study.meaning: salvation, deliverance, victory; from yasha (to save, deliver). In Isaiah's context, it encompasses both spiritual redemption and political/national restoration.
word_study.significance: This is the central term of the book of Isaiah. It appears 27 times in Isaiah (more than in any other biblical book) and encompasses multiple dimensions: rescue from enemies, restoration to homeland, forgiveness of sins, and ultimately the redemptive work of the Messiah. The promise 'thy salvation cometh' is the culmination of Isaiah's entire message.

word_study.meaning: comes, arrives, approaches; a participle indicating present/imminent action.
word_study.significance: The participle form suggests active, ongoing arrival. Salvation is not a distant abstraction but something approaching, imminent, increasingly near. The present tense creates urgency and certainty.

word_study.meaning: his reward, his wages, his compensation; skar (reward, wage, recompense). The possessive suffix indicates this is the reward that belongs to Him or that He brings.
word_study.significance: The 'reward' is likely the reward that God has prepared for His faithful people. The Savior comes bearing this reward, the compensation promised to the faithful. This echoes Matthew 16:27, 'For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.'

word_study.meaning: his work, his deed, his accomplishment; peulah (work, labor, accomplishment). From the root meaning to work or labor.
word_study.significance: This refers to the Savior's redemptive work—His labor of love for the salvation of humanity. The work of atonement and redemption is complete ('his work before him') when He comes. This anticipates Hebrews 10:14, 'For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.'

cross_references.connection: That passage states, 'Behold, the Lord GOD will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him: behold, his reward is with him.' Isaiah 62:11 echoes this language, confirming that salvation arrives as a person bearing reward and having completed His redemptive work.

Matthew explicitly references Isaiah 62:11 when describing Jesus' entry into Jerusalem: 'All this was done...that it might be fulfilled which was spoken...Say ye to the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh.' The New Testament identifies Jesus as the salvation/King announced in Isaiah 62:11.
John's account of the entry also echoes this passage, with the crowd welcoming Jesus with branches. John interprets this as the fulfillment of the ancient promise of the coming King.

Zechariah prophesies, 'Behold, thy King cometh unto thee...lowly, and riding upon an ass.' This passage and Isaiah 62:11 together form the composite portrait of the coming Messiah-King arriving in humility.
John's vision shows the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the bride (the Church/Zion) is prepared to meet her Bridegroom. This echoes the 'daughter of Zion' awaiting her salvation/King.
Nephi applies Isaiah's prophecies of Zion's salvation to Christ's redemptive work, showing that the Book of Mormon interprets Isaiah's eschatological language Christologically.

commentary.historical_context: In the Persian post-exilic period, the Jewish community would have been acutely aware of their subordinate status. They were not an independent nation but a small community within the Persian empire, later under Greek and eventually Roman rule. The proclamation of salvation 'to the end of the world' would have been profoundly aspirational: a tiny, marginalized community was promised that their vindication would become known everywhere. The 'daughter of Zion' language would have resonated with those who remembered Jerusalem's glory (as described in the earlier chapters of Isaiah) and were now living in modest, rebuilt circumstances. The promise that 'thy salvation cometh' spoke to the existential hope of a people whose national identity was constantly threatened. The New Testament writers, living centuries later, recognized that Jesus' entry into Jerusalem as a Messiah-King was the fulfillment of this prophecy. Yet the final, complete fulfillment remains eschatological: when Christ returns, the proclamation to the end of the world will be fully realized.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the Restoration brings the message of salvation to all peoples. Nephi's vision (1 Nephi 13-14) shows the gospel going forth to all nations, which is the fulfillment of Isaiah's proclamation 'to the end of the world.' The Book of Mormon also applies Isaiah's prophecies of Zion's restoration to the gathering of Israel in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:16-21 describes the Savior coming with His reward and His work complete. D&C 1:35-36 emphasizes that the gospel is being proclaimed 'to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.' This is the modern expression of Isaiah 62:11's proclamation to the end of the world. D&C 15:6 promises that those who preach the gospel will have eternal life, echoing the reward that comes with salvation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is where members make covenants of salvation. When members enter the temple, they are responding to the proclamation of salvation. The temple endowment is a dramatization of the plan of salvation and the coming of the Savior. The bride symbolism (daughter of Zion awaiting her salvation/King) is central to temple theology, where the Church is the Bride of Christ.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 11 is explicitly Christological. The 'salvation' that comes is personified—it is not abstract but a Being who arrives. This Being comes with reward (compensation for the faithful) and with His work complete (His atonement and redemption accomplished). Jesus is identified in the New Testament as exactly this salvation. Matthew 1:21 states that Jesus was named because 'he shall save his people from their sins.' The daughter of Zion awaiting salvation is ultimately the Church awaiting her Bridegroom. The 'proclamation to the end of the world' is the gospel message that has been preached from Pentecost through the last dispensation.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern members to understand that our salvation is not an impersonal force but a personal relationship with a Savior who comes for us, bearing reward. The phrase 'thy salvation cometh' speaks to each individual and to the community: Christ comes for you. Furthermore, the verse calls us to understand the Restoration as the outworking of this prophecy. When Joseph Smith proclaimed the gospel 'to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people' (through missionary work), he was fulfilling Isaiah's vision of the proclamation reaching the end of the world. Members engaged in missionary work, temple building, and family gathering are participating in the fulfillment of this verse. Finally, the verse invites personal reflection on what it means that 'thy salvation cometh.' In moments of difficulty, loss, or spiritual trial, this proclamation reminds us that the Savior comes to us with His reward (grace, forgiveness, exaltation) and with His work complete (atonement is finished; redemption is available). We wait not for salvation to be accomplished but to be fully manifested.

text_kjv: And they shall call them, The holy people, The redeemed of the LORD: and thou shalt be called, Sought out, A city not forsaken.

commentary.narrative: Verse 12 completes Isaiah 62 with four final names that describe the restored community. The TCR translator notes the profound reversal: 'Four final names for the restored community: Holy People, Redeemed of the LORD, Sought Out, City Not Forsaken. Each name directly reverses the exile condition. Not Forsaken (lo ne'ezavah) answers the Forsaken (Azuvah) of verse 4—the old name is not merely replaced but explicitly negated.' This verse thus echoes and completes the renaming theme introduced in verses 2-4 (Hephzibah, 'My Delight Is in Her,' and Beulah, 'Married'). The shift from 'they' (plural) to 'thou' (singular) in the second half shows that the restoration applies both to the community as a whole and to the city personified as an individual woman. These names are not merely poetic but constitute a new identity that transforms how the people understand themselves and how others perceive them.
commentary.narrative_continued: The first name, 'The Holy People' (am ha-qodesh), establishes that restoration involves sanctification. Holiness is not a distant ideal but the defining characteristic of the restored community. This echoes the promise in Exodus 19:6 that Israel would be 'a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.' After exile's degradation and foreign domination, being called 'holy' is restoration of covenantal identity. The second name, 'The Redeemed of the LORD' (geulei YHWH), emphasizes that this people belong to God through redemption. The verb 'redeem' (gaal) carries the sense of being bought back, recovered, restored to family. A redeemed people is one that God has personally claimed and restored. The third name, 'Sought Out' (drushah), suggests active seeking: the people who were lost, scattered, and forsaken are now sought after. God Himself seeks them out; the nations recognize their worth and seek them.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The final name, 'A City Not Forsaken' (ir lo ne'ezavah), directly negates the name 'Forsaken' (Azuvah) from verse 4. This is not mere replacement but deliberate negation—the curse is explicitly overturned. In verse 4, Jerusalem was called 'Desolate' (Shemamah) and 'Forsaken' (Azuvah), representing the exile condition where the city lay in ruins and the people were scattered. Now the opposite is declared: 'Not Forsaken.' This is the ultimate promise: despite the centuries of abandonment, despite the seeming silence of God during exile, the people will receive assurance that they are neither abandoned nor forgotten. Each name carries a corrective force: they were treated as profane, but they are holy; they were enslaved, but they are redeemed; they were lost, but they are sought out; they were forsaken, but they are restored. The accumulation of four names emphasizes the completeness and multidimensional nature of the restoration.

word_study.meaning: holy people, sanctified people; qodash (holy, set apart, sanctified); am (people, nation).
word_study.significance: Holiness in Hebrew means separation for sacred purpose. The 'holy people' are those separated to God's service. This echoes Exodus 19:6 and Leviticus 20:26, establishing that Israel's fundamental identity is covenantal holiness. The restoration includes restoration of this identity.

word_study.meaning: redeemed ones, those who have been redeemed/restored; from gaal (to redeem, buy back, restore, avenge).
word_study.significance: The verb gaal is rich with meaning. It refers to the kinsman-redeemer who restores family property and recovers family members. The 'redeemed of the LORD' are God's people whom He has personally recovered and restored to covenant relationship. This vocabulary is used throughout Isaiah (e.g., 43:1, 44:22-23, 51:10, 52:9).

word_study.meaning: The LORD, the covenant God of Israel; the personal name of God revealed at Sinai.
word_study.significance: The use of the name YHWH (not merely 'God') emphasizes covenant relationship. These people are redeemed by the covenant God Himself, indicating personal, binding relationship.

word_study.meaning: sought out, searched for, desired; from darash (to seek, search, inquire, require). The participle form indicates an ongoing or completed state of being sought.
word_study.significance: This name suggests that the people, though scattered and lost, are the objects of active seeking. Both God and the nations 'seek them out'—recognize their value, search them out. This is the inverse of being forsaken: instead of being abandoned and unwanted, they are actively pursued.

word_study.meaning: city, town, urban settlement; often used metaphorically for community or people.
word_study.significance: The use of 'city' rather than 'people' emphasizes Jerusalem specifically. The city itself, its walls and structures, are restored. This is not merely spiritual restoration but physical, embodied, geographical restoration.

word_study.meaning: not forsaken, not abandoned, not left desolate; from azav (to abandon, forsake, leave behind).
word_study.significance: The negative particle lo intensifies the contrast with the 'Forsaken' (Azuvah) of verse 4. The TCR translator notes: 'Not Forsaken (lo ne'ezavah) answers the Forsaken (Azuvah) of verse 4—the old name is not merely replaced but explicitly negated.' This is not merely a new name but the deliberate negation of the old curse. The God who appeared to forsake His people during exile now declares that appearance a lie: the people were never truly forsaken.

cross_references.connection: Verses 4 and 12 form an inclusio (opening and closing bracket) around the entire chapter. Verse 4 establishes the old names (Forsaken, Desolate); verse 12 establishes the new names that explicitly negate the old ones. This bracket shows the entire motion of the chapter: from exile to restoration, from abandonment to redemption.

God tells Israel at Sinai, 'And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.' Isaiah 62:12 echoes this foundational promise, confirming that the restored community will be what God originally intended them to be.

Moses reminds Israel that they are 'an holy people unto the LORD thy God' and that the LORD 'hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself.' Isaiah 62:12 affirms this covenantal election and identity after exile has tested it.

Peter applies these names to New Testament believers: 'But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people...which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God.' This shows how the promises to Israel are extended through the gospel.

The vision of the New Jerusalem includes the promise that God 'will dwell with them...and God himself shall be with them, and be their God.' This fulfills the restoration promised in Isaiah 62:12: a people where God dwells, not forsaken.

The Lord promises that the righteous 'shall inherit the earth, and it shall be called the sons of lod Zion, a city of the saints, even the city of my people.' Isaiah 62:12's promise of a restored city is fulfilled in the latter-day vision of Zion.

commentary.historical_context: The post-exilic community lived under the weight of the names mentioned in verse 4: they were small, economically struggling, and politically insignificant. The names in verse 12 would have seemed aspirational and eschatological—promises for a future age. Yet they also served a psychological and spiritual function in the present: the exiled community could begin to claim these identities even before full restoration was materially evident. The practice of re-naming to mark transformation was common in ancient cultures (Abram to Abraham, Saul to Paul). For the post-exilic community, the new names provided a way to understand themselves not as permanently diminished but as on the trajectory toward the promised restoration. The excavated ruins and modest rebuilding projects of Persian-period Jerusalem would have contrasted sharply with these grand promises, yet they offered hope that God's purposes were not thwarted by exile.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently applies Isaiah's naming language to the restoration of Israel. In 1 Nephi 22:28, Nephi affirms that the dispersed of Judah will be gathered, establishing that the restoration spoken of in Isaiah includes a literal gathering. The principle that God's people can claim new identities in covenant relationship appears throughout the Book of Mormon (Alma 5:38-40, where members are asked if they have been born of God and become His sons and daughters).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Restoration brings new names to God's people. Members who enter the temple receive new names as part of their endowment, symbolizing their restored and exalted identity. D&C 130:11 discusses how names in heaven relate to identity and authority. The Latter-day Saint understanding of 'covenant identity' is rooted in this same principle: in the temple, we are no longer merely individuals pursuing salvation but members of God's people, sealed into covenant relationship, recipients of His promises. D&C 45:71 promises that 'they are they who are the church of the Firstborn' and shall inherit all things.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment is essentially a drama of naming and transformation. Those who enter the temple progress from the fallen condition to receive new names and vestments representing their redeemed state. This is the literal enactment of Isaiah 62:12: moving from a state of exile and loss (the fallen human condition) to a state of redemption, holiness, and belonging (the covenant state). The temple teaches that we are 'the holy people, the redeemed of the LORD,' sought out by God Himself and no longer forsaken.

commentary.christological_typology: The four names that describe the restored community ultimately describe the redeemed Church/Bride. The 'holy people' are sanctified through Christ's atonement (Hebrews 10:10). The 'redeemed of the LORD' are those whom God has bought back at the price of Christ's blood (1 Corinthians 6:20). The 'sought out' people echoes Jesus' parable of the lost sheep (Luke 15:4-7), where the shepherd actively searches for the lost. Finally, 'not forsaken' speaks to Jesus' promise in Matthew 28:20, 'Lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.' The person of Christ is the fulfillment of the restoration promised in verse 12.
commentary.application: This verse invites Latter-day Saints to understand their identity as fundamentally rooted in covenant relationship with God. When we enter covenants—baptism, temple endowment, sealing—we are not merely joining an organization but claiming the identity described in verse 12: we become 'the holy people, the redeemed of the LORD, sought out, not forsaken.' This identity is not earned by perfection but received through faith and covenant. The practical application is that members should understand themselves through this covenantal lens rather than through the world's categories. We are not defined by worldly status, wealth, or popularity but by our standing before God as His holy, redeemed, sought-out people. This is particularly relevant for those who feel marginalized, forgotten, or undervalued by the world: verse 12 assures them that God has sought them out and has not forsaken them. The four names also invite us to ask: How do I see myself? As holy? As redeemed? As sought by God? As belonging to His people? To claim these identities is to step into the restoration promised here. Finally, verse 12 calls the Church collectively to understand itself as the literal fulfillment of Isaiah's promise. The gathering of Israel, the restoration of temples, the preaching of the gospel to all nations—these are the modern manifestations of the people being 'sought out' and called by the names that Isaiah promised.

text_kjv: Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.

commentary.narrative: Isaiah opens chapter 63 with one of Scripture's most vivid theophanies — a divine warrior approaching from the southeast, stained with blood. The scene begins as a watchman's question: 'Who is this?' The answer comes directly from God Himself, who identifies not by name but by action and attribute: 'I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.' This is not a conquering king of human armies but God alone, striding in His strength. The geographical reference to Edom (a perpetual enemy of Israel) and Bozrah (its principal city) signals that this judgment is directed at those who have oppressed God's people. The TCR rendering emphasizes the theatrical drama: 'crimson garments' rather than merely 'dyed garments' — the blood-staining is the point, not royal embroidery.
commentary.narrative_continued: The prophecy stands at the climax of Third Isaiah (chapters 56–66), a section addressing the exilic and post-exilic community with promises of God's ultimate vindication. After 62 chapters of legal contestation, complaint, and covenant renewal, Isaiah finally presents the divine warrior in action. But notice the peculiar claim: God speaks 'in righteousness' (tzedaqah) — His judgment is not arbitrary cruelty but the fulfilment of covenant obligation. He is 'mighty to save' (yeshuah), a term that encompasses both deliverance and vindication. The rhetorical form — a question and immediate self-identification — creates intimate encounter: the reader is positioned as the watchman, asking the question that Isaiah has been building toward for chapters.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The image would have carried profound resonance for exilic and post-exilic Judah. After decades of dispossession, they are presented with a vision of divine retribution against the nations that exulted over their suffering. Edom, in particular, had rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 1:11-12) and had come to embody all hostile powers in prophetic imagination. God's appearance 'from Edom' thus signals judgment executed at the point of greatest offense — the exile is being reversed not through human military might but through God's personal, wrathful action.

word_study.meaning: From the root adam ('red'), Edom was the nation descended from Esau, occupying territory southeast of the Dead Sea. The name itself carries the sense of redness, which the TCR notes creates a deliberate wordplay with the crimson-stained warrior.
word_study.significance: Edom functions in biblical prophecy as the archetypal enemy — representative of all nations hostile to God's covenant people. Its mention here signals that judgment is directed at those who have persecuted Israel during exile.

word_study.meaning: The KJV 'dyed garments' obscures the specific sense of chamuts, which indicates garments stained or dyed in red — specifically the red of blood. The TCR rendering makes this explicit: 'crimson garments.'
word_study.significance: This is not ceremonial royal dress but battle-stained clothing. The redness derives from judgment executed, not from dye vats. This detail anchors the winepress metaphor that dominates verses 2-6.

word_study.meaning: From a root suggesting majesty, splendor, or excellence. The term carries the sense of something magnificent or worthy of honor, though here in a martial rather than ceremonial context.
word_study.significance: The paradox is intentional: God's majesty is displayed not in courtly finery but in the awfulness of righteous judgment. The splendor consists in His terrible strength and the flawlessness of His justice.

word_study.meaning: Often translated 'righteousness,' but semantically encompasses both moral rightness and covenant fidelity. God's judgment is righteous because it fulfills the obligations of His covenant — He is keeping faith with His people and punishing those who have broken covenant by harming them.
word_study.significance: This single word encapsulates the theological claim of the passage: God's violence is not capricious but covenantally grounded. He judges because He is faithful to His promises to Israel.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'great/mighty to save.' The verb yasha (ישע) encompasses deliverance, salvation, and vindication. The adjective rab (great/mighty) emphasizes the supreme sufficiency of God's power.
word_study.significance: This phrase holds together the entire passage: God's judgment against enemies is simultaneously God's salvation of the oppressed. The same act that treads down Edom redeems Zion.

cross_references.connection: The risen Christ is depicted as clothed in a vesture 'dipped in blood' (cf. Matthew 14:26), directly echoing this passage. The connection shows how early Christian interpretation applied Isaiah's divine warrior imagery to Christ's parousia.

Isaiah earlier depicts God wondering 'that there was no intercessor' and working salvation by His own arm—the same solitary agency emphasized in 63:3 and 63:5. This forms a deliberate echo within Third Isaiah.
The psalmists call for judgment on Edom for its role in Jerusalem's desolation. Isaiah 63:1-6 presents the prophetic answer to this plea: God Himself executes the vengeance the Psalms petition.
Obadiah's prophecy against Edom finds fulfillment imagery here. The specific judgment against Edom's 'mighty men' echoes through Isaiah's vision of the divine warrior's work.
The Doctrine and Covenants applies Isaiah's imagery of the coming in blood-stained garments to Christ's last judgment: 'I have trampled them in my wrath, and my fury, it upheld me' (D&C 133:51).

commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with an uncomfortable claim: divine righteousness sometimes manifests as wrath. We live in an era that emphasizes God's mercy and universalism, often downplaying judgment. But Isaiah insists that God's righteousness encompasses both salvation for the faithful and vengeance against the stubborn oppressor. For covenant-keeping Latter-day Saints, the application is twofold: first, trust that God's justice is ultimately vindicated—wrongs done to you and your community are not ignored but will be answered by God. Second, recognize that standing in covenant with God requires more than passive faith; it demands active fidelity. To call upon God as 'mighty to save' is also to accept His role as judge. The righteousness that saves is the same righteousness that condemns rebellion.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of the divine warrior figure. Just as Isaiah 63's warrior comes alone in righteousness and mighty to save, Christ comes as the sole sufficient source of redemption and judgment. The blood upon His garments in Revelation 19:13 explicitly connects this prophecy to Christ's return. Moreover, Christ's atoning blood and His eventual judgment both flow from the same righteous power: He shed His blood to save His people (covenant fulfillment) and will shed the blood of His enemies at His return (covenant enforcement). The paradox—that the same figure both redeems and judges—finds its fullest expression in Christ, who is 'the Lamb' (redeemer) and 'the Lion' (judge) simultaneously.
commentary.historical_context: The vision of a divine warrior in blood-stained garments derives from ancient Near Eastern warrior iconography, where gods and kings are depicted as splattered with the blood of vanquished enemies—a mark of victorious power rather than dishonor. However, Isaiah subverts this motif: the warrior is alone ('no one with me'), without human allies or armies. This emphasizes that divine judgment operates independently of geopolitical power and cannot be resisted by human military might. Edom's specific mention reflects historical animosity: Edomite bands had harassed Judah during the Babylonian siege (586 BCE) and had subsequently encroached on formerly Judahite territory. For exilic and post-exilic Judah, Edom became the symbolic representative of all nations that rejoiced in Israel's suffering. The winepress metaphor (introduced in verse 2) also carries ancient Near Eastern weight: grape harvest and wine-making were agricultural labors, but the language of treading grapes in a winepress becomes, in prophetic hands, a grotesque metaphor for the crushing of human bodies and the spilling of blood. The physical imagery would have been viscerally powerful to an audience familiar with both viticulture and warfare.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon preserves similar language of divine judgment in 1 Nephi 22:15-19, where Nephi sees the coming of the Lord to judge both the righteous (whom He brings to Zion) and the wicked (whom He overthrows). The parallelism between salvation for the covenant people and judgment for the rebellious—both acts of the same divine warrior—appears consistently in Nephite prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 133:41-51 directly cites and applies Isaiah 63:1-6 to Christ's final return: 'Who is this that cometh down from God in heaven with dyed garments; yea, from the regions which are not known, clothed in his glorious apparel, traveling in the greatness of his strength?' (D&C 133:46). The revelation makes explicit that Isaiah's warrior is Christ Himself at the Second Coming. This Restoration application reads Isaiah's prophecy not as historical judgment alone but as an archetype of Christ's ultimate vindication.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of the divine warrior returning in blood-stained garments evokes the temple's sacrificial system and the Day of Atonement, when the high priest enters the Holy of Holies bearing blood. However, Isaiah inverts the direction: rather than blood carried into the holy place, blood flows from God as He executes judgment. This suggests a transcendent judgment that supersedes and fulfills the Levitical atonement system.

text_kjv: Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?

commentary.narrative: The dialogue continues as the watchman presses his question: 'Why is Your apparel red?' The questioner has identified the figure and now demands explanation for the specific detail that made identification necessary—the crimson staining. This interrogative form ('Wherefore...?') creates dramatic tension: the reader is invited into the investigation. The watchman has recognized the warrior but not yet grasped the significance of the bloodstaining. The comparison to 'him that treadeth in the winefat' introduces the controlling metaphor that will dominate verses 3-6: God's judgment of His enemies is portrayed as the solitary crushing of grapes in a winepress.
commentary.narrative_continued: The TCR rendering emphasizes the interrogative precision: 'Why is Your apparel red, and Your garments like one who treads in the winepress?' This is not casual inquiry but pointed questioning. The watchman is asking God to explain the violence. The answer that follows (verses 3-6) will reveal that this is not random bloodshed but calculated, purposeful judgment—the deliberate execution of divine vengeance. The winepress metaphor is crucial: just as grapes are crushed to release their juice, so are the enemies of God's people crushed to release their lifeblood. But the metaphor does more: it suggests inevitability, cyclical necessity, and the transformation of one substance into another (grapes into wine). Here, human bodies are transformed into spilled blood.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: In the original Hebrew context, the winepress (gat) would have carried immediate resonance for an agricultural people. Winemaking was a communal, seasonal labor that every Judean family understood. The image of someone treading grapes alone (as verse 3 will specify) would have been unusual—winepress work was typically done communally, with music and celebration. The solitary treader thus emphasizes divine isolation and determination. This verse serves as the threshold between identification (verse 1) and explanation (verses 3-6). The watchman has asked 'Who?' and received a name. Now he asks 'Why?'—and God's answer will unfold the whole cosmic purpose of His wrath.

word_study.meaning: The adjective 'red,' derived from the root meaning both the color and the nation of Edom. The TCR notes that this creates a deliberate wordplay: Edom/adom—the nation that will be judged (Edom) is identified by the color of blood (adom).
word_study.significance: This pun is untranslatable in English but powerful in Hebrew: the judgment of Edom is literally written in the redness of blood. The connection between place-name and color suggests that divine judgment is not arbitrary but inscribed in the very language God uses.

word_study.meaning: Lilbushkha (apparel, dress, raiment) and begadim (garments, clothes) are near-synonymous terms. The parallelism emphasizes repetition and fixation on the visual detail of blood-stained clothing.
word_study.significance: The repeated focus on garments serves a rhetorical function: the external marker (blood-staining) makes invisible divine wrath visible and undeniable. What God has done is written on His body for all to witness.

word_study.meaning: A pit or vat for treading grapes, often hewn from stone. The term carries connotations of labor, seasonal cycle, and the transformation of one substance (grapes) into another (wine).
word_study.significance: The gat functions as the concrete image through which Isaiah makes violence intelligible: crushing, inevitable, transformative. It is not beautiful, but it is necessary and purposeful.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah earlier prophesies that the winepress ceases in the judgments against Moab—but here the winepress becomes the instrument of God's judgment, suggesting that divine judgment repurposes human labor and agricultural cycles.

An angel gathers the vintage of the earth and 'trod the winepress' outside the city, and 'blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles.' This is direct typological application of Isaiah's metaphor to Christ's return.

Lamentations uses the same winepress image to describe how God 'hath trodden the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress,' depicting judgment against Israel itself. Isaiah subverts this: now the winepress is used not against God's people but against their enemies.

Joel prophesies 'Put ye in the sickle: for the harvest is ripe' and 'come, tread; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great'—another application of harvest and winepress imagery to divine judgment.

commentary.application: When you witness injustice—oppression, cruelty, corruption—and see the perpetrators apparently unpunished, Isaiah 2 invites you to recognize that you are observing only the beginning of the story. The blood-stained warrior approaches. God does not leave violence unanswered or oppression unavenged. Your call is twofold: first, trust that God's justice, though delayed, is absolute. Do not lose faith because the wicked prosper temporarily. Second, ensure that you are not the one standing in the winepress. The blood-staining is not generic; it comes from the crushing of specific enemies of God's covenant people. Remain faithful to covenant, and you will be preserved when the treading begins.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the solitary treader who comes to execute judgment alone. Matthew 26:39 captures Christ's isolation in Gethsemane: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.' Here, Christ faces the winepress of judgment—drinking the bitter cup of the world's sin—in profound solitude. Yet this is the inverse of Isaiah 63's warrior: Christ drinks judgment not to execute wrath on enemies but to bear the consequences of humanity's rebellion in place of others. At His return, however, the two converge: Christ will tread the winepress of the nations' judgment as the solitary divine warrior.
commentary.historical_context: The winepress was a standard feature of ancient Judean agriculture. Grape harvest occurred in late summer, and communal winemaking was a significant social and religious occasion. Winepresses were often hewn from bedrock and could be quite large—capable of processing the yield from an entire village's vineyards. The image of a solitary figure treading grapes in a winepress would have struck an ancient audience as unusual and ominous: winemaking was supposed to be communal and celebratory, accompanied by singing and social bonding. An alone treader suggested something gone wrong—isolation, darkness, separation from community. This made the metaphor particularly potent for expressing divine judgment as a solitary, terrible act. The Canaanite and Israelite religious calendar both marked grape harvest with festival observance, making it a season of gratitude and communal celebration. To reimagine the winepress as an instrument of divine judgment was thus to invert an expected season of joy into one of terror.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob in 2 Nephi 9:46 uses harvest and vintage imagery when discussing judgment: 'O that ye would awake; awake from a deep sleep, yea, that ye would awake from the sleep of hell, and shake off the awful chains by which ye are bound; for the pains of a carnal state are to be cast away.' While not explicitly using winepress language, Jacob employs similar metaphors of separation and judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants returns to this image when describing the Lord's work: in D&C 76:107, the perdition is described using imagery of separation and outer darkness. The contrast between the winepress of salvation (for the faithful) and the winepress of judgment (for the wicked) appears throughout Restoration revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The winepress can be understood as an inversion of temple-centered ritual: where the temple is the place of communal covenant renewal and communion, the winepress of judgment is a place of absolute isolation and destruction. The solitude of the treader parallels the high priest's solitary entry into the Holy of Holies, but with opposite intention—the priest intercedes and atones; the warrior judges and destroys.

text_kjv: I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.

commentary.narrative: God now responds directly to the watchman's question. He speaks His explanation of the blood-staining in emphatic solitude: 'I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me.' This repeated emphasis on divine isolation is crucial to understanding Isaiah's theodicy. God does not require human armies, allies, or co-laborers to execute judgment. The entire work of redemption and vengeance belongs to God alone. The verse then shifts tense—from past completed action ('I have trodden') to future purpose ('I will tread them')—revealing that what the watchman has already witnessed (the blood-stained warrior) is both a finished act of the past and a prophetic sign of future, comprehensive judgment. The 'anger' and 'fury' are not blind rage but purposeful, measured responses to covenant violation.
commentary.narrative_continued: The TCR rendering clarifies the parallelism: 'I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with Me. I trampled them in My anger and trod them down in My wrath; their lifeblood spattered on My garments, and I stained all My clothing.' Notice the shift from treading (hophal, passive sense of being trodden) to active trampling and treading—the verbs accumulate in intensity. The repetition ('trodden' / 'trampled' / 'trod down') emphasizes the thoroughness and relentlessness of the judgment. The lifeblood spattering and staining is not accidental splash but the inevitable result of the crushing action.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For an exilic community, this message carries extraordinary power: you have felt abandoned by God during Babylon's conquest. You have waited decades for vindication. But now God reveals that His apparent absence was not failure but strategic withdrawal—He was alone because this was His work exclusively, not requiring human cooperation or assistance. The judgment against Babylon and its allies (including Edom) will not be executed by returning Jewish armies but by God's own personal action. This eliminates any doubt about whether the scattered people can reconquer their homeland by force. They cannot. But God can and will. The solitude of judgment is the guarantee of its effectiveness.

word_study.meaning: Darach means to tread or march, often used of treading grapes or walking a path. Ramas means to trample or tread down with destructive intent. The combination emphasizes the crushing force of the action. The Dead Sea Scrolls show no variant here.
word_study.significance: These verbs move from the agricultural (treading grapes) to the martial (trampling enemies). The metaphor seamlessly becomes literal: the grapes represent the peoples being crushed.

word_study.meaning: Alone, by oneself, apart from companions. The term emphasizes isolation and singular agency.
word_study.significance: This word appears three times in Isaiah 63:3-5, forming a deliberate hammer-stroke: God works alone. No human can assist. No coalition of nations can join. This solitary agency underwrites God's absolute power over history.

word_study.meaning: The plural of 'am (people), referring to nations or ethnic groups collectively. The term encompasses all who stand opposed to God's covenant people.
word_study.significance: The judgment is not directed at a single nation but at all peoples—all the nations arrayed against Israel. This universal scope makes the judgment eschatological, not merely historical.

word_study.meaning: Aph is anger or wrath, literally 'nostrils' (the physical locus of anger in ancient Near Eastern thought—flaring nostrils). Chemah is burning wrath, often rendered 'fury.' Together they form a merism of divine displeasure.
word_study.significance: These are not abstract concepts but visceral, embodied experiences of divine wrath. God's fury is not cold calculation but hot indignation at covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: Dam is blood, the substance of life. Nitsacham (from natzach, to gush or spray) is specifically lifeblood, emphasizing the vital fluid that gushes from the crushed bodies.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on blood as a flowing, active substance—spattering, gushing—makes the judgment visceral and undeniable. This is not metaphorical violence but the literal spilling of life-force.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah states 'I wondered that there was no intercessor' and 'his arm brought salvation unto him,' establishing a parallel theme: God's solitary agency and the absence of human helpers. This echo suggests deliberate theological construction within Third Isaiah.

John's Revelation explicitly applies Isaiah's imagery: the risen Christ is 'clothed with a vesture dipped in blood' and 'treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God.' This confirms Christological interpretation of Isaiah 63.

Moses' Song describes God's judgment: 'I will make mine arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh' and 'he will avenge the blood of his servants.' The theme of God's solitary judgment and blood-spilling appears across the biblical corpus.

The Doctrine and Covenants directly quotes Isaiah: 'I have trodden the wine-press alone, and have brought to pass the vengeance and the judgment of which the Father spake.' This Restoration text makes explicit that the divine warrior is Christ.

Nahum proclaims 'God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries.' This echoes Isaiah's emphasis on God's personal, wrathful execution of justice.

commentary.application: You live in an age of collective solutions and collaborative projects. Businesses, governments, and civic organizations operate on the principle that large problems require large coalitions. But Isaiah teaches that God's ultimate judgment and salvation are not collaborative. God works alone. What does this mean for you? First, do not place your ultimate trust in human leadership or political movements to solve the world's fundamental problems. These may serve administrative purposes, but the final judgment and redemption belong to God exclusively. Second, recognize that when you are isolated in your faith—when your community doesn't understand, when you stand alone in keeping covenants—you are not weak but aligned with the pattern God Himself exemplifies. Faithfulness may require solitude. God sanctifies solitude; He walks it Himself.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ fulfills the role of the solitary divine warrior. In Gethsemane, Christ is alone ('Could ye not watch with me one hour?'—Matthew 26:40)—a prefigurement of His solitary bearing of humanity's judgment in His body. Yet this is the inverse of Isaiah's warrior: Christ bears judgment upon Himself for others' sake. At His return, however, Christ will be the treader in the winepress, the solitary executor of cosmic judgment. Hebrews 10:12-13 captures this: 'One sacrifice for sins for ever sat down on the right hand of God... For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.' The work of salvation is complete and singular—Christ's work alone, with none assisting, with full efficacy.
commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern military context influences this passage significantly. Accounts of Assyrian and Babylonian military campaigns often describe the conquering king personally treading enemies underfoot—literally stepping on defeated foes or their bodies. However, Isaiah's inversion is profound: rather than a human king claiming military victory, the divine being Himself executes judgment. This elevated the stakes from geopolitical to cosmic. Moreover, the Dead Sea Scrolls show no textual variants in this verse, indicating that the imagery was stable and accepted throughout the Second Temple period. The solitude of divine judgment would have resonated particularly with exilic Judah, which felt abandoned by God and yet was being promised that this very absence of human military support signified God's intention to work directly. When nations fall, when dynasties crumble, when enemies are destroyed, ancient Near Eastern political theology attributed this to the intervention of the gods. Isaiah transposes this framework: the God of Israel works alone because He has no need for human assistance and because His work encompasses not merely the political but the soteriological (salvific) dimension.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi in 1 Nephi 22:15-19 describes God's personal work: 'He will preserve the righteous by his power, even if it so be that the fulness of his wrath must come upon the people... He shall judge all men according to their works, according to the desire of their hearts.' Like Isaiah, Nephi emphasizes God's personal, individual work in judgment and salvation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:12-14 contains similar language of God's solitary judgment: 'I say unto you, even as I have said, all things unto me are spiritual, and not at any time have I given unto you a law which was temporal; neither any man, nor the children of men; neither Adam, your father, whom I have taken from your bosom' (though this is not directly about winepress judgment). More directly, D&C 76:103-106 describes God's judgment of the wicked in solitude—the sons of perdition face judgment that no human can mitigate or interrupt.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The solitary treader echoes the high priest's solitary entry into the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). However, the high priest's solitude is for intercession and atonement, while the divine warrior's solitude is for judgment and destruction. Yet both are sacred acts performed alone before God. The temple thus provides the framework for understanding divine solitude as appropriate and necessary.

text_kjv: For the day of vengeance is in mine heart, and the year of my redeemed is come.

commentary.narrative: This verse is the theological hinge upon which the entire passage turns. God explains the motivation and meaning of the judgment just described. The 'day of vengeance' and the 'year of my redeemed' are not two separate events but one simultaneous divine action viewed from two perspectives: from the standpoint of the oppressor, it is vengeance; from the standpoint of the covenant people, it is redemption. This simultaneity is extraordinarily important—it means that God's judgment is not arbitrary cruelty toward enemies but necessary liberation of the enslaved. The vengeance is 'in mine heart,' suggesting it is not impulsive but long-considered, covenantally grounded. The TCR rendering clarifies the temporal shift: 'the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redeemed had come'—the perfect tense suggests not a future event but one that has entered the sphere of divine determination and is now entering the sphere of historical fulfillment.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'year of my redeemed' (shnat ge'ulai) employs the kinsman-redeemer concept central to Israelite covenant theology. A go'el (redeemer) is a family member who buys back the enslaved or impoverished relative, restoring them to covenant status and family property. Here, God claims to be Israel's go'el—their kinsman-redeemer. The judgment against Edom and the enemy nations is simultaneously the ransom-purchase that restores Israel to freedom. This explains the dual image of violence and salvation: the same act that crushes the enemy frees the captive. One people's catastrophe is another people's liberation.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The temporal language is crucial: 'the day of vengeance' and 'the year of my redeemed' are known quantities—specific, appointed times fixed in divine counsel. This addressing an exilic community that has experienced the 'day of wrath' inflicted upon them (when Babylon conquered Jerusalem). Now God promises that just as His wrath had its appointed day, so shall His redemption have its appointed year. The parallel structure suggests that judgment and redemption follow the same divine timetable. For the community waiting in exile, this verse offers a theodicy: your suffering has meaning, not because you deserve it but because God's purposes encompass both judgment of the wicked and restoration of the righteous in one coordinated action.

word_study.meaning: Vengeance, retribution, the execution of justice against wrongdoing. The root carries the sense of avenging a wrong or reestablishing balance. It is not mere revenge but the restoration of covenant order.
word_study.significance: Naqam is a legitimate divine prerogative in biblical theology. God avenges the blood of the righteous (Psalm 79:10), the oppressed (Deuteronomy 32:43). Vengeance here is not petty but covenantally mandated justice.

word_study.meaning: Day, a 24-hour period, or in prophetic usage, a divinely appointed season of action. In eschatological contexts, it often refers to a specific moment of divine intervention.
word_study.significance: The 'day of vengeance' appears paired with the 'year of redemption.' These are not meteorological days and years but covenant-determined times when God acts decisively in history.

word_study.meaning: Ge'ulai means 'my redeemed' (people). Ga'al is the kinsman-redeemer verb meaning to buy back, redeem, or restore to family status. The noun ge'ulah encompasses the act of redemption itself.
word_study.significance: The TCR notes this derives from family law: a go'el (redeemer) rescues a relative who has fallen into slavery or debt bondage. God positions Himself as Israel's kinsman-redeemer. This personalizes redemption—it is not abstract liberation but familial rescue performed by a relative.

word_study.meaning: A year, a full cycle of seasons. In prophetic usage, it can denote a season of divine action or, as with the Jubilee, a appointed time of restoration and release.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'day' (sudden, concentrated divine action) with 'year' (a season of sustained restoration) suggests that the moment of vengeance is concentrated while the restoration of the redeemed unfolds over an extended period.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 61 speaks of 'the year of the LORD's favour, and the day of vengeance of our God.' The same terminology appears, suggesting these are coordinated events within Third Isaiah's theological vision of end-time judgment and restoration.

Leviticus establishes the institution of kinsman-redeemer (go'el) who buys back enslaved Israelites. Isaiah applies this family-law concept to God's redemption of Israel, suggesting God is Israel's ultimate go'el.

The Doctrine and Covenants quotes Isaiah and applies it eschatologically to Christ's last day: 'For the day of vengeance is in my heart, for I have sworn an oath unto you that the wicked shall not stand up against the righteous; therefore, if ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall be blessed.'

The psalmists petition God: 'Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed.' Isaiah's promise of vengeance answers this petition.

Jeremiah announces judgment on Babylon: 'Because the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken: for the LORD God of recompences shall surely requite.' Vengeance and recompense belong to God.

commentary.application: The simultaneity of vengeance and redemption challenges any easy optimism about universal salvation. Isaiah insists that the same event that liberates the righteous condemns the wicked. For you as a covenant keeper, this verse means: (1) Your redemption is certain—God has appointed it and will fulfill it. Do not doubt that your covenant faith will be vindicated. (2) But the vindication of the righteous necessarily involves the judgment of the wicked. You cannot have resurrection without accounting for sin. (3) Live accordingly. The year of redemption has come near (in Latter-day Saint understanding, it is approaching in our own epoch). Ensure you stand on the side of the redeemed, not the judged.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate go'el—the kinsman-redeemer. Hebrews 2:14-15 captures this: 'Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.' Christ assumes kinship with humanity (takes on flesh and blood) precisely to redeem us from bondage. Yet Christ is also the executor of judgment: Matthew 25:31-46 depicts Christ as the judge who separates righteous from wicked at the parousia. In Christ, vengeance and redemption converge: His death is our redemption (kinsman-redeemer work); His return is the world's judgment (divine warrior work).
commentary.historical_context: The concept of the kinsman-redeemer (go'el) derives from ancient Near Eastern family law, specifically mechanisms for protecting the property and dignity of vulnerable family members. When an Israelite fell into debt slavery, his kinsman had the right (and eventually the duty) to ransom him. When a man died without heirs, his kinsman had the obligation to produce an heir for the family line (as in Ruth). This institution undergirds much of Israelite social cohesion and covenant theology. By applying go'el language to God's relationship with Israel, Isaiah transposed family law into cosmic history: God becomes Israel's ultimate kinsman, bound by loyalty (hesed), obligated to rescue the enslaved, responsible for restoring what was lost. This would have resonated profoundly with exilic Judah, who felt cast off and abandoned. God's claim to be their go'el meant that they were still family, still under His care, and still destined for restoration according to the deepest structures of covenant relationship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi in 2 Nephi 10:24-25 speaks of redemption through Christ: 'Wherefore, redemption cometh in and through the Holy Messiah; for he is full of grace and truth. Behold, he offereth himself a sacrifice for sin, to answer the ends of the law, unto all those who have a broken heart and a contrite spirit.' The Day of Atonement (the central redemptive act) is paired with the judgment of those who reject it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:40-48 describes the 'celestial kingdom,' where the redeemed dwell, set in contrast to outer darkness reserved for the sons of perdition. The simultaneous vindication of the faithful and judgment of the wicked appears as a Restoration principle: 'And thus we saw the glory of the celestial, which surpasses all understanding' (D&C 76:89) alongside 'And this is the condemnation... that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light' (D&C 84:53).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The go'el concept is central to the temple's redemptive theology. In the endowment, participants enact the restoration of covenant relationship—the redemption of humanity through Christ's role as the ultimate Redeemer. The simultaneous announcement of judgment (for those who reject covenant) and redemption (for the faithful) mirrors temple theology: one baptismal font, one covenant, but two eternal destinations based on the response to God's redemptive offer.

text_kjv: And I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold: therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; and my fury, it upheld me.

commentary.narrative: The theme of divine solitude reaches its crescendo. God turns inward, reflecting on the isolation that characterized His work. The verb 'looked' (waise't) suggests divine survey or assessment—God examined the cosmos to see if any being could assist in the work of redemption and judgment. The result: 'there was none to help.' The second line deepens this: 'I wondered that there was none to uphold'—God's wonder (washtomem) expresses astonishment, the impossibility of finding a co-laborer. This is not sadness but confirmation that the work of cosmic redemption falls exclusively within God's purview. No human army, no angelic coalition, no created being can assist.
commentary.narrative_continued: The turn to positive agency is sharp: 'therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me.' The arm (zero'i) is the instrument of God's power—it appears throughout Scripture as the metaphor for divine action (God's mighty arm in Egypt, God's arm to save, etc.). Here, God's own arm is sufficient; no external support is needed. The final clause introduces a paradox: 'and my fury, it upheld me.' Wrath becomes the sustaining force. While humans might weaken or falter, God's fury—His righteous indignation at covenant violation—strengthens and sustains Him. The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ) show a minor variant here: the scroll adds a final he to the pronoun, reading 'hi'ah' instead of 'hi',' but this is merely a scribal convention and carries no theological shift.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The TCR rendering clarifies the reversal: 'I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one upheld Me. So My own arm brought salvation, and My wrath — it sustained Me.' The structure moves from (1) divine survey and disappointed expectations, through (2) pivotal recognition ('therefore'), to (3) self-sufficiency and empowerment.
