These practitioners of abomination—sitting in graves, eating swine—are constructing an identity of superiority and separation. The TCR rendering captures the arrogance perfectly: 'Keep to yourself — do not come near me, for I am too holy for you!' This is not humility but pride masquerading as piety. It echoes the Pharisaical self-righteousness that Jesus would later condemn: those who distance themselves from others on grounds of supposed spiritual purity while remaining internally corrupt (Matthew 23:25–28).
commentary.narrative_continued: The mechanics of this false holiness are worth examining. These individuals may have developed an elite spirituality: secret initiations, hidden wisdom, communion with the dead (which they may have claimed gave them access to divine truth). From their perspective, their distance from ordinary Torah observers is justified—they possess esoteric knowledge. From Isaiah's perspective, they have simply inverted righteousness. The gap between their self-perception and reality is absolute. They claim to be 'too holy' (qedashtiykha—more consecrated, more set apart than others), when in fact they are defiled. This is the fundamental spiritual danger Isaiah identifies: sincere people convinced of their own righteousness while systematically violating covenant.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: God's response is visceral and immediate: 'These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burneth all the day.' The Hebrew phrase 'ashan be'appi' (smoke in my nostrils) is an image of irritation and sustained anger. Smoke is not a clean smell; it is an irritant that causes discomfort and does not dissipate but lingers. The doubled phrase 'a fire that burneth all the day' intensifies the image: God's anger is not momentary rage that cools, but a smoldering, persistent heat. The 'all the day' (kol hayom) echoes verse 2's 'all the day' (kol hayom), connecting God's perpetual outstretched arms (v. 2) with God's perpetual, smoldering anger (v. 5). One cannot reject the outstretched arms indefinitely without encountering the burning fire. The verse marks the transition from indictment (vv. 1–5) to judgment (v. 6).

word_study.term_english: Stand by thyself, come not near
word_study.term_original: קְרַב אֵלֶיךָ אַל־תִּגַּשׁ־בִּי (qrav aleikha al tigash bi)
word_study.meaning: Stand near you, do not approach me. A command to keep distance, to separate.
word_study.significance: The grammar is slightly unusual (imperative + negative imperative), but the meaning is clear: 'You stay back; don't come near me.' This is a command to separation based on claimed spiritual superiority. The irony is that those practicing abomination are commanding others away on grounds of holiness.

word_study.meaning: I have consecrated/sanctified you (or I am sanctified/more holy). Can be reflexive ('I have made myself holy') or comparative ('I am holier than you').
word_study.significance: The root qadash (holy, sanctify, set apart) is being claimed by those who have actually desecrated themselves. True qedusha (holiness) means separation from defilement and consecration to God. These people claim it while practicing defilement. This is the climax of irony in verses 1–6: those most defiled claim the highest holiness.

word_study.meaning: smoke in my nostrils/nose. An image of irritation, displeasure, or smoldering anger.
word_study.significance: Ashan (smoke) is not a flattering metaphor. Smoke is an irritant that lingers, obscures, and causes distress. God is not merely displeased but actively irritated by these people. The image is visceral: God's anger is as real and immediate as the irritation of smoke in one's nostrils.

word_study.term_english: a fire that burneth all the day
word_study.term_original: אֵשׁ יֹקֶדֶת כָּל־הַיּוֹם (esh yokedet kol hayom)
word_study.meaning: a fire that burns/blazes all day long. Yokedet conveys active burning, flames, heat.
word_study.significance: The fire is not momentary indignation but sustained judgment. The phrase 'all the day' (kol hayom) has appeared twice before: in verse 2 ('all the day' God stretched out His arms) and implicitly throughout the passage. Here it appears again in the judgment section. The contrast is stark: God's mercy is unceasing, but so is His justice toward those who reject it.

cross_references.connection: Jesus condemns the Pharisees: 'Ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess... Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.' This is Jesus applying Isaiah 65:5's principle to His own time.

The Pharisee in the parable stands and prays 'God, I thank thee that I am not as other men...' This is precisely the attitude Isaiah 65:5 condemns: false holiness based on separation from and contempt for others.

Proverbs warns against 'a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness.' Isaiah 65:5 is the prophetic application of this proverb to Israel's covenant community.

Earlier in Isaiah, God declares to Israel: 'When ye spread forth your hands, I will hide mine eyes from you... Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes.' The same God who offers cleansing (ch. 1) now expresses smoldering anger at those who reject it (ch. 65).

King Benjamin teaches: 'And now, my brethren, I would that ye should do as ye have hitherto done. And I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be led to a place on the right hand of God, in the kingdom of his Father.' The Book of Mormon contrasts true covenant keeping with the false holiness Isaiah condemns.

commentary.historical_context: The scenario Isaiah describes reflects real tension in post-exile Judean society. Some members of the returning community had maintained strict Torah observance during exile and upon return. Others had accommodated themselves to Mesopotamian religious and cultural practices. As these communities re-integrated, conflict emerged. The strict observers viewed the accommodationists as defiled; the accommodationists viewed themselves as cosmopolitan and sophisticated. Some may have developed an elite spirituality—secret cult practices, esoteric wisdom—that they believed elevated them above ordinary Torah keeping. For these practitioners, their distancing of themselves from 'ordinary' Jews was not arrogance but justified separation of the pure from the impure. Isaiah exposes this as inversion: the 'pure' are actually defiled; the 'impure' whom they reject may be more faithful to covenant than they are. The historical parallels are instructive: religious elites in many times and places have claimed superior spiritual status based on hidden knowledge, esoteric practice, or claimed access to divine truth unavailable to the masses—while living in ways incompatible with the revealed covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 28:12–15 describes a similar apostasy: 'And they shall contend one with another; and their priests shall contend one with another; and they shall teach with their precepts the doctrines of men... And they shall clothe themselves with robes of seeming sanctity... And there shall be many which shall say: Eat, drink, and be merry, for tomorrow we die; and it shall be well with us.' The parallel is not exact, but the pattern of claimed holiness masking actual violation of covenant is similar.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 50:7–9 offers guidance on discerning true spiritual authority: 'Wherefore, by this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them... By this ye may know if a man is of God: If a man loveth God with all his heart, and trusteth in God, and serveth him with all his might, mind and strength, then is man of God.' The measure is not claimed holiness but actual covenant keeping and love.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple covenant includes promises to consecrate oneself to God's work. False holiness—claiming spiritual superiority without actual consecration—is a violation of that covenant. The progression from verse 2 (outstretched arms, available mercy) to verse 5 (smoldering fire, unavailable judgment) tracks the response of those who repeatedly reject the covenant mercy offered at the Temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies true holiness—a holiness that is not separative but inclusive. Jesus regularly violated the purity boundaries the Pharisees maintained (eating with tax collectors, touching the woman at the well, healing on the Sabbath) not because He disrespected holiness but because He understood that true qedusha (holiness) is a matter of the heart and covenant commitment, not external observance divorced from inner transformation. Yet Christ also made clear that this inner transformation must result in moral reformation: 'Go, and sin no more' (John 8:11). The false holiness of Isaiah 65:5 is condemned; the true holiness of repentance and covenant keeping is celebrated.
commentary.application: Isaiah 65:5 is perhaps the most convicting verse in this passage for modern members. It addresses the subtle danger of spiritual pride—the way people can violate covenants while maintaining a sense of superior righteousness. This might manifest as: (1) claiming deep spirituality while maintaining relationships or habits that violate covenants; (2) distancing oneself from fellow members deemed 'less righteous' while harboring secret transgressions; (3) adopting counterfeit spiritual practices (meditation divorced from gospel principles, dabbling in alternative spiritualities) while maintaining outward Church adherence; (4) claiming special knowledge or revelation unavailable to Church leaders and members. The verse demands radical honesty: Am I maintaining a false self-image of holiness? Do I distance myself from others on grounds of spiritual superiority while actually violating my own covenants? Am I smoke in God's nose—an irritant that provokes not approval but sustained anger? The verse teaches that God's response to sustained false holiness is not patience but 'a fire that burneth all the day.' Repentance must include not only stopping the transgression but confronting and confessing the false holiness that accompanied it.

text_kjv: Behold, it is written before me: I will not keep silence, but will recompense, even recompense into their bosom,

commentary.narrative: After the extended indictment of verses 1–5, verse 6 announces God's judgment with finality and inevitability. The phrase 'Behold, it is written before me' (hinne ketuva lephanai) invokes the image of a divine ledger or record. The verb 'written' suggests that these offenses have been recorded—they are not forgotten, not overlooked, not subject to excuse or mitigation. In ancient Near Eastern context, both Egyptian and Mesopotamian mythologies depicted divine recording of human deeds. The phrase 'before me' (lephanai—literally, 'to/toward my face') emphasizes that the record is not hidden or at a distance; God has it constantly before Him, sustaining His memory and informing His judgment. The TCR rendering 'Behold, it is written before Me: I will not keep silent' stresses the connection: the existence of the written record compels God's speech and action.
commentary.narrative_continued: God's declaration 'I will not keep silence' (lo echeshe) is the inverse of the silence God maintained through Israel's rebellion (chapters 63–64 implicitly asked, 'Why is God silent?'). The answer is: not because God is absent but because God was extending mercy and opportunity for repentance. But silence cannot continue indefinitely. God must speak, must judge, must act according to justice. The doubled 'I will recompense' (shillamti veshillamti—literally 'I will repay, I will repay' or with fuller grammatical form 'I will recompense, even I will recompense') intensifies the certainty and emphasis. There is no ambiguity: judgment is certain, proportional, complete. This is not personal vengeance but legal recompense, the payment due for contracted violation.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The phrase 'into their bosom' (al cheiqam) is visceral and immediate. The 'bosom' (cheiq) is the front of the body where one holds something close—it represents the most intimate space. Judgment is not distant or abstract; it is placed directly into the hands and lives of the transgressors, impossible to evade or escape. The verse marks the transition from indictment to consequence. Verses 7–16 will elaborate on the specifics of that judgment, but verse 6 announces the fundamental principle: God's patience is finite, His memory is eternal, and His justice is inescapable. The verse also echoes Psalm 69:28 ('Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous') and anticipates Revelation 20:12 ('And the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life'). The image of divine bookkeeping recurs throughout scripture as a way to express God's comprehensive knowledge and inevitable justice.

word_study.meaning: written before me, inscribed in my presence. Ketuva is the feminine passive participle of katav (to write). Lephanai literally means 'to/toward my face.'
word_study.significance: The image suggests a divine ledger or record kept before God's face. The verb is passive—the record is written (by some force of cosmic accountability) and kept by God. This is not human recording but divine, comprehensive recording.

word_study.meaning: I will not keep silent, I will not refrain from speaking. Chashah means to be silent, to refrain, to hold back.
word_study.significance: The verb asserts God's determination to speak and act. God has not been indifferent but has (until now) extended patience. The breaking of silence marks a decisive shift from mercy to judgment.

word_study.meaning: I will recompense, I will repay. The doubling intensifies: not merely 'I will repay' but 'I will repay with certainty and completeness.'
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'I will repay — I will repay' captures the emphasis perfectly. This is not tentative or conditional; it is absolute and inevitable. The doubled verb creates a rhetorical effect of overwhelming certainty.

word_study.meaning: into their lap/bosom, into their breast. Cheiq refers to the front of the body, the lap, or the breast—the area one holds close or nurtures.
word_study.significance: The image is intimate and unavoidable. Judgment is not imposed from a distance but placed directly into the hands of the transgressors. The TCR rendering 'into their lap' emphasizes this immediacy. There is no escape; judgment is as close as one's own body.

cross_references.connection: David petitions: 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.' Isaiah 65:6 invokes the same image of divine bookkeeping as the basis for judgment.

John's vision describes: 'And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.' This is the eschatological fulfillment of Isaiah 65:6's principle.

The prophet describes: 'Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.' This is the inverse of Isaiah 65:6: the righteous are written in God's book; the wicked face judgment.

The Lord speaks: 'For I the Lord, in the beginning believed in your faith; and I have covenanted with you... that you might receive whatsoever you should ask the Father in my name.' The inverse: those who break covenant by rejecting God's outstretched hands face recompense rather than blessing.

Alma teaches the principle of restoration (recompense): 'Therefore, my son, see that you are merciful unto your brethren... And see that all these things are done in wisdom and order; for it is not requisite that a man should run faster than he has strength.' The principle of divine recompense operates universally: good is rewarded, evil is punished, according to what one has done.

commentary.historical_context: The imagery of divine bookkeeping is ancient and cross-cultural. Egyptian theology included the weighing of the heart against Ma'at (truth); Mesopotamian thought involved divine recording of deeds. In the Hebrew tradition, God's comprehensive knowledge and memory is expressed through metaphors of writing and records. The post-exile context is crucial: Judah is under Persian rule and subject to Persian legal and administrative systems, which were famous for their written records and archives. Isaiah may be drawing on this cultural familiarity—just as the Persian king maintains records for administrative justice, so God maintains records for cosmic justice. The verse would have resonated powerfully with a community recently returned from exile, acutely aware that historical events are recorded and that those records determine what is remembered and what is forgotten.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41:3–4 teaches: 'Now, it is plain that it was appointed unto men to die; and after death, they must come to judgment, even the Lord God, the Eternal Judge of both quick and dead... Now, there is a death which is called a temporal death; and the death of Christ shall loose the bands of this temporal death, that all shall be raised from this temporal death.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that divine judgment is inescapable and universal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:110 declares: 'That you may be prepared in all things when I shall send you again to magnify the office of your calling.' The written record of obedience determines one's preparation and worthiness. Conversely, the record of transgression determines judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple endowment teaches that all actions are witnessed—by God, by angels, by the cosmos. Nothing is hidden from the divine record. The Temple covenant is made with full knowledge that one stands before witnesses and that one's covenant-keeping or covenant-breaking will be recorded eternally. Isaiah 65:6 reinforces this: the written record is comprehensive and determines eternal consequence.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate expression of both God's silence and God's speech regarding judgment. Through His earthly ministry, Christ extended grace and opportunity for repentance, embodying God's patience and outstretched arms. Yet Christ also taught extensively about divine judgment and accountability. In Matthew 25:31–46, Christ describes the final judgment, where deeds are rewarded or punished according to one's actions toward the least of His brethren. The 'book of life' (Revelation 3:5, Revelation 20:12) in which names are written or blotted out is ultimately Christ's determination—He is the judge before whom the books are opened. Christ breaks God's silence not through condemnation but through redemption; yet for those who reject that redemption, His final word is judgment.
commentary.application: Isaiah 65:6 confronts modern members with the seriousness of covenant. The phrase 'it is written before me' suggests that God does not forget, does not overlook, and does not treat our actions as irrelevant. Every violation of covenant is recorded; every acceptance of the gospel and subsequent turning away is noted. For some members, this verse offers comfort: the righteous are remembered and will be rewarded. For others, it offers warning: hidden transgressions are not actually hidden. The verse also teaches that God's patience, while real and extended, is not infinite. The phrase 'I will not keep silence' warns that a time comes when judgment must be rendered. The principle operates both personally and collectively: individuals who reject mercy face judgment; societies that persist in wickedness eventually face divine consequence. The modern application might be phrased thus: What is being written in God's record regarding my covenant keeping? What transgressions am I maintaining despite my claimed faith? When will I stop drifting and return to full covenant commitment? The verse offers no escape—judgment is 'written before' God, inevitable and inescapable. Yet it also offers opportunity: repentance can change what will be written before Him. The record is not sealed until death.

text_kjv: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry: behold, my servants shall drink, but ye shall be thirsty: behold, my servants shall rejoice, but ye shall be ashamed:

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens God's response to the lament of chapters 63–64 with a sharp, threefold judgment. The structure is deliberately antithetical: every promise to God's servants is shadowed by its inverse for the rebels. The 'servants' (avadai) are those who have called upon God's name (65:1); the 'you' are those who have rejected Him for Fortune and Destiny (65:11). This is not a future judgment delayed—the tone suggests an immediate reality. The parallelism (eat/hunger, drink/thirst, rejoice/shame) creates an overwhelming sense of relational consequence: covenant fidelity brings provision; covenant violation brings deprivation.

The word 'therefore' (laken) ties this entire passage back to the preceding indictment. God is not issuing an arbitrary punishment but a lawful response to those who have actively sought what He did not appoint (65:12). The threefold repetition of 'behold, my servants' emphasizes that the distinction is entirely relational—it is membership in God's household, not merit or effort, that determines outcome. To eat, drink, and rejoice are the basic goods of human flourishing; to hunger, thirst, and be ashamed are their reversal. The contrast is absolute because the covenant choice is absolute.

word_study.meaning: My servants; those bound in covenant relationship to the master. The term denotes not servility but intimate household membership and responsibility.
word_study.significance: Throughout Isaiah, God's servants are those who obey His word and seek Him. Here, avadai stands in stark contrast to those who 'call upon a name which I have not appointed' (65:11). The repetition ('my servants... my servants... my servants') hammers home that belonging to God is the single decisive factor.

word_study.meaning: To be ashamed, put to shame, confounded. A state of public exposure and loss of honor before God and others.
word_study.significance: Shame is the inverse of the 'glory' (kabod) promised to God's servants in 65:14. The rebels will be exposed for their rebellion; their cover will be stripped away. In covenant theology, shame is separation from God's honor.

word_study.meaning: You will hunger; lack sustenance. The verb can be physical or spiritual—the deprivation of what sustains life.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves 'hungry' to highlight the absolute reversal: those who rejected God's provision will find themselves without it. This echoes Deuteronomy's covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:48–57).

cross_references.connection: These verses identify the rebels as those who 'prepare a table for Fortune and fill a drink-offering unto Destiny,' establishing the context for why verse 13's judgment falls upon them.
The covenant curses in Deuteronomy establish the pattern of deprivation (hunger, thirst, shame) that Isaiah 65:13 echoes—confirming this as a lawful response to covenant violation.
Nephi applies Isaiah's servants/rebels contrast to the righteous and wicked in the last days, confirming the Restoration reading of this passage as a judgment applicable to all covenant peoples.
The theme of a 'new name' (verse 15) has its NT counterpart in Revelation's promise of a new name to the faithful, reinforcing the eschatological arc from judgment to renewal.
The Lord's voice through Joseph Smith echoes the structure and tone of Isaiah 65:13, warning the wicked and promising the faithful—demonstrating the continuing application of this covenant principle.

commentary.historical_context: The historical backdrop of Isaiah 65 is the post-exilic community's struggle with syncretism. By the late 6th century BCE, some Judeans had begun incorporating foreign religious practices (evidenced by the 'Fortune' and 'Destiny' deities mentioned in verse 11, likely Gad and Meni, Aramaic-derived gods). Meanwhile, a faithful remnant continued in covenant obedience. The distinction Isaiah draws—between God's servants and the apostates—reflects the social and religious fracture within the returning community. The threefold contrast (eating, drinking, rejoicing versus their opposites) would have been unmistakable to an audience living near subsistence: these are not abstract spiritual conditions but daily realities. Hunger and thirst were not metaphors in the ancient world; they were the most pressing forms of social punishment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 22:15-16 cites and applies this passage, interpreting the 'servants' as the righteous in the last days and the 'ye' (rebels) as the wicked who will be destroyed. Nephi's application affirms that Isaiah's judgment applies across covenant dispensations. 2 Nephi 30:10 also echoes the theme of the righteous receiving what they need while the wicked are cut off.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14-16 uses similar antithetical language: 'I have called upon the faithful and the elect of my church, whom I have appointed with all the powers and keys of this priesthood, to seal up the testimonies, and to seal up the law, and to testify unto the world against their wickedness. Wherefore, I the Lord God will send forth flies upon the face of the earth, which shall eat their flesh, and cause them to sting because of their iniquity—in like manner as I have sent forth the fierce anger of my wrath upon all nations.' The pattern of covenant reward for the faithful and judgment for rebels is consistent throughout Restoration scripture.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The 'servants' who eat, drink, and rejoice anticipate the temple's function as a place of covenant nourishment and joy. Those who partake of the Lord's table in righteousness are sustained; those who break covenant are cut off from that sustenance. The contrast prefigures the separation of righteous from wicked that the temple's ordinances enact symbolically.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 65:13 typologically prefigures the separation at Christ's return when the righteous (His servants) receive eternal life (sustenance, joy) and the wicked receive judgment (deprivation, shame). The 'servants' are those who have entered into covenant with the Servant of servants—Jesus Christ—and thus share in His exaltation. Those who reject Him find themselves hungering in His absence.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse poses a clarifying question: Am I living as one of God's servants, or am I seeking provision from other sources? The verse invites honest examination of what we truly depend on for sustenance—not just physical food but spiritual nourishment. Covenant fidelity brings a sufficiency that those outside covenant cannot access. The judgment here is not arbitrary vindictiveness but the natural consequence of covenant choice: the God we serve is the God who provides. If we serve another, we find ourselves empty.

text_kjv: Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart, but ye shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall howl for vexation of spirit.

commentary.narrative:
The judgment continues into the emotional and spiritual register. If verse 13 addressed the physical deprivations of hunger and thirst, verse 14 penetrates to the heart and spirit—the inward reality. The 'servants shall sing for joy of heart' presents an image of spontaneous, irrepressible gladness. The Hebrew 'joy of heart' (tub lev) suggests not a fleeting emotion but a deep, settled contentment rooted in right relationship. By contrast, the rebels 'cry for sorrow of heart and howl for vexation of spirit.' The escalation from 'cry' to 'howl' (yalilu) conveys a loss of composure, a breakdown of restraint—the sound of desperation.

The Covenant Rendering notes that 'broken spirit' (shever ruach) is precisely the inverse of the 'contrite spirit' God cherishes (66:2). The same brokenness can lead either to repentance (if met with God's grace) or to despair (if stubbornly maintained in rebellion). For Isaiah's audience, this distinction would have been viscerally clear: the faithful sing; the faithless wail. The contrast moves from external goods (food, drink) to internal states (heart, spirit), suggesting that the judgment penetrates the whole self. To be severed from God is not merely material deprivation but spiritual desolation.

word_study.meaning: Shall sing/cry out in exultation from gladness/goodness of heart. Yaron denotes a loud, jubilant cry; tub lev denotes the inner condition of wholeness and well-being.
word_study.significance: This is the sound of covenant blessing—unforced, spontaneous joy. The Covenant Rendering preserves 'glad heart' to emphasize that the joy springs from an inward condition of shalom (peace, wholeness), not from external circumstance.

word_study.meaning: You will cry out/shriek from pain/grief of heart. Ke'ev denotes acute pain or anguish.
word_study.significance: The mirror-image verb tzaka (cry out, shriek) is the same root used for distress and desperation. The 'pain of heart' (ke'ev lev) stands as the exact opposite of the gladness ('joy of heart') promised to the servants.

word_study.meaning: You will wail from brokenness/shattering of spirit. Telil is an onomatopoeia for wailing/howling; shever ruach denotes a shattered, crushed inner self.
word_study.significance: The escalation from 'cry' to 'howl' (telil) suggests an abandonment of dignity, a regression into animal-like desperation. Shever ruach—'broken spirit'—is contrasted in 66:2 with the 'contrite spirit' that God receives with honor. The difference is crucial: a spirit broken in repentance opens to God; a spirit broken in despair closes upon itself.

cross_references.connection: This verse promises that God regards 'him that is of a contrite and humble spirit' (ruach niddakah). The contrast with 65:14's 'broken spirit' clarifies that repentance opens the way to God's favor, while hardened rebellion leads only to despair.
The psalmist's call to 'make a joyful noise' echoes the 'singing' of God's servants in Isaiah 65:14, establishing a liturgical pattern of covenant joy.
Nephi warns that the wicked 'shall come down in sorrow, yea, even to a terrible awful doom, because they have rejected the Lord'—echoing Isaiah's image of the rebels' howling and anguish.

Alma's account of his spiritual wretchedness before repentance ('and this is the torment of the wicked') parallels the 'sorrow of heart' and 'vexation of spirit' Isaiah describes for those who reject God.

The promise that the righteous's 'confidence shall wax strong in the presence of God' invokes the same assurance as Isaiah's 'servants shall sing'—a deep, inward confidence rooted in covenant standing.

commentary.historical_context:
In ancient Near Eastern thought, the 'heart' (lev) and 'spirit' (ruach) were understood as seats of will, intention, and emotional capacity—not merely subjective feeling but the operative center of the self. An individual whose heart was glad and spirit whole was said to be in right relationship; one whose heart ached and spirit broke was thought to be under divine judgment or demonic assault. The contrast Isaiah draws between singing and howling would have been understood not as personality types but as signs of covenantal standing. A community that sang together in festivals and processions (as depicted in Psalm 100, 1 Samuel 10:5) demonstrated its harmony with God; a people reduced to wailing evidenced their rupture from covenant.

Archaeological evidence from post-exilic Judah shows signs of both religious consolidation (around the Jerusalem temple cult) and persistent syncretism (adoption of Aramaean and Persian religious elements). Isaiah's vivid contrast may well reflect the audible reality of this divided community: the faithful worshipping with gladness in the temple, while the syncretists pursued foreign rites in desperation, finding no peace.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36's description of spiritual anguish ('My soul did quicken, and I remembered my pains no more; yea, my soul was filled with joy as exceeding as my pain') inverts Isaiah's judgment: those who repent move from the wailing of verse 14 to the singing of verse 14's promise. The Book of Mormon shows that the same potential for either joy or anguish depends on covenant choice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 18:10-11 affirms that the souls of the faithful matter infinitely to God, suggesting that their internal state—their joy or sorrow—is precious to Him. The singing of the righteous in Isaiah 65:14 anticipates the celestial chorus praised in D&C 84:98 ('And they who remain shall also be quickened; nevertheless, they shall return again to their own place, to enjoy that which they are worthy of; For a man who is put into prison by the manifestation of my word is not my servant').
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The singing in the temple (as described in 1 Chronicles 25, where David appointed singers 'to prophesy with harps, stringed instruments, and cymbals') exemplifies the 'joy of heart' promised to God's servants. By contrast, those who reject covenant access to the temple are cut off from that liturgical joy. The temple is the space where God's servants sing together; exclusion from it brings spiritual desolation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate 'servant' who 'shall sing' in the midst of the assembled righteous (Hebrews 2:12, citing Psalm 22:22). His resurrection singing—joy in the presence of the Father—becomes the model and source of all joy for those who enter covenant with Him. Conversely, those who reject Him face the 'outer darkness' where there is only 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' (Matthew 25:30)—the 'howling' Isaiah describes.
commentary.application: This verse invites self-examination about our inner state. Are we living with the 'joy of heart' that covenant fidelity brings, or are we experiencing the spiritual anguish that separation from God produces? The passage suggests that our emotional and spiritual condition is not incidental but diagnostic—a sign of our actual covenant standing. If we find ourselves in despair, Isaiah offers not judgment but a way back: the contrite spirit of verse 66:2 is still received by God. Our current interior condition is not our destiny unless we refuse repentance.

text_kjv: And ye shall leave your name for a curse unto my chosen: for the Lord GOD shall slay thee, and call his servants by another name:

commentary.narrative:
The judgment escalates from personal deprivation and internal anguish to social obliteration. The rebels' name becomes a byword—a formula of cursing used by God's chosen. To have one's name become a curse is, in ancient Israelite thought, the ultimate erasure. A name carried identity and lineage (Genesis 48:16; Ruth 4:10-11); it was how one endured after death. To have one's name become a curse is to be remembered only for what one opposed, to become a cautionary tale rather than an ancestor. The phrase 'ye shall leave your name' suggests a deliberate abandonment—the rebels lose their own name and it is repurposed as an instrument of judgment against them.

The verse then shifts to an affirmation: God 'shall call his servants by another name.' The contrast here is between annihilation and renewal. The rebels lose their name; the servants receive a new one. This is not a casual renaming but a covenant act—a public declaration of changed status and identity. The Covenant Rendering notes that 'another name' (shem acher) anticipates Revelation 2:17 ('To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written'). In both cases, a new name signals a new identity granted by God Himself—a belonging that transcends human genealogy.

word_study.term_english: leave your name for a curse
word_study.meaning: Your name as a curse/oath of cursing. Shbua can denote both an oath formula and a curse formula—here, your name will be invoked in curses by the faithful.
word_study.significance: This reverses the Abrahamic blessing (Genesis 12:2-3): 'I will make of thee a great nation; and I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee.' The rebels find their name invoked not in blessing but as a curse—they become an anti-type of the patriarchs.

word_study.meaning: Put you to death; cause you to die. The verb hemit carries the sense of active termination, not mere natural death.
word_study.significance: This is judicial execution—the consequence of covenant breach. The term emphasizes that God, not chance or fate, effects the judgment.

word_study.meaning: A different name; a new identity. In covenant theology, a new name signifies transformation of status and destiny.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves this term deliberately because it echoes throughout scripture: Abram becomes Abraham (Genesis 17:5), Sarai becomes Sarah (Genesis 17:15), Saul becomes Paul (Acts 13:9), Simon becomes Peter (Matthew 16:18). A new name marks a new covenant bond. The phrase appears again in 62:2 ('Thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name') and in Revelation 2:17 and 3:12.

cross_references.connection: Christ promises to write 'a new name' upon the overcomer—directly echoing Isaiah 65:15's covenant renewal through divine renaming. The new name marks transfer from one household (the world) to God's household (the New Jerusalem).
Earlier in Isaiah, the same promise appears: 'Thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.' This establishes renaming as a consistent pattern of covenant restoration.
Abram and Sarai's renaming as Abraham and Sarah exemplify the covenant renewal through new names that Isaiah 65:15 promises—a pattern repeated throughout scripture as the sign of changed standing.

Lehi's promise to his sons includes the assurance that their seed will prosper 'if they keep the commandments of the Lord,' establishing the same covenant causality: obedience leads to a name and place; rebellion leads to erasure.

The doctrine that each celestial glory has 'a new name' written upon it affirms the Restoration understanding that covenant membership carries a divine name written upon us—anticipating the 'another name' promised in Isaiah 65:15.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel and the Near East, a curse formula often took the form 'May you be like [name of the cursed]'—meaning the name itself became proverbial for ruin. Examples include the biblical phrases 'an Amalekite' (one who wars against God's people), 'a Philistine' (one who resists God's purpose), or later, 'a Judas' (one who betrays). To have one's name become such a formula was the gravest social death. Conversely, to receive a new name from the deity was a mark of extraordinary favor—it meant being incorporated into the divine household with a new status and mission. The practice appears in Egyptian coronation texts (new pharaohs received throne names) and in Persian court tradition (favored officials received new names by royal decree). Isaiah's promise of a new name for God's servants places them in this honorific tradition—they are not merely spared but elevated to a status beyond their former identity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon echoes this principle in 1 Nephi 13:37, where the Gentiles 'shall be numbered among the seed of thy father' if they accept covenant—a new name and identity, essentially. Also, Alma 32 describes how faith 'becometh more and more fruitful,' suggesting a transformative naming or identity shift through covenant commitment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 130:11 explicitly teaches that in the celestial kingdom, each person receives 'a new name.' D&C 109:36 (part of the Kirtland Temple dedication) speaks of God's people being 'called by a new name, which is the covenant that [God] has made with [them].' This Restoration teaching confirms that the 'new name' in Isaiah 65:15 is not metaphorical but literal—an actual name given at covenant renewal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where one's name is sealed and made eternal—where the 'new name' promised in Isaiah becomes operative. At endowment, one receives a new name not to be spoken outside the temple, signifying a new identity before God. This directly fulfills Isaiah's promise: God's servants receive 'another name' that marks them as His in a way transcending earthly genealogy.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus receives a 'new name' (Revelation 3:12, Philippians 2:9-11: 'Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name') as the ultimate overcomer. All who are sealed to Him likewise receive a new name—incorporation into His household and identity. The 'another name' of Isaiah 65:15 is ultimately the name of Christ, the true sealer and namer of the faithful.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse speaks to the power of covenant identity. Our membership in God's household is not incidental but constitutive of who we are. We are 'called by a new name'—not merely 'Latter-day Saint' as a label, but a transformed identity that places us in a new relationship with God. This also cautions us: if we turn from covenant, we risk becoming a 'byword'—known not for what we were called to be but for what we rejected. Conversely, fidelity to covenant means we are being sealed with a name that endures eternally, written in the records of heaven.

text_kjv: That he who blesseth himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he that sweareth in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hid from mine eyes.

commentary.narrative:
The vision shifts from judgment to restoration. After the series of inversions (servants eat/rebels hunger, servants rejoice/rebels are ashamed, servants receive new names/rebels' names become curses), verse 16 announces a transition into a new age where all swearing and blessing are directed to God. The Covenant Rendering's preservation of 'God of Amen' rather than translating it as 'God of truth' is crucial: 'amen' is not merely an abstract truth but faithful, reliable keeping of covenant. God is the one upon whom all oaths are sworn, the foundation of all blessing. Those who invoke blessings and oaths in the new creation do so by invoking the God of absolute reliability.

The second half of the verse—'the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hid from mine eyes'—shifts the perspective from what humans shall do to what God shall do. God forgets the troubles; God hides them from His sight. This is not amnesia in the modern sense but the complete cessation of sorrow in the presence of overwhelming new joy. The old order (exile, suffering, division between servants and rebels) passes away; God's attention moves entirely to the new creation. This verse is the hinge between judgment (verses 13–15) and the new creation vision (verses 17–18).

word_study.meaning: He who invokes blessing upon himself; uses a blessing formula. The reflexive form (mitbarak) suggests self-directed blessing or blessing sought from a power source.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern thought, blessing was not mere sentiment but a conferral of fertility, prosperity, and divine favor. To bless oneself 'in the God of Amen' is to appeal to the true source of blessing—a radical reorientation from the false deities (Fortune, Destiny) mentioned in verse 11.

word_study.meaning: The God of Amen; a unique divine title in the Hebrew Bible. Amen (אָמֵן) derives from the root aman, 'to be firm, faithful, true.' As a divine title, it means 'the God whose word is firm, whose covenant is unbreakable, who keeps what He promises.'
word_study.significance: This is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where God bears this specific title. The Covenant Rendering preserves 'Amen' rather than translating it to 'truth' because amen carries liturgical resonance—it is the congregational response affirming that God's word is reliable. By calling Him 'the God of Amen,' Isaiah declares that God's essential nature is covenantal trustworthiness. This title anticipates Revelation 3:14, where Christ is called 'the Amen, the faithful and true witness.' The term signals that in the new creation, all swearing and blessing flow from the one source of absolute reliability.

word_study.meaning: He who takes an oath; invokes a sworn promise. Oath-swearing was the most binding form of human covenant-making.
word_study.significance: In the new creation, all oaths are sworn by the God of Amen—meaning there is one source of binding truth, one standard of reliability. All human promises are validated by reference to God's unfailing nature.

word_study.meaning: The former troubles/distresses. Tzarot (troubles) encompasses both external oppression and internal anguish; rishnot (former) marks a definitive break with the past era.
word_study.significance: This phrase encompasses the entire history of exile, division, and covenant breach—all will be erased from God's memory and sight in the new creation. The parallelism with verse 17 ('the former things shall not be remembered') establishes that the new heavens and new earth erase the old order entirely.

cross_references.connection: Christ is called 'the Amen, the faithful and true witness'—directly echoing Isaiah's unique title 'God of Amen.' In Revelation, the title affirms Christ as the guarantor of all truth and the foundation of all blessing in the new creation.

In John's vision of the new creation, 'God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying'—fulfilling Isaiah's promise that 'former troubles are forgotten and hid from my eyes.'

Peter quotes Isaiah 65:17 directly and adds that 'we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness'—confirming that the 'God of Amen' of verse 16 is the source of all covenantal promises.

The Shema ('Hear, O Israel, the LORD thy God is one LORD') establishes God as the sole source of blessing; Isaiah 65:16 reaffirms this principle in the eschatological age—all blessing and swearing flow from one God.

The Lord promises that in the celestial kingdom, 'the Father and I are one. The truth and the light by which the Spirit is enlightened is Christ.' This Restoration passage echoes Isaiah's 'God of Amen'—one God, one truth, one foundation of all covenants.

commentary.historical_context:
In ancient Near Eastern covenant practice, oath-swearing and blessing-pronouncing were formal, liturgical acts. An oath sworn was binding upon the gods themselves (according to Mesopotamian thought) or upon God in Israelite covenant theology. When Isaiah speaks of all swearing and blessing being 'in the God of Amen,' he is proposing a radical theological reorientation: in the new age, there is one and only one source of covenantal validation. The false deities (Fortune and Destiny in verse 11) will be utterly displaced. This would have resonated powerfully with post-exilic Judeans navigating a syncretic, pluralistic religious landscape (as suggested by the references to Gad and Meni). Isaiah's vision promises a future age where such confusion is impossible—all oaths and blessings acknowledge one God.

The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the textual stability of 'God of Amen,' using plene spelling for elohei but preserving the identical title. This suggests that even centuries before the Christian era, interpreters recognized the significance of this unique divine epithet.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 4:8 affirms that 'we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ'—establishing the Book of Mormon pattern that all truth and all binding covenants flow from Christ, who is the 'Amen' of Isaiah 65:16. 2 Nephi 2:8 teaches that 'all things are done in the wisdom of him who knoweth all things'—affirming one source of ultimate reliable truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:6 declares that 'the light which is in all things, which giveth life to all things, which is the law by which all things are governed, even the power of God'—this is Jesus Christ, the 'Amen' of Isaiah. D&C 1:39 affirms that 'the voice of the Lord is the voice of truth and the voice of Christ'—one source of binding covenant truth. D&C 110:1-4 records Joseph Smith's vision of Christ in the Kirtland Temple, with Christ explicitly affirming His role as the keeper of all truth and the guarantor of all covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, all covenants are sworn in the name of the God of Israel—the 'God of Amen.' Every oath taken in the temple is validated by reference to His unfailing character. The temple is the space where humans invoke 'the God of Amen' most solemnly, binding themselves to Him through covenants sworn in His name. The endowment teaches that all priesthood authority flows from this one source of reliability.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the 'Amen'—the faithful and true witness, the guarantee of all God's promises. In Hebrews 6:16-20, Christ is presented as the 'anchor of our souls,' the one by whom all covenants are ratified. All who enter covenant with Christ swear by the 'God of Amen,' participating in His faithfulness. The new creation is the age in which all swearing and blessing acknowledge Christ as the foundation of truth.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites reflection on the source of our blessings and the binding power of our oaths. When we take covenants in the temple, we swear by 'the God of Amen'—the God of absolute, proven reliability. This means our covenants are not provisional or fragile but are grounded in the character of God Himself. It also means that all our blessings—spiritual, familial, temporal—flow from the one source of Amen, the one being who keeps every promise. In a world of many competing voices and authorities, Isaiah's vision centers us on a single reality: God is the God of Amen, and all that matters is aligned with Him.

text_kjv: For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.

commentary.narrative:
This is one of the most consequential verses in the Hebrew Bible for eschatology. Isaiah announces not renovation but new creation (bara)—the same verb used in Genesis 1:1 ('In the beginning God created [bara] the heavens and the earth'). God is not refurbishing the old order but generating an entirely new cosmos. The use of the present tense ('I create') rather than future ('I will create') suggests that from God's perspective, this act is already underway, already accomplished in the divine mind and will.

The phrase 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind' does not mean literal amnesia but the complete psychological displacement of the old by the overwhelming newness of the new. When standing in the presence of infinite new joy, the old sorrows cease to have any psychological reality. This is not forgetting in the sense of losing information but the natural human response to being overtaken by something so much greater. The verse is quoted directly in Revelation 21:1 ('And I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away') and invoked in 2 Peter 3:13, making it the scriptural foundation for Christian eschatology.

The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the text without significant variant. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on 'I am creating' (present progressive) rather than 'I will create' (future) captures an important nuance: God's creative word is already effective, already accomplishing what it announces. This aligns with the NT understanding that the new creation is both future ('I create') and already breaking into the present through Christ's resurrection.

word_study.meaning: To create, bring into being from nothing. This verb appears exclusively with God as the subject in the Hebrew Bible—humans can 'make' (asah) or 'form' (yatzar), but only God can 'create' (bara).
word_study.significance: The use of bara—identical to Genesis 1:1—establishes that the new heavens and new earth are not improvements to the old but a wholly new divine act of cosmos-making. This is the language of God's absolute creative power, not of human renovation or restoration.

word_study.term_english: new heavens and a new earth
word_study.term_original: שָׁמַיִם חֲדָשִׁים וָאָרֶץ חֲדָשָׁה (shamayim chadashim va-arets chadashah)
word_study.meaning: Fresh/new heavens and a fresh/new earth. Chadash denotes not 'recent' but 'renewed, restored to original vigor, made new.' The heavens and earth together denote the entire cosmos.
word_study.significance: This is the comprehensive scope of God's re-creation: not just a new Jerusalem (though that follows in verse 18) but a new cosmos. Every level of reality—the physical, the spiritual, the moral—will be remade.

word_study.meaning: The former things, the first things, the earlier things. This encompasses the entire old creation, with all its history of exile, suffering, and division.
word_study.significance: The parallelism with verses 13–15 suggests that 'the former things' include not only the physical cosmos but the entire old order marked by judgment and separation between servants and rebels. In the new creation, all of that passes away.

cross_references.connection: John's vision explicitly quotes Isaiah: 'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away'—providing the NT fulfillment of Isaiah's prophetic announcement.

Peter invokes Isaiah's promise: 'Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness'—affirming that the new creation is the consummation of God's covenant promise.
The use of bara (create) in Isaiah 65:17 directly echoes Genesis 1:1, establishing that the new creation is as foundational an act as the original creation—a return to God's original creative power.

The revelation to Joseph Smith describes the celestial glory: 'These are they whose bodies are celestial, whose glory is that of the sun, even the glory of God, the highest of all'—the new heavens and earth populated by those who inherit celestial glory.

Paul discusses the resurrection body and the transformation of all things into spiritual form, grounding his teaching in the principle that God creates (bara) a wholly new order, not a renovation of the old.

commentary.historical_context:
In Second Temple Judaism, the announcement of a new creation (bar bara) was not unique to Isaiah—it appears in apocalyptic literature (1 Enoch, 2 Enoch, 4 Ezra) as a common expectation of the end times. However, Isaiah's formulation is the most authoritative and the most frequently cited. The verse would have resonated powerfully with exilic and post-exilic Judeans: after the destruction of the First Temple and the Babylonian exile, the hope for a cosmic renewal—not merely a rebuilt city or restored temple, but a new heavens and new earth—expressed the depth of restoration hoped for. It was not restoration of the status quo ante but transformation into something altogether new.

The DSS evidence confirms that 1QIsaᵃ (dated c. 125 BCE) preserves the same reading as the Masoretic Text, with only minor spelling variations (kia instead of ki). This textual stability across a thousand years suggests the verse was recognized as theologically central and carefully preserved. By the 1st century CE, this verse was foundational to Christian eschatology, as evidenced by its direct quotation in Revelation 21:1, written c. 95 CE.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:2 speaks of a day when 'that which is rotten cannot inherit the kingdom of God; therefore, ye must be purged that ye may become sanctified, that ye can dwell in the presence of God'—affirming that in the new creation (symbolized by the celestial kingdom), only those who are renewed can inherit it, just as only a new earth can be created when the old has passed away.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:17-19 reveals: 'And again, verily I say unto you, he hath given a law unto all things... And unto every kingdom is given a law; and unto every law there are certain bounds also and conditions. All beings who abide not in those conditions are not justified... But they are destroyed according to the law of a celestial kingdom.' This teaches that the new creation operates under laws different from the present order—confirming Isaiah's vision that an entirely new cosmos is being established.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents in microcosm the new creation—a space where heaven and earth intersect, where the old order (sin, death, separation) is ritually overcome and a new order (covenant, eternal life, exaltation) is enacted. The temple endowment traces the fall and restoration, prefiguring the cosmic restoration promised in Isaiah 65:17. Those who inherit the celestial kingdom will dwell in the new heavens and new earth, the culmination of all that the temple teaches.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the inaugurator of the new creation. His resurrection is the 'first-fruits' of the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:20-23)—the initial breaking in of the new order into the old. All who are resurrected in Christ are part of the new creation. 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares: 'If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.' The new heavens and new earth announced in Isaiah 65:17 are the cosmic expansion of what Christ's resurrection initiates: the wholesale re-creation of reality under His authority.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites us to hold two truths simultaneously: we are living in the old creation, with all its sorrows and limitations, yet we are already participating in the new creation through our covenants with Christ. Our temple covenants place us on the trajectory toward the new heavens and new earth. This verse also liberates us from the illusion that the current world order is permanent or that merely reforming existing structures will solve fundamental human problems. Only God's re-creative power can accomplish that. Our task is not to perfect the old order but to prepare ourselves to inhabit the new one—to become 'sanctified that [we] can dwell in the presence of God.'

text_kjv: But be ye glad and rejoice for ever in that which I create: for, behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy.

commentary.narrative:
The vision descends from cosmic abstraction to concrete reality. While verse 17 announces the new heavens and new earth in sweeping terms, verse 18 centers everything on a city and a people: Jerusalem and her inhabitants. This is characteristic of Isaiah's eschatology: the universal is always particulars, the cosmic is always embodied. The new creation is not an invisible, purely spiritual realm but a place where God's covenant people—centered in Zion—dwell in eternal joy.

The structure of the verse is remarkable: 'Be glad and rejoice forever in what I create'—a command to joy that stretches into eternity. 'Forever' (ad-ei ad) denotes endless duration; the joy is not provisional or conditional but permanent. Then follows the explanation: 'I am creating Jerusalem as a delight and her people as a joy.' The city and people are not merely recipients of joy from outside but are themselves the embodiment of delight and joy. The feminine noun 'Jerusalem' (Yerushalayim) takes feminine pronouns and verbs in the Hebrew, suggesting Jerusalem is a woman or mother—and she is being created, remade, as a person of delight. Her children, her people, are created as joy itself.

This is radically incarnational: the new creation is not a realm of disembodied spirits but a transformed city with a transformed people. The Dead Sea Scrolls confirm the reading without significant variant. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on 'creating' (present progressive) rather than 'will create' emphasizes that God's word is already in effect, already accomplishing the transformation.

word_study.meaning: Be glad/exultant and rejoice/be delighted. Sis denotes exultation and joy; gilu denotes rejoicing, dancing, being moved with delight.
word_study.significance: The parallel imperatives command not merely internal emotion but public, bodily rejoicing—the whole self engaged in response to God's creative work. This echoes the liturgical joy of temple festivals (Deuteronomy 12:12, 1 Chronicles 15:25).

word_study.meaning: Forever, unto eternity, endlessly. Literally 'unto eternity upon eternity'—an intensified expression of endless duration.
word_study.significance: This is not temporary joy but joy that characterizes the entire age to come. In Latter-day Saint understanding, this corresponds to 'eternal life'—not mere endless duration but life lived in God's presence.

word_study.meaning: Delight, rejoicing, exultation. A state of joy and celebration.
word_study.significance: Jerusalem herself becomes the embodiment of delight—not merely a city that contains joyful inhabitants but a city whose very character is delight. This anthropomorphizes Jerusalem, making her the bride or mother of those who dwell in her.

word_study.meaning: Her people, her inhabitants. The possessive pronoun (ha—her) establishes Jerusalem as a collective mother, and 'her people' as her children.
word_study.significance: The relationship is familial: Jerusalem is not merely a geographical location but a covenant community bound to their city as children to a mother. In the new creation, this bond is permanent and constitutive.

word_study.meaning: Joy, gladness, rejoicing. Often used for the joy of festival celebrations or covenant blessings.
word_study.significance: The people are not merely in a state of joy; they are created as joy—their very existence embodies the joy God intends for His covenant community. The Covenant Rendering's 'a joy' (singular) emphasizes that the people collectively form one unified joy.

cross_references.connection: John's vision directly echoes Isaiah 65:18: 'And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.' The city is remade, and her people (the Bride) are her joy.

The psalm celebrates 'the city of the great King' (Jerusalem), 'beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth'—establishing Jerusalem as the center of covenant joy, which Isaiah 65:18 promises will be eternally true in the new creation.

Earlier in Isaiah, God promises: 'The LORD hath called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit... as a young wife... For thy Maker is thine husband... and thy God thy joy and delight.' Isaiah 65:18 fulfills this: Jerusalem and her people become the joy of God in the new creation.

The revelation to Joseph Smith describes the New Jerusalem (Zion) that shall be built 'in the last days,' where the righteous shall 'see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, clothed with power and great glory' and shall be 'caught up to meet him'—fulfilling Isaiah's vision of Jerusalem as the place of eternal joy.

Jacob promises that in the latter days, Jerusalem shall 'become a holy place' and 'shall be established in righteousness,' echoing Isaiah's vision of Jerusalem remade as the center of joy and blessing.

commentary.historical_context:
For Judeans, Jerusalem was not merely a political capital but the cosmic center—the place where heaven and earth intersected at the temple. The destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE was not merely a military defeat but a theological crisis: Had God abandoned the city? Was the covenant null? Isaiah 65:18, written in or after the exile, reasserts that God's ultimate purpose centers on Jerusalem. The new creation will be Zion-centered. This resonated profoundly with post-exilic returners and later with 1st-century Jews anticipating Messiah. By the time the book of Revelation was written (c. 95 CE), Christians understood the 'New Jerusalem' to be the fulfillment of all that Isaiah promised—the ultimate vindication and transformation of the holy city.

The Dead Sea Scrolls show no textual variant in verse 18—the promise of Jerusalem as delight and her people as joy was so central that it was carefully preserved across copyings. The scroll evidence suggests that even centuries before Christianity, Jewish interpreters recognized Isaiah 65:17–18 as the culmination of all eschatological hope.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly promises that Zion shall be established in the last days (3 Nephi 16:18-20; 3 Nephi 21:23-29). Nephi prophesies that 'in that day that the Son of Man shall come, he shall sit in his throne in heaven' while His covenant people gather 'in the lands of their inheritance, upon all the face of the earth, unto the day of judgment.' The Zion-centered eschatology of Isaiah 65:18 is echoed and amplified in the Book of Mormon's vision of a celestial Zion in the Americas.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:64-71 contains Joseph Smith's revelation about the New Jerusalem that shall be built 'in the last days, at the time of the coming of the Son of Man. And the Lord said unto me: It shall be called the New Jerusalem, a land of peace, a city of refuge, a place of safety for the saints of the Most High God.' This reveals that the 'Jerusalem created as delight' of Isaiah 65:18 is an actual city to be established by God's people in preparation for the Second Coming. D&C 57:1-3 specifies that this city shall be built 'in the land of Missouri'—concretizing Isaiah's vision in latter-day covenant geography.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the seed of the New Jerusalem. Within the temple, heaven and earth meet, the old creation (the world, sin, death) is transcended, and the new creation (covenant, exaltation, eternal life) is enacted. Those who receive their endowment are being prepared to dwell in the New Jerusalem—in Jerusalem as delight, and as part of her people, created as joy. The temple teaches that the destination of all covenant keeping is the celestial Zion, where God dwells with His people.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the 'joy' that fills Jerusalem—the Bridegroom who comes to make His Bride (the Church/Zion) His delight (Ephesians 5:25-27). Christ is Himself the 'stone which the builders rejected' that becomes 'the head of the corner' (1 Peter 2:7), and upon this stone Zion is built. In Revelation, the New Jerusalem is 'the Bride, the Lamb's wife' (Revelation 21:9)—Christ's people remade as His joy and His delight. All who are covenant with Christ dwell in the city He is establishing, participants in the joy of Jerusalem remade.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites us to understand that the ultimate destiny of God's covenant people is communal and particular: we are not disembodied spirits in an abstract heaven but inhabitants of the New Jerusalem, a real city populated by a real people, centered in Zion. Our temple covenants bind us to this city and people. We are being prepared to dwell there. This has profound implications: it means our salvation is not purely individual but corporate—we are part of a people, a city, a bride being prepared for the Bridegroom. It also means that our current work of building Zion—establishing righteous communities, creating institutions of learning and worship, caring for the poor and afflicted—is not separate from the new creation but is its seed and prototype. We are already creating the Jerusalem of Isaiah 65:18 in miniature, through faithfulness to covenant.

text_kjv: The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock: and dust shall be the serpent's meat. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Isaiah 65:25 stands as the capstone of the entire book of Isaiah, returning full circle to the messianic vision of chapter 11. After depicting God's restoration of the cosmos—new heavens, new earth, new Jerusalem—the prophet concludes by painting shalom visible in the animal kingdom itself. This is not merely poetic embellishment; it is the theological climax of Isaiah's entire witness. The natural order, fractured by sin and the Fall, is restored to its Edenic harmony. The wolf and lamb, natural predators and prey, graze side by side without violence. The lion, apex predator, becomes a herbivore. Even the serpent, cursed in Genesis 3, finds its place in the new creation—eating dust, its power to harm rendered impotent.

The verse's final declaration—'They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain'—echoes Isaiah 11:9 verbatim, creating an intentional inclusio that frames the entire prophetic book. This repetition signals that what was promised in chapter 11 to the messianic age is now being realized in the eschatological consummation. The phrase 'my holy mountain' refers to God's kingdom, the dwelling place of His people, a space so thoroughly sanctified that even predatory instinct is transformed. This is not restraint born of fear or coercion, but genuine transformation—the very nature of creatures is altered by God's creative power.

The specific detail about the serpent eating dust carries profound theological weight. Unlike the other animals, whose nature is transformed into peace (wolf grazing, lion eating straw), the serpent remains under judgment—yet in a way that renders it harmless. The curse from Genesis 3:14 ('thou shalt eat dust all the days of thy life') is not rescinded but contained, domesticated. The serpent's degradation becomes a guarantee of safety for God's people. This suggests that redemption does not mean the erasure of all consequences for rebellion, but rather their recalibration into a cosmos where sin's power is broken and God's peace reigns absolutely.

word_study.meaning: Wolf; a predatory animal symbolizing violence, cunning, and danger in Near Eastern and biblical literature (cf. Matthew 7:15, 10:16; Jeremiah 5:6). The term evokes both literal threat and metaphorical representation of evil.
word_study.significance: The wolf's transformation from hunter to herbivore represents the reversal of the Fall's curse upon creation. In Isaiah's vision, the hierarchy of predator-prey gives way to horizontal coexistence. The Covenant Rendering notes that this pairing with the lamb echoes Isaiah 11:6, establishing continuity between the messianic age and the final eschatological state.

word_study.meaning: A young sheep, typically vulnerable and defenseless. In biblical symbolism, the lamb represents innocence, meekness, and sacrificial purity (Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29).
word_study.significance: The lamb's safety alongside the wolf symbolizes the vindication of the righteous and the powerless in God's kingdom. That the vulnerable creature needs no protection from its natural enemy demonstrates perfect peace, not through domination but through transformed nature.

word_study.meaning: To graze, to feed as livestock. The root רעה (rʿh) carries connotations of shepherding, tending, and pastoral care. The imperfect form suggests ongoing, habitual action—not a momentary truce but a permanent state.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'shall graze together,' emphasizing continuous, companionable feeding rather than mere absence of conflict. This echoes God as shepherd (Isaiah 40:11; Psalm 23) and suggests that even in the new creation, God's shepherding care extends to all creatures, bringing them into harmonious unity.

word_study.meaning: Lion; the supreme predator of the ancient Near East, embodying power, dominion, and ferocity. In biblical symbolism, the lion can represent both God's majesty (Psalm 29:1) and the power of evil (1 Peter 5:8).
word_study.significance: The lion's herbivory ('shall eat straw like the bullock') represents the most radical transformation in the verse—the mighty rendered gentle. This echoes Isaiah 11:7 and suggests that in the new creation, power itself is reordered toward gentleness rather than domination.

word_study.meaning: Straw; the dried stalks of grain, fit only for animal fodder, not for human consumption. It represents lowliness and the most basic sustenance.
word_study.significance: The irony is deliberate: the apex predator sustains itself on the meanest food. This signifies a complete inversion of the natural hierarchy. Where once the lion consumed flesh and dominated creation, it now eats straw and dwells in peace. The transformation is not mere behavioral restraint but fundamental reordering.

word_study.meaning: Dust, earth, ground. Semantically linked to humiliation, degradation, and death (Genesis 3:19, 'dust thou art'). In Isaiah 29:4, the word connotes weakness and powerlessness.
word_study.significance: The serpent eating dust directly recalls God's curse in Genesis 3:14: 'upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat.' Rather than lifting this curse, the new creation ratifies it—the serpent remains humiliated and grounded. Yet this degradation serves a restorative purpose: it ensures the serpent cannot harm God's people. The curse becomes protective.

word_study.meaning: Food, bread, sustenance. The word לחם (lachm) originally denotes bread but broadens to mean any food or nourishment. The possessive suffix -ו (o) makes it 'its food.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'food' rather than 'meat' clarifies that the serpent, like all creatures in the new creation, sustains itself on what is provided—not through predation or venom, but through assigned diet. This reinforces the theme of divine provision and order.

word_study.meaning: To do evil, to cause harm, to injure. The root רעע (rʿʿ) means badness or wickedness. In the context of animals, it means to maul, attack, or otherwise inflict harm.
word_study.significance: This verb is critical: it denotes not merely absence of violence but the impossibility of harm. The new creation is not simply a restraint on predatory instinct but a fundamental alteration such that harm cannot occur. Evil intent becomes impossible.

word_study.meaning: To destroy, to corrupt, to ruin. The root שחת (scht) carries connotations of decomposition, decay, and systematic ruination. It appears in the Flood narrative (Genesis 6:11-13) and connotes wholesale corruption.
word_study.significance: Paired with 'hurt,' this verb encompasses both momentary violence and systemic destruction. In the new creation, neither temporary harm nor cumulative damage can occur. The cosmos itself is immune to the corruption that has characterized creation since the Fall.

word_study.meaning: Holy mountain; God's sanctified place of dwelling. In Isaiah, this refers to Zion and, eschatologically, the entire renewed creation. The adjective קדוש (qadosh, holy) denotes separation, purity, and dedication to God.
word_study.significance: The 'holy mountain' is not merely a geographical location but a cosmic space wholly consecrated to God's purposes. That this peace pervades 'all My holy mountain' means that the entire renewed creation is a sanctuary, a space where God's holiness—and therefore peace—is complete and inviolable. There is no secular or profane space in the new world; all is holy.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah 11 provides the original vision of the peaceable kingdom that Isaiah 65:25 recapitulates and fulfills. The wolf-lamb pairing and the closing declaration 'they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain' are quoted verbatim, creating an intentional inclusio that brackets Isaiah's entire prophecy.

God's curse on the serpent ('thou shalt eat dust') is echoed and reaffirmed in Isaiah 65:25. Rather than being lifted, the curse is contained and rendered harmless in the new creation, ensuring perpetual safety for God's people while the serpent remains humiliated.

John's vision of the new heavens and new earth directly parallels Isaiah 65:17-25, including the absence of pain and crying. Both passages depict cosmic restoration and the removal of the consequences of sin, though Revelation does not detail the animal kingdom's transformation.

Paul quotes Isaiah 65:1 in Romans 10:20 as evidence that God revealed Himself to the Gentiles. While not directly referencing verse 25, Paul's engagement with Isaiah 65 as a whole affirms its importance in the apostolic understanding of God's inclusive redemptive purpose.

Peter echoes Isaiah 65:17 ('new heavens and new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness'), confirming that Isaiah's eschatological vision was understood by New Testament writers as the authoritative template for the final consummation.

The image of God as shepherd of the flock resonates with Isaiah 65:25's depiction of all creatures grazing together in divine care. Both passages emphasize God's tender, protective shepherding over creation.

commentary.historical_context:
The vision of the peaceable kingdom drew on ancient Near Eastern mythology and wisdom traditions. Mesopotamian texts and Egyptian poetry occasionally depicted idealized states where natural order was suspended—though always mythologically and never eschatologically as the permanent future state of the cosmos. Isaiah's innovation is theological and radical: he uses the language of primordial peace to describe not mythic eternity but the *future* vindication of God's people and the cosmos itself.

The wolf-lamb pairing would have struck an ancient Near Eastern listener with particular force. Wolves were present throughout the Levantine wilderness and were genuine threats to flocks. The lamb, correspondingly, was a primary sacrificial animal and staple of pastoral economy. To imagine them grazing in perfect harmony was not sentimental but revolutionary—it promised that the threats defining daily life would be unmade.

The reference to the serpent eating dust connects to the Genesis 3 curse, which all Israelites would have known. However, Isaiah's vision does not depict the curse being reversed; rather, it is domesticated and rendered safe. This reflects a sophisticated theological understanding: redemption involves the recalibration of consequences, not their erasure. The serpent's humiliation—forced to crawl and eat dust—becomes a perpetual guarantee that it cannot rise up against humanity again.

The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ, col. LI, line 9) preserve this verse without meaningful textual variation from the Masoretic Text, indicating that Isaiah 65:25 was understood with remarkable consistency from the second century BCE onward.
