The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'that I am making,' underscoring present divine action: the making of the new creation is already underway, not merely a future prospect.

word_study.meaning: To stand, endure, remain, persist. The root conveys both literal standing and figurative endurance or stability. When used of covenants or divine promises, it means 'to continue in force' or 'to be reliable.' The Psalms frequently use amad to describe God's word standing forever (Psalm 119:89).
word_study.significance: The verb amad is crucial: Israel's 'seed and name' do not merely exist, they amad—they stand firm, like pillars. They endure like the mountains. This is not tentative survival but covenantal permanence. The Covenant Rendering's 'shall endure' captures this stability.

word_study.meaning: Offspring, descendants, lineage; both biological succession and covenant continuity. In Genesis 12:7 ('unto thy seed will I give this land'), zera' becomes the foundation of the Abrahamic covenant—the promise that Abraham's line will continue and inherit blessing. Here, zera' affirms that the covenant line survives eschatological transformation.
word_study.significance: The promise to Abraham of numberless offspring (Genesis 15:5-6, 22:17) finds its ultimate affirmation here. Even in the age of new creation, the seed endures. This is not biological determinism but covenantal assurance: God's purposes through Abraham's line will not be thwarted by judgment or exile.

word_study.meaning: Name; but in Hebrew, shem implies reputation, identity, legacy, and renown. When God says 'I will make my name great' (Genesis 12:2), He means His reputation and work will be known. When Israel's name endures, it means their identity as God's covenant people persists.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'seed and name' invokes the Abrahamic covenant twice over: 'I will make thee a great nation' (a people—zera') and 'I will make thy name great' (reputation and legacy). Isaiah is saying: The promises given to Abraham will be fulfilled perpetually in the new creation.

word_study.meaning: Before Me, in My presence, in front of Me. It conveys standing in God's direct gaze, subject to His scrutiny and care. When something stands 'before' God, it is under His watch and jurisdiction.
word_study.significance: Israel's seed and name endure 'before Me' (lefanay)—not hidden or forgotten, but perpetually in God's presence and within His care. This echoes Psalm 41:12, 'in thy presence shall I be satisfied,' and affirms that covenant endurance is covenantal presence.

cross_references.connection: The Abrahamic covenant promises that Abraham's seed will be numberless and his name will be great. Isaiah 66:22 affirms that this covenant endures even in the new creation—the ultimate fulfillment of God's word to Abraham.

The introduction of the new heavens and new earth: 'Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.' Isaiah 66:22 repeats this foundation to anchor the promise of Israel's perpetuity.
'For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven.' Both Isaiah and the Psalmist use the language of permanence and endurance to describe the reliability of God's covenant word.

John's vision of the new heaven and new earth echoes Isaiah 65-66: 'And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away.' The Revelation realizes Isaiah's eschatological vision.

Paul argues that Abraham's inheritance is not merely the earthly Land but the entire renewed cosmos: 'For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world... by the law of faith.' This is Isaiah 66:22 interpreted through Christ: Abraham's seed inherits the new creation.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 22 addresses a community traumatized by exile and diaspora. The Babylonian destruction (586 BCE) and subsequent dispersion created an existential crisis: Did Israel have a future? The loss of the Temple, the exile of the royal line, and the scattering of the people made covenantal continuity seem impossible. The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel had warned of judgment; now Isaiah promises restoration, but with a cosmic scope: the restoration is not merely political or territorial—it is cosmic. The new heavens and new earth framework (itself influenced by ancient Near Eastern mythology, where cosmic renewal was a divine prerogative) becomes the container for Israel's everlasting promise. By linking Israel's perpetuity to cosmic transformation, Isaiah elevates the nation's future from mere historical contingency to metaphysical necessity. The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ col. LIV) attest this verse unchanged, confirming that even late Second Temple Judaism, with its apocalyptic expectation of cosmic transformation, preserved this verse as central eschatological promise.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes the eternal nature of covenantal promises. In 1 Nephi 13:37, Nephi learns that the gospel will 'go forth among all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people,' and in 15:13-16, he sees that Jews and Gentiles will be 'numbered with the seed of thy father.' In 2 Nephi 29:8-14, the Lord declares that He will bring forth His word to all peoples, and the book of the Lamb (Book of Mormon) will testify of the New Testament, and together they will convince all the world that the Holy One of Israel has spoken. The eternal nature of these covenantal promises is woven throughout: 'thy seed and thy name remain' (Isaiah 66:22) is echoed in Nephi's vision that the covenant extends to the last days and to 'all peoples.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:22-25 contains the revelation regarding the new heavens and new earth: 'And again, verily, verily, I say unto you that when the thousand years are ended, and men again begin to deny their God, then will I spare the earth but for a little season.' Then follows the final judgment and 'a new heaven and a new earth, wherein all things are restored to their proper use.' Most importantly, D&C 130:8-9 teaches that this restored earth 'shall be quickened, and shall abide the celestial law, and be the place of the residence of the sanctified.' The Restoration affirms Isaiah 66:22 by stating that God's covenant people will inhabit and endure upon the renewed creation forever. D&C 76:62 and D&C 132:19 promise the celestial-bound saints that they 'shall inherit thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, dominions, all heights and depths... forever and ever.' This is Isaiah's promise realized: seed and name endure eternally.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the microcosm of the new creation and the place where covenants are sealed 'for time and all eternity.' In Latter-day Saint theology, Temple covenants are not temporal but eternal—they extend beyond mortality into the resurrection and the celestial kingdom. The sealing of families (the ultimate expression of 'seed' enduring) is performed in the Temple under divine authority. Endowment ordinances teach that God's people are clothed with covenantal authority and glory, preparing them for the celestial kingdom where they will 'dwell with God' (Revelation 21:3). The Temple grounds the eternality of the covenant in sacred ritual and space.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 66:22 ultimately points to Christ as the foundation of all everlasting covenant. Hebrews 13:8 affirms, 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.' The apostle Paul writes that in Christ, all God's promises are 'yea' and 'Amen' (2 Corinthians 1:20). Christ's resurrection and exaltation inaugurate the new creation; in Him, all things are reconciled and made new (Colossians 1:15-20, 2 Corinthians 5:17). The promise that 'seed and name remain' finds ultimate fulfillment in the elect, who are 'the seed of Christ' (Galatians 3:29) and who bear His name as Christians. The new heavens and new earth are established through Christ's redemptive work, and in that renewed creation, all who are in Christ endure eternally.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, verse 22 offers both security and responsibility. The security: our covenants with God endure forever. The marriage sealed in the Temple, the adoption into Israel through baptism and confirmation, the priesthood held and exercised—these are not temporary or probationary; they are written into the fabric of creation itself. No failure, no struggle, no external threat can erase our identity in Christ if we endure to the end. The responsibility: we are to live as though we believe this. Covenant endurance requires fidelity. If 'seed and name' endure, we are accountable for the legacy we leave. The 'seed' suggests that our spiritual lineage extends forward—our children and their children will inherit the covenants we have made and the example we have set. The 'name' implies that our character and reputation will continue to speak. What will our name mean? What legacy are we building? Verse 22 is both eschatological comfort and present-tense call to faithful covenant-keeping.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 23 completes the vision of eschatological worship by depicting it as universal, rhythmic, and perpetual. The repeated cycles—'from one new moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another'—establish a cosmic liturgy. Every month, every week, without exception, 'all flesh' (kol basar) streams to worship before the LORD. This is the realization of Isaiah 56:7 ('my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples') and the echoing of Isaiah 2:2-4 ('many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD'). The universal worship described here is not coerced or cynical; it is the voluntary, rhythmic convergence of all humanity—Jew and Gentile, near and far—upon the holy mountain, drawn by reverence for God's character.

The language deserves close attention. 'All flesh' (kol basar) is not merely all nations but all embodied beings—the entire created order in its physical, material reality. This is not a purely spiritual or otherworldly vision; it is carnal, earthly, real. The worship occurs 'from new moon to new moon'—the monthly festival marking the renewal of time—and 'from Sabbath to Sabbath'—the weekly rhythm of rest and covenant remembrance. Together, these cycles suggest completeness: both the cosmic calendar (moon) and the divine calendar (Sabbath) structure worship. No one is exempt; all flesh comes. The verb 'come' (bo, to come or enter) is in the habitual future tense—not a one-time event but a perpetual pattern. The Dead Sea Scrolls attest this verse with plene spelling (chodesh, 'month/new moon'), emphasizing clarity of language.

word_study.meaning: All flesh; the totality of living, embodied creatures. Basar (flesh) emphasizes the physical, material nature of existence. In Genesis 6:12, 'all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth'; here, all flesh is redeemed and sanctified. The phrase appears frequently in Isaiah (40:5, 40:6, 45:25, 66:16, 66:23, 66:24) to emphasize the inclusivity of God's redemptive work.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering preserves 'all flesh,' underscoring materiality and universality. This is not merely all nations or all peoples—it is the entire created order, in its bodily, tangible reality. Resurrection language echoes through the phrase: if flesh endures and gathers in worship, bodies are raised and renewed. This affirms the doctrine of physical resurrection and vindication.

word_study.meaning: Month; the lunar cycle. In Hebrew, chodesh derives from a root meaning 'to renew' (chadash), so a 'new moon' (chodesh) is literally 'the renewal.' In ancient Israel, the new moon (Rosh Chodesh) was observed as a festival and a marker of sacred time. It is mentioned in Amos 8:5 as a festival that merchants wanted to end so they could resume trading, indicating it was a significant observance.
word_study.significance: The new moon is not arbitrary; it marks the renewal of time itself. By prescribing worship 'from new moon to new moon,' Isaiah affirms that the entire cycle of renewal—every month—is consecrated to God. Time itself becomes liturgical. The Dead Sea Scrolls use plene spelling here (chodesh), emphasizing the clarity of the term.

word_study.meaning: The seventh day, day of rest; from the root 'to cease' or 'to rest' (shabat). The Sabbath is the foundation of Jewish sacred time and the sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:13, 16). It commemorates God's rest on the seventh day of creation and is the day of cessation from labor and turning toward God.
word_study.significance: By invoking Sabbath, Isaiah is saying that the eschatological worship is not novel but is the fulfillment of the Sabbath principle given in the Torah. The Sabbath, which once was the privilege of Israel alone, becomes the rhythm for all flesh. This is Sabbath universalized—the entire cosmos enters into the rest and worship that Israel practiced.

word_study.meaning: To come and bow down / prostrate oneself. The verb bo means 'to come' or 'to enter'; lehistachawot is the hitpael infinitive of shachah, 'to bow down, prostrate, worship.' The combination emphasizes both the physical act of coming and the physical gesture of worship—bowing, kneeling, prostration.
word_study.significance: This is not abstract or purely spiritual worship; it is embodied, physical, visceral. The worshipers come in their flesh and bow down in their flesh. This grounds eschatological worship in the material, bodily reality affirmed by verse 23's emphasis on 'all flesh.'

word_study.meaning: Before Me, in My presence; standing directly in front of God. Lefanay conveys immediate proximity and direct encounter. To worship 'before Me' is to worship in God's presence, not remotely or by proxy.
word_study.significance: The repetition of lefanay (also in verse 22, 'remain before Me') creates a thread: God's covenants endure before Him (verse 22), and all worship occurs before Him (verse 23). This emphasizes divine presence as the constant reality underlying both covenant and worship.

cross_references.connection: The LORD's house is called 'a house of prayer for all peoples.' Isaiah 66:23 is the full realization: all peoples, at regular intervals, come to that house to worship, making it perpetually a house of prayer.

In the last days, the mountain of the LORD's house shall be exalted, and many people shall flow unto it; 'out of Zion shall go forth the law.' Isaiah 66:23 depicts that same flow of people realized as a perpetual, rhythmic pilgrimage.
'Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee.' The vision of perpetual dwelling and continuous praise in God's presence echoes through Isaiah 66:23.

'After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and peoples, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands.' This is Isaiah 66:23 realized in John's vision: all flesh standing before God in endless worship.

After the final judgment, 'it shall come to pass, that every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts.' This echoes Isaiah's vision: all nations gathering for prescribed, rhythmic worship.

commentary.historical_context: The historical background involves Jewish sacred time-keeping and the challenge of diaspora. In the Temple period, pilgrims traveled to Jerusalem for the three great festivals (Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles). Every Sabbath was observed locally or in community; every new moon was marked as a festival. However, after the Babylonian exile and the scattering of the Jewish people, not every Jew could journey to Jerusalem for every observance. The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ) preserve this verse with attention to the lunar and Sabbatical calendar—the Qumran community itself was deeply concerned with exact chronology and proper calendar observance. Isaiah 66:23 is a vision in which geographic distance is no obstacle: all flesh, everywhere, gathers perpetually to worship. The new moon and Sabbath are still observed, but they are universalized—not merely Israel's practices but the cosmic liturgy. Later, in synagogue practice, this verse became central to the readings after the haftarah; it affirmed that even after the Temple's destruction (70 CE), the rhythm of worship continued through prayer and study.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes perpetual worship and temple ordinances. In 1 Nephi 1:8-9, Nephi sees the throne of God and the multitude of angels praising Him. In 2 Nephi 26:13, the Lord promises to go forth 'among all nations' with His gospel. In 3 Nephi 18:27-32, Jesus teaches His disciples to pray always and to 'come unto me that ye may partake of the waters of life freely' (verse 32, alluding to baptism and the sacrament). The Nephite people are commanded to gather regularly for worship and sacrament, and in 4 Nephi 1:12, after Christ's visit, 'all the people were righteous and there were no manner of -ites' (divisions)—a preview of the universal worship of Isaiah 66:23.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 50:40 teaches that those who are 'sanctified by the Spirit' receive 'all things as his gift.' D&C 101:23 promises that the faithful shall 'see the Lord's face in His own house' in the New Jerusalem. The Restoration restores the practice of regular, rhythmic worship through sacrament meetings (every Sabbath), monthly fast days, and periodic Temple attendance. D&C 109:8-10 dedicates the Kirtland Temple as 'a house of prayer, a house of fasting, a house of faith, a house of learning, a house of glory, a house of order,' anticipating the eschatological house of prayer of Isaiah 66:23. The rhythm of weekly Sabbath worship and annual Temple attendance by the faithful mirrors the 'new moon to new moon, Sabbath to Sabbath' pattern of verse 23.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the focal point of verse 23's eschatological vision. In Latter-day Saint theology, the Temple is literally 'the Lord's house'—the place where worshipers come into His presence to receive covenants and ordinances. The endowment ceremony and sealing ordinances are performed regularly (often daily in large temples), making the Temple a perpetual house of prayer. The dedication of the Salt Lake Temple (D&C 109) and every temple dedication since emphasizes that the Temple is 'a house of prayer, a house of fasting, a house of faith,' for 'all people.' The vision of Temples dotting the earth—from Nauvoo to Salt Lake City, from Kirtland to dozens of current temples—is Isaiah 66:23 beginning to be realized: multiple sanctuaries where all flesh can come to worship before the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 66:23 depicts the eschatological worship of Christ as King and High Priest. Hebrews 8:1-2 describes Jesus as 'a minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man.' In Revelation 21:22-23, there is no temple in the New Jerusalem because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it.' Yet this does not diminish worship; rather, worship becomes universal and unmediated. Every person, all flesh, worships before the presence of God and the Lamb. The rhythm of new moons and Sabbaths points to the perpetual worship of the eternal Godhead (Revelation 4:8-11, where the four beasts 'rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty').
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 23 invites reflection on the meaning and practice of worship. First, worship is not optional or sporadic; it is rhythmic and perpetual—a regular, intentional turning toward God. Attending sacrament meeting every Sabbath, making Temple covenants, gathering with the Saints—these are not burdensome obligations but the privilege of entering God's presence. Second, the phrase 'all flesh' challenges us to see worship as inclusive and welcoming. The vision is not of an elite few in an inner sanctum, but of 'all flesh'—all people, all nations, all ages, all conditions—coming before God. This should shape how we extend hospitality in our chapels and welcome people of all backgrounds. Third, verse 23 is eschatological promise that encourages us to persevere in worship even when it feels difficult or routine. The 'new moon to new moon, Sabbath to Sabbath' suggests that faithful worship creates a pattern, a rhythm that sanctifies time itself. Our regular attendance at sacrament meeting, our family home evening, our personal and family prayer—these are participations in the cosmic liturgy of verse 23, prefiguring the eschatological worship. Are we worshiping with full presence and intention? Are we gathering not out of habit but out of love for God and desire for His presence?

text_kjv: And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of Isaiah delivers an unflinching conclusion—not comfort but cosmic contrast. Immediately following the vision of universal, perpetual worship (verse 23), Isaiah depicts the worshipers going out from the house of God to witness the fate of the rebellious. This is not gratuitous violence but the theodicy of judgment: those who refuse covenant are separated from those who accept it, and their judgment is permanent and visible. 'The carcases of the men that have transgressed' (pigrei ha'anashim haPosh'im) are displayed—a ghastly sight that contrasts with the purity of those entering God's presence. The metaphor of 'worm' and 'fire' becomes the defining image of divine judgment in later Jewish and Christian theology. The worm (tolaat) suggests decay, corruption, and the disgrace of being exposed and eaten by maggots—the worst imaginable death in ancient Levantine culture (being denied proper burial meant the body was abandoned to scavengers). The fire (esh) is unquenched—perpetual, unstoppable, consuming endlessly without mercy. The phrase 'shall be an abhorring unto all flesh' (v'hayu dera'on lekol basar) uses a rare word (dera'on, abhorrence, loathing) that appears only here and in Daniel 12:2.

The verse is deliberately jarring and unresolved. It does not end with comfort or redemption but with the starkness of judgment. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve this final verse unchanged, confirming that even ancient Jewish scribes, copying the text near the end of the greatest scroll ever discovered, did not soften the conclusion. Both texts end Isaiah with judgment hanging over the cosmos. The rabbinical tradition eventually developed a liturgical workaround: the haftarah (prophetic reading) would re-read verse 23 after verse 24, ending on the note of worship rather than judgment. But the text itself permits no such escape. This is Isaiah's theological boldness: mercy and judgment are not alternatives; they coexist. The same God who welcomes all flesh to worship turns away those who have rejected His covenant, and their judgment is irrevocable.

word_study.meaning: To go out, come forth, exit. The verb conveys movement from one place to another, often with purpose. In Exodus 12:42, 'a night to be much observed unto the LORD for bringing them out,' yatsa describes liberation; here it describes a grim procession.
word_study.significance: The worshipers don't merely see judgment from a distance; they 'go forth' to witness it. This is active, intentional observation—a recognition of the finality of the judgment and the fate of the unredeemed.

word_study.meaning: Corpses, dead bodies, carcasses. Pigger (plural pigrei) specifically denotes the body of a person who is dead—not merely lifeless but shamefully so, unburied and exposed. This word appears in Leviticus 26:30 ('I will cast your carcasses upon the carcasses of your idols') as a sign of ultimate degradation.
word_study.significance: The term pigrei emphasizes absolute death and shame. These are not the honored deceased in tombs but corpses exposed to decay and defilement—the ultimate dishonor in the ancient Levantine world, where proper burial was essential to dignity.

word_study.meaning: Those who rebel, transgress, or break covenant (from the root pashat, to rebel or spread open). A pashat is not merely a sinner but a rebel—one who has actively broken covenant relationship. This word carries moral and relational weight beyond mere transgression.
word_study.significance: The use of posh'im rather than chote (sinners) emphasizes that these are not people who stumbled but those who actively rebelled against God's covenant. They knew the way and chose to reject it.

word_study.meaning: Worm, maggot; that which eats flesh and causes decay. Tolaat is used in Job 25:6 ('man, that is a worm...and the son of man, which is a worm') to signify human vulnerability and degradation. In the context of unburied corpses (Isaiah 66:24), the worm becomes the agent of decay.
word_study.significance: The worm is not figurative but literal—the embodied reality of corruption. By saying the worm 'shall not die,' Isaiah means that the process of decay is perpetual; the body is never allowed to rest. This is the opposite of sheol, where the dead sleep; here, judgment means endless degradation.

word_study.meaning: Their fire shall not be extinguished. Fire (esh) is quenched (kabah) only if water is applied or fuel is exhausted; an unquenched fire burns endlessly. In Isaiah 50:11, those who kindle their own fire are told 'ye shall lie down in sorrow'—but the fire remains. Here, there is no suggestion of exhaustion or extinguishing; the fire is eternal.
word_study.significance: The image of unquenched fire becomes central to the Christian concept of Gehenna/Hell (Mark 9:43-48, where Jesus quotes this verse three times). It suggests punishment that does not end because the rebellion itself does not repent. If repentance is impossible (or forbidden), punishment endures.

word_study.meaning: Abhorrence, loathing, an object of contempt or horror. This is a rare word appearing only in Isaiah 66:24 and Daniel 12:2. The root is disputed, but it clearly conveys extreme revulsion.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'abhorrence to all flesh'—a final, utter rejection. Not merely punishment or removal, but revulsion. This is the psychological and social consequence of judgment: the redeemed see the rebels not with pity but with horror at their choice and fate.

cross_references.connection: Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24 three times: 'where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.' Christ's teaching on Gehenna explicitly invokes Isaiah's final image of unending judgment to emphasize the seriousness of rejecting the kingdom.

'And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (dera'on).' Daniel uses the same rare word as Isaiah 66:24 to describe the ultimate fate of the wicked in the resurrection.

'The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God...and shall be tormented with fire and brimstone...and the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever.' The Revelation realizes Isaiah's image of perpetual, visible judgment.

'I will cast your carcasses upon the carcasses of your idols,' says God as the consequence of breaking covenant. Isaiah 66:24 echoes this Levitical threat: covenant-breaking results in shameful exposure of the body.

The Enochic apocalyptic tradition describes the fate of sinners in terms similar to Isaiah 66:24: their bodies are tormented and their names blotted out. Isaiah's eschatological imagery becomes central to Second Temple Judaism's theology of judgment.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 24 reflects the ancient Levantine horror at improper burial and exposure of the body. In ancient Israel and the Near East, being denied burial was considered the worst possible fate—worse than death itself. A corpse left exposed to birds and beasts of prey, or to maggots, was not merely a physical degradation but a cosmic humiliation. The prophets often invoked this image as the ultimate curse (Jeremiah 8:1-3, where God threatens to scatter the bones of those who reject Him). In the exile period and afterward, the question of divine justice became acute: If God is righteous, why do the wicked prosper? Isaiah 66:24 provides an answer: their judgment is deferred, not denied. They will be exposed and degraded eternally. The image of the worm and fire became so central to Jewish and Christian thought that it generated elaborate eschatologies of judgment (Sheol, Gehinnom, Hades, Tartarus). The Dead Sea Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ col. LIV) preserve verse 24 unchanged at the very end of the Great Isaiah Scroll—the final words of Isaiah and the final words on the manuscript. The fact that the scroll ends here, with judgment and horror, suggests that the scribes viewed Isaiah's stark conclusion as irremovable truth. Later synagogue practice developed the custom of re-reading verse 23 after verse 24 to avoid ending the haftarah on judgment, but the text itself stands unchanged.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains parallel imagery of divine judgment. In 1 Nephi 15:33-35, Nephi describes hell as a state of torment: 'the lake of fire and brimstone, which is the second death...a state of perfect knowledge of his guilt, which must cause him to shrink from the presence of the Lord into a state of darkness, and awful awful awfulness.' In 2 Nephi 9:26-27, Jacob teaches that those who reject Christ's atonement 'shall have their names blotted out, that the names of the wicked shall not be numbered among the names of the righteous.' The Nephite text affirms Isaiah's theology: judgment for covenant-breaking is irrevocable, and the wicked are separated eternally from the righteous.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:32-49 describes in detail the fate of 'those who deny the Son after the Father has revealed him'—they 'shall go away into the lake of fire and brimstone, with the devil and his angels, and the only ones on whom the second death shall have any power' (verses 36-37). D&C 19:10-12 teaches that the 'awful' judgment is real and that transgression against covenants results in suffering. D&C 88:32-35 affirms that 'the Lord knoweth all things' and that judgment is according to works. Most pointedly, D&C 29:41 warns that 'the end of the wicked is to be burned,' echoing Isaiah's image of unquenched fire. The Restoration reinforces Isaiah's stern teaching: judgment is not merely philosophical but literal and ultimate.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Temple is the place where covenants are made that either lead to life or—if broken—to judgment. The sealing ordinances include the warning that those who break their covenants will be subject to divine judgment. The endowment ceremony presents the contrast between those who obey God and those who rebel (the plot involving Lucifer and his followers). The Temple grounds the reality of judgment by making clear that covenants are not casual but binding, with real consequences for fidelity or infidelity. Doctrine and Covenants 132:19 teaches that celestial marriage and eternal life are granted to those who keep the covenant; verses 41-42 warn that 'if any man or woman shall be found not willing to abide by my law' they shall be damned. The Temple makes concrete what Isaiah 66:24 expresses symbolically: covenant-keeping leads to eternal life; covenant-breaking leads to judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: Isaiah 66:24 points to Christ's role as both Savior and Judge. In Revelation 19:11-16, Christ appears as 'Faithful and True... and in righteousness he doth judge and make war.' His garments are dipped in blood (verse 13), indicating that judgment is His sacred function. In Matthew 25:31-46, the Son of Man judges the nations, and the wicked are sent into 'everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels.' Christ's dual role as Savior and Judge is the framework for understanding Isaiah 66:24: those who accept Christ's covenant and redemption experience the perpetual worship of verse 23; those who reject it face the judgment of verse 24. The worm and fire are not primarily metaphorical torture but the consequence of separation from God's presence—a state Jesus understood as 'outer darkness' (Matthew 8:12). Christ bore this judgment Himself (Romans 8:1-4, 'There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus'), so that those who accept His atonement escape verse 24's fate.
commentary.application: Verse 24 is deliberately uncomfortable, and it should be. It is Isaiah's final word, and it is a warning. The verse does not say judgment is temporary or provisional; it is final and visible ('they shall look upon... they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh'). For modern disciples, this verse is a call to seriousness about covenants. The sealing power (D&C 110:16) is real, which means the bonds created by Temple covenants are real, which means the consequences of breaking them are real. We should not enter into covenants lightly. The verse also addresses a subtle temptation in modern theology: the idea that eventually 'all is well' and judgment is abolished. Isaiah 66:24 says this is not so. The redeemed will forever see the consequence of rejection; they will be witnesses to the finality of God's justice. This is not sadistic; it is the ultimate validation that God's justice is real and irreversible—the only ultimate guarantee that righteousness matters. The final application is personal: Am I living as though I take my covenants seriously? Am I entering into Temple ordinances with full awareness that these are binding, celestial contracts? Am I endeavoring to be a worthy vessel for God's blessings, or am I presuming upon God's mercy while neglecting obedience? Verse 24 ends Isaiah with a summons: Choose covenant; choose righteousness; choose fidelity to God's word. The alternative is not annihilation but exposure—a state of everlasting regret and shame, eternally separated from those who loved God and kept His commandments.
